stages.title: The Raw Data
stages.text:
STAGE 01 · OBSERVE
The Raw Data
BEFORE YOU START

You only need a basic understanding of means and variance. ANOVA asks whether differences among group means are large compared with the variation inside the groups.

Imagine we are comparing test scores across three different teaching methods (Group A, B, and C).

If you look at the raw data in the visual panel, you'll notice that not everyone in Group A scored exactly the same. There is a natural spread, or noise, within every group. This is everyday biological, psychological, or measurement variation.

stages.title: The Research Question
stages.text:
STAGE 02 · OBSERVE
The Research Question

Our question isn't about individuals; it's about the group averages (the black lines).

Are the gaps between these group means large enough to confidently say the teaching methods have different effects? Or are the means just slightly off from each other by pure chance, drowning in the natural noise of the students?

Teaching Interaction: Shape the Data

stages.title: The Rules of the Game
stages.text:
STAGE 03 · PREPARE
The Rules of the Game

Before we build an ANOVA model, we must check our assumptions. If the data breaks the rules, standard ANOVA might mislead us.

Normality

Technically, ANOVA assumes the residuals (the error or distance of each point from its group mean) are normally distributed. In practice, researchers often check if the data within each group resembles a bell curve.

Homogeneity of Variance

The spread (variance) of scores should be roughly equal across all groups. ANOVA is robust to minor violations, provided sample sizes are equal.

Independence

Data points must not influence each other. If the same student is tested multiple times, you must use a Repeated-Measures ANOVA instead.

stages.title: Variance Decomposition
stages.text:
STAGE 04 · BUILD
Variance Decomposition

ANOVA answers our question by splitting the total variation in the data into two components. Look at the canvas to see these distances visualized.

Between-Group Variance (Signal)
The systematic variance associated with the independent variable. Measured by how far each group mean (black line) deviates from the Grand Mean (dashed line).
Within-Group Variance (Noise)
The unsystematic variance or error. Measured by how much individual dots deviate from their own group mean.

stages.title: The F-Statistic
stages.text:
STAGE 05 · UNDERSTAND
The F-Statistic

ANOVA summarizes this decomposition into a single ratio, the F-statistic. It compares the size of the treatment effect to the size of the error.

stages.title: Degrees of Freedom
stages.text:
STAGE 06 · UNDERSTAND
Degrees of Freedom

Before we can calculate our variance estimates (Mean Squares) for the F-statistic, we need to divide our Sum of Squares by our Degrees of Freedom (df).

In statistics, df simply means how many values are still free to vary once a constraint has been imposed. Imagine picking 3 numbers that must average to 10. You can freely choose the first two (say, 8 and 15), but the third is locked (-13). You have 2 degrees of freedom.

In our specific teaching example, we have N = 36 total students spread across k = 3 groups:

dfbetween = k - 1 = 3 - 1 = 2
Once the overall Grand Mean is set, only 2 of our 3 group means are free to vary.
dfwithin = N - k = 36 - 3 = 33
Within each group, the students' scores must average out to their respective group mean. We lose 1 degree of freedom per group constraint.
dftotal = N - 1 = 36 - 1 = 35
If we only knew the Grand Mean, 35 out of the 36 students' scores would be free to vary.

stages.title: A Worked Example
stages.text:
STAGE 07 · UNDERSTAND
A Worked Example

Let’s bring this together using the data currently on display. We divide our sums of squared deviations (Sum of Squares, SS) by our degrees of freedom to get the Mean Squares (MS), which are variance quantities used in F = MS_between / MS_within. Under the null hypothesis and standard ANOVA assumptions, both estimate the same error variance.

FROM THE DISPLAYED SCORES

Group means: A = 80, B = 68, C = 56. Grand mean = 68. Each group has n = 12, so N = 36.

BETWEEN-GROUP SIGNAL

SSbetween = 12[(80 - 68)2 + (68 - 68)2 + (56 - 68)2] = 3456

WITHIN-GROUP NOISE

SSwithin = 132 + 132 + 132 = 396

APPLYING DEGREES OF FREEDOM

dfbetween = 2; dfwithin = 33.
MSbetween = 3456 / 2 = 1728.
MSwithin = 396 / 33 = 12.
F = 1728 / 12 = 144.

Scroll down to see these quantities organized into the universal language of statisticians: the ANOVA table.

stages.title: Reading the ANOVA Table
stages.text:
STAGE 08 · UNDERSTAND
Reading the ANOVA Table

When you run ANOVA in software like R, SPSS, or Python, the output is standardized into this table format.

Interact with the table in the visual panel: Tap or hover over the column headers (SS, df, MS, F, p) and the rows to understand exactly what each number represents and how they mathematically connect.

The Conclusion:

Because our p-value (< 0.001) is less than our threshold (0.05), we reject the null hypothesis. We conclude that at least one teaching method has a significantly different mean score.

stages.title: Post-Hoc Testing
stages.text:
STAGE 10 · UNDERSTAND
Post-Hoc Testing

A significant ANOVA is an omnibus test—it tells you a difference exists, but not where. Is A different from B? Is B different from C?

The Multiple Comparisons Problem

If you run three separate t-tests, your 5% chance of a false positive (Type I error) compounds. The more tests you run, the higher the Family-Wise Error Rate.

To follow up safely, we use Post-Hoc tests like Tukey's HSD. Under its assumptions, Tukey's controls the family-wise error rate at the chosen alpha level across the full set of pairwise comparisons. Look at the visual panel for the breakdown.

stages.title: Enter Two-Way ANOVA
stages.text:
STAGE 11 · UNDERSTAND
Enter Two-Way ANOVA

So far, we've used a One-Way ANOVA to ask a single question: Does the teaching method matter? But reality is complex.

Let's extend our example. We take our original three teaching methods (A, B, and C) and introduce a second factor: the student's Sleep Level (High vs. Low).

Two-Way ANOVA now asks three questions at once: Does teaching method matter? Does sleep matter? And crucially, does the effect of one depend on the other? We are no longer comparing only 3 group means, but 6 distinct cells (3 methods × 2 sleep levels).

This allows us to explore how both variables simultaneously influence test scores.

stages.title: Cells & Marginal Means
stages.text:
STAGE 12 · UNDERSTAND
Cells & Marginal Means

To understand a two-way design, it helps to see how the data is organized. Look at this numeric structure for our extended teaching example:

TWO-WAY DATA STRUCTURE

SLEEP \ METHOD	A	B	C	SLEEP MEAN
High Sleep	82	74	66	74
Low Sleep	62	66	70	66
Method Mean	72	70	68	Grand: 70
Cell Means (The middle grid)
A cell mean is the average score for one exact combination—like the students who received Method A AND High Sleep (82). Our design has 6 distinct cells.
Marginal Means (The outer edges)
A marginal mean averages across one factor while ignoring the other. The marginal mean for Method A (72) combines both sleep levels. "Main effects" look only at these outer marginal means.

stages.title: The Interaction Effect
stages.text:
STAGE 13 · UNDERSTAND
The Interaction Effect

If the gap between methods stays consistent regardless of sleep, the lines in our plot will be roughly parallel. That suggests no interaction.

But if the lines are not parallel, it suggests an interaction. Crossing lines are not technically required for an interaction, but this example uses a strong crossing pattern to make the concept visually obvious: the effect of Method completely flips depending on Sleep.

How to Read the Interaction Plot

Step 1: Check for parallel lines. If lines are roughly parallel, there is likely no interaction. If they cross or clearly change relative position, an interaction is present.
Step 2: Look at overall height. If one line tends to sit higher on average, that suggests a main effect of Sleep.
Step 3: Look at how the ranking changes. Notice which method is best under High Sleep, and then notice how that changes under Low Sleep. Here, the best method completely reverses!
No Interaction (Parallel)
Interaction (Crossover)

stages.title: Building the ANOVA Table
stages.text:
STAGE 14 · UNDERSTAND
Building the ANOVA Table

How do we get from our six cells to the statistical output? We partition the total variation into four distinct buckets:

1
Method (Main Effect)
Variation among the three Method marginal means (72 vs 70 vs 68). It asks if one teaching method is better on average.
2
Sleep (Main Effect)
Variation between the two Sleep marginal means (74 vs 66). It asks if well-rested students do better on average.
3
Method × Sleep (Interaction)
The leftover structured variance when the gaps between methods change across sleep levels. For High Sleep, A beats C by +16 points. But for Low Sleep, C beats A by +8 points.
4
Error (Within-Cell Noise)
The natural random noise of individual students within each of the six specific cells.

To turn these buckets into our final results, each source gets its own Sum of Squares (SS). We divide each SS by its degrees of freedom (df) to get a Mean Square (MS). Finally, we compare each effect's MS to the Error MS to produce an F-ratio.

Why Averages Can Hide The Truth

Notice that our Method marginal means are quite close (72, 70, 68). Because the crossover pattern partly cancels out when averaged across sleep levels, the main effect of Method looks modest. But the interaction is large because the best method changes completely depending on sleep! This is why we always read the interaction row first.

stages.title: Reading the Two-Way Table
stages.text:
STAGE 15 · REFLECT
Reading the Two-Way Table

Notice how the ANOVA table expands in the visual panel. Our single "Between Groups" signal is now cleanly split into three specific rows: Method, Sleep, and Method × Sleep.

Correct Reading Order

Read the interaction row first. If the interaction is significant, the effect of one factor depends on the other.
Be careful with main effects. If the interaction is significant, interpreting the main effect of Method or Sleep on its own can be highly misleading.
Then read the main effects. Look at Method and Sleep to see if they matter on average across all conditions.

Our Example's Conclusion: The Interaction is highly significant (p < 0.001). This confirms what we visually saw—the lines clearly cross between Method B and Method C. Method A provides a large advantage for well-rested students, but Method C becomes the best option for tired students. The main effects (Method and Sleep) are also significant, but the interaction tells us the true story of how they combine.

stages.title: Caveats & Recap
stages.text:
STAGE 16 · REFLECT
Caveats & Recap

ANOVA is a beautiful, mathematically elegant tool for partitioning variance. But it is only a model of reality.

Assumptions are Key

ANOVA is robust, but severe violations of normality or independence will produce a completely meaningless F-statistic. Always check your residuals.

Look at the Data

Never rely solely on the p-value, tables, or bar charts. Plot the raw data (like our dot plot), check the boxplots, and ensure extreme outliers aren't driving the omnibus result.

Choose the ANOVA variant from the design: use standard one-way ANOVA for similar variances, Welch ANOVA for unequal variances, Kruskal–Wallis or a robust alternative for strong non-normality or ordinal outcomes, and repeated-measures or mixed models for repeated observations. After a significant omnibus test, use planned contrasts or multiplicity-corrected post-hoc comparisons. Report group intervals and a named effect size such as eta-squared or omega-squared.

In one sentence: ANOVA asks whether the observed between-group variation would be unusual under an equal-means null model, assuming the chosen model and design conditions hold.

COMPLETE THE PICTURE
Choosing the right follow-up

An omnibus ANOVA can tell you that at least one group differs, but not which groups differ. Use a corrected post-hoc procedure such as Tukey HSD for pairwise comparisons.

If the assumptions are badly violated, consider Welch's ANOVA for unequal variances or a rank-based alternative such as Kruskal–Wallis. The method should follow the data, not the other way around.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
ANOVA compares between-group signal with within-group noise.
A significant F-test is an omnibus result, not a list of differing groups.
Report the test, effect size, assumptions, and any corrected follow-up comparisons.

Practical method checklist

Before you finish
Assumptions

Independent observations and assumptions appropriate to the ANOVA variant.

When the method fails

Unequal variance, dependence, strong non-normality, outliers, and multiplicity.

Validation and leakage

Analysis and resampling must respect the sampling or experimental design.

Interpretation cautions

An omnibus p-value neither measures importance nor identifies differing groups.

What to report

Group estimates, intervals, ANOVA variant, effect size, contrasts, and correction.

stages.title: The Prediction Problem
stages.text:
STAGE 01 · OBSERVE
The Prediction Problem
BEFORE YOU START

Generalisation is performance on new data, not performance on the examples used to fit the model.

PLAIN ENGLISH

Every dataset contains two things: the true signal we want to learn, and random static we should ignore.

TECHNICAL MEANING

A model's goal is to capture the underlying function F(X) while ignoring the irreducible error Ε.

For our concrete example, let's predict a person's Income based on their Years of Education.

Notice on the right: The dots are our raw historical data. The horizontal axis is Years of Education, and the vertical axis is Income. We need to draw a reliable line through them.

stages.title: High Bias (Underfitting)
stages.text:
STAGE 02 · BUILD
High Bias (Underfitting)
PLAIN ENGLISH

The model is too stubborn. It assumes the relationship is completely straight and simple, ignoring reality.

TECHNICAL MEANING

Bias is the error introduced by choosing a model that lacks the complexity to represent the true data distribution.

WHY IT MATTERS

A high bias model makes the exact same systematic mistake over and over again, regardless of how much data you feed it.

Quick Check: Does a high-bias model memorize the noise?
Notice on the right: The rigid red line forces a straight path through curved data. It is completely missing the underlying wave.

stages.title: High Variance (Overfitting)
stages.text:
STAGE 03 · BUILD
High Variance (Overfitting)
PLAIN ENGLISH

The model is too easily distracted. It memorizes every single typo and random bounce in our training data.

TECHNICAL MEANING

Variance is the amount by which our model's curve would change if we estimated it using a different set of training data.

WHY IT MATTERS

Like a student who memorizes a practice exam but fails the real test, an overfitted model cannot generalize to unseen future data.

Notice on the right: The erratic blue line twists wildly to touch almost every single dot. It has learned the noise alongside the signal.

stages.title: The Error Decomposition
stages.text:
STAGE 04 · BUILD
The Error Decomposition

We cannot minimize both perfectly. Mathematically, the expected prediction error on a new observation breaks down into exactly three components:

Err(x) = [E[f̂(x)] - f(x)]² + E[(f̂(x) - E[f̂(x)])²] + σ²
Bias²
The Stubbornness Error: How much the model's rigid average assumption misses the true reality.
Variance
The Distraction Error: How wildly the model's curve jumps around when given slightly different training sets.
Irreducible Error (σ²)
The Baseline Noise: The inherent randomness in the real world that no model can ever predict.

Conditions for this exact equation: the familiar decomposition applies most directly to squared-error prediction at a fixed input, across repeated training samples, with an irreducible-noise model. Bias and variance remain useful ideas in classification, but the same algebra does not automatically apply to classification loss.

Notice on the right: The green dashed line is the sweet spot—a gentle curve that follows the main trend but ignores the random static.

stages.title: The Testing Problem
stages.text:
STAGE 06 · UNDERSTAND
The Testing Problem
PLAIN ENGLISH

A model that aces the practice quiz might still fail the final exam.

TECHNICAL MEANING

Training error often underestimates test error and is not a reliable estimate of future performance.

WHY IT MATTERS

If we use all our finite data to train the model, we are flying blind. We must safely evaluate models on data they haven't seen yet.

The Solution: Resampling Methods. Resampling is how we practically estimate where the sweet spot lies using finite data. We strategically recycle our data by making repeated splits, rotating held-out folds, or redrawing samples.

COMPLETE THE PICTURE
Keep the test set genuinely untouched

Use cross-validation or a validation set to choose features, complexity, and hyperparameters. Use the test set once, after those decisions are complete.

If model selection itself is extensive and you need an unbiased estimate of the full procedure, use nested cross-validation: the inner loop tunes and the outer loop evaluates.

stages.title: 1. The Validation Set
stages.text:
STAGE 07 · UNDERSTAND
1. The Validation Set
PLAIN ENGLISH

Think of this as a practice exam used to choose a study strategy. A separate final exam remains hidden until that strategy is locked.

TECHNICAL MEANING

The dataset is randomly partitioned into two mutually exclusive sets: a "training set" to build the model, and a "validation set" to test it.

WHY IT MATTERS

It is simple but noisy. If the validation pile happens to contain unusually hard cases, the score changes substantially. The estimate depends on one random split.

The Process:
1. Shuffle eligible independent observations.
2. Split development data into training and validation piles.
3. Fit candidate models on training data.
4. Choose among them using validation data.
5. Keep the separate final test set untouched.

The Trade-off: We use a 50/50 development split below so it is easy to see. An 80/20 training/validation split is common, but the right choice depends on sample size and structure. A small validation set produces a noisy selection score; the final test set is separate.

stages.title: 2. k-Fold Cross-Validation
stages.text:
STAGE 08 · UNDERSTAND
2. k-Fold Cross-Validation
PLAIN ENGLISH

Instead of risking one lucky or unlucky test, we take turns. We divide the class into groups. Every single group gets exactly one chance to be the test group while everyone else studies.

TECHNICAL MEANING

The data is divided into k equal chunks (folds). We train k separate models, holding out a different chunk for validation each time, then average the k validation errors.

WHY IT MATTERS

By averaging multiple different tests together, we dilute the "luck of the draw" from any single random split. It gives us a much fairer, more stable picture of how the model will actually perform in the real world.

The Process:
1. Chop the data into 5 equal chunks (folds).
2. Train a new model on 4 chunks. Test it on the 1 chunk left out.
3. Rotate. Pick a new chunk to be the test.
4. Repeat until every chunk has been the test exactly once.
5. Average all 5 test scores together.

Train Model 1 (Test on Fold 1)
RUNNING ERROR RECORD
Awaiting first fold...
Notice on the right: Step through the folds. The orange test block slides down automatically. We build 5 entirely different models and log their scores. By averaging them all, we smooth out the jumps and find the truth.

stages.title: 3. Leave-One-Out (LOOCV)
stages.text:
STAGE 09 · UNDERSTAND
3. Leave-One-Out (LOOCV)
PLAIN ENGLISH

Imagine a class of 100 students. We send exactly one student out of the room. We teach the other 99. Then we test that single missing student. We repeat this 100 times.

TECHNICAL MEANING

This is cross-validation taken to the absolute extreme. We leave out just one data point, train on the rest, and do this for every point in the dataset.

WHY IT MATTERS

It uses almost all the data to train, which gives the model the best chance to learn perfectly. But training 100 separate models takes a massive amount of computing power.

The Hidden Flaw: Because we only leave out one point, the 100 models we build are almost perfectly identical. Their answers are incredibly similar to each other. When you average answers that are highly correlated, their mistakes don't cancel out well. The final error estimate can still be surprisingly jumpy.

Compared to 5-fold CV: LOOCV uses more training data. But it takes vastly longer to compute and rarely gives a better, more stable answer.

Notice on the right: Slide the slider to move the orange test block. Look at the 99 blue training blocks—they barely change! This means all 100 tests are too mathematically similar to average out noise effectively.

stages.title: 4. The Bootstrap
stages.text:
STAGE 10 · UNDERSTAND
4. The Bootstrap
PLAIN ENGLISH

Imagine tasting a giant pot of soup. You take a spoonful and score it a 7.0. Is that score reliable, or was that just a lucky scoop? To find out, you stir the soup and taste it multiple times, getting slightly different scores: 6.8, 7.2, 6.9, 7.1. Bootstrap checks how much these scores vary or "wiggle."

TECHNICAL MEANING

Bootstrap is about generating many possible answers from the exact same data to check for stability. We repeatedly sample our original data with replacement, and recalculate our target number on each new sample.

WHY IT MATTERS

If our taste scores stay tightly packed together (e.g., 6.8–7.2), our answer is highly stable. If they spread out wildly (e.g., 5.0–9.0), our result is unreliable. This gives us our margin of error.

The Process:

Start with your original dataset (say it’s got 100 points).
To make one ‘bootstrap sample,’ randomly pick one data point from your original set.
Write it down, but don’t remove it. Put it back, so all points stay equally available.
Repeat this random picking (with putting back) until you have a new sample the same size as the original. So if you started with 100 points, you pick 100 times.
Now, calculate the average (or whatever metric you’re checking) from that new sample.
Repeat this entire process hundreds or thousands of times. Each time, you get a slightly different average.
Finally, look at all those averages. Their spread tells you how stable (or not) your original estimate is.

stages.title: Limitations in Practice
stages.text:
STAGE 11 · REFLECT
Limitations in Practice

Each method carries trade-offs. Here is what they mean for your daily work:

Validation Set: Be cautious with this when data are small; your results will change randomly every time you run the script.
LOOCV: Takes forever to run on large data. It tends to have very low bias, but averaging nearly identical models makes the final estimate jumpy.
k-Fold CV: In practice, 5-fold or 10-fold CV is often a strong default because it balances stability and computation well.
Bootstrap: Excellent for answering "how confident are we in this specific number?", but not the first choice for estimating pure test error.
Micro-Check: If I want to publish the uncertainty of my new variable, which do I use?

stages.title: Summary & Synthesis
stages.text:
STAGE 12 · REFLECT
Summary & Synthesis

A successful model must navigate the error puzzle. It requires enough complexity to avoid Bias, but enough restraint to avoid Variance. We rely on computational resampling to estimate how our model will generalize to the real world.

Memory Checklist
Bias:
The model is too rigid (Underfitting).
Variance:
The model is too jumpy (Overfitting).
Cross-Validation:
Used to estimate future Test Error.
Bootstrap:
Used to estimate Uncertainty and Std Errors.
METHOD	BEST USE CASE	KEY TRAIT
Validation Set	Quick, rough checks	HIGH VARIABILITY
k-Fold CV	Model selection & Test Error	BALANCED
LOOCV	Very small datasets	LOW BIAS
Bootstrap	Uncertainty / std errors	WITH REPLACEMENT
KEY TAKEAWAYS
High bias underfits; high variance overfits.
Resampling estimates performance variation, not merely one lucky split.
Tuning and final evaluation must use separate information.

Practical method checklist

Before you finish
Assumptions

Squared-error decomposition at a fixed input across repeated training samples.

When the method fails

Using the exact algebra for unrelated losses or ignoring dependence in resampling.

Validation and leakage

Use data-appropriate CV and an outer evaluation when selection occurs.

Interpretation cautions

Classification bias and variance need not share the same formula.

What to report

Loss, resampling design, fold distributions, selection rule, and final uncertainty.

title: Chi-Square Test of Independence | StatML Academy

stages.title: The Raw Counts
stages.text:
STAGE 01 · OBSERVE
The Raw Counts
BEFORE YOU START

Chi-square uses counts in categories. Each observation must contribute to one cell only, and the expected counts must be large enough for the reference distribution to work well.

The Chi-Square test evaluates categorical data—data placed into distinct bins or groups without an inherent numeric value.

Imagine we survey 50 students to see if there is a relationship between two categorical variables: Club Choice (Art vs. Sports) and Favorite Snack (Apples vs. Chips).

Rule of thumb: Chi-Square works with frequencies (counts), not averages. Every individual belongs to exactly one cell in our table.

stages.title: Hypotheses & Marginals
stages.text:
STAGE 02 · PREPARE
Hypotheses & Marginals

Are club choice and favorite snack related, or are they completely independent? We formalize this question using hypotheses.

H₀
Null Hypothesis: Club choice and favorite snack are independent. (No relationship).
H₁
Alternative Hypothesis: Club choice and favorite snack are not independent. (There is a relationship).

To test this, we must first look at the margins. The row totals and column totals tell us the overall preferences of the group, ignoring the split between the variables.

stages.title: Expected Counts
stages.text:
STAGE 03 · UNDERSTAND
Expected Counts

If the Null Hypothesis is perfectly true, the counts inside the table should be directly proportional to the totals on the margins. This gives us our Expected Counts—the baseline of what we would expect if there were no relationship at all between club choice and snack preference.

To find the expected count for any cell in our table, we use this simple formula:

Expected Count = (Row Total × Column Total) ÷ Grand Total

In standard algebraic shorthand, it is written as:

E = (Row Total × Column Total) / Grand Total
STEP-BY-STEP CALCULATION: ART & APPLE

Let's calculate the expected value for the first cell (Art students who prefer Apples):

Row Total (Art) = 30
Column Total (Apple) = 25
Grand Total = 50

E = (30 × 25) / 50 = 750 / 50 = 15

Why does this work?

Out of 50 total surveyed students, 25 like apples. That is exactly half (50%) of all students. If snack preference and club choice are completely unrelated (independent), then apples should be spread proportionally across both clubs.

Since 50% of the entire sample likes apples, we expect 50% of each club to like apples. Art has 30 students, and half of 30 is 15.

"If everything were random, about half of the Art students should like apples."

INTERACTIVE: BUILD AN EXPECTED COUNT

Select a cell to see how expected frequencies are generated under the assumption of independence:

-- Choose a cell to calculate --
Art & Apple
Art & Chips
Sports & Apple
Sports & Chips
CALCULATING THE REMAINING CELLS

We apply the exact same formula to the other three cells:

Art & Chips: E = (30 × 25) / 50 = 15
Sports & Apple: E = (20 × 25) / 50 = 10
Sports & Chips: E = (20 × 25) / 50 = 10
WHAT IS REALLY HAPPENING?

The total number of apples is 25. If independent, we split these apples across the rows based on the size of each club:

Art has 30 out of 50 students (60% of the sample). Therefore, Art gets 60% of the expected apples: 60% of 25 = 15.
Sports has 20 out of 50 students (40% of the sample). Therefore, Sports gets 40% of the expected apples: 40% of 25 = 10.

The same logic applies to the chips category, which also has a column total of 25.

Expected count means: how much this row deserves × how much this column deserves.
Warning: Expected counts are not guesses from our opinion. They are calculated from the table totals under the assumption that the variables are independent.
CHECK YOUR PROGRESS: EXPECTED COUNTS

B. 10
C. 15

stages.title: Residuals & Contributions
stages.text:
STAGE 04 · UNDERSTAND
Residuals & Contributions

The core intuition of Chi-Square is to compare what we Observed (O) with what we Expected (E). We square the residuals and divide by the expected count to scale the difference.

χ² = Σ [ (O - E)² / E ]
WORKED EXAMPLE: ART & APPLE CONTRIBUTION

Let's calculate the individual score contribution for Art students who prefer Apples:

Observed (O) = 20
Expected (E) = 15
Residual (O - E) = 20 - 15 = 5
Square the residual: 5² = 25
Divide by expected: 25 ÷ 15 = 1.67

This cell contributes exactly 1.67 points to the overall Chi-Square statistic. Bigger contributions mean that cell is more responsible for the overall relationship.

Interactive Matrix: Hover over any cell in the table to inspect its Observed, Expected, Residual, and individual χ² contribution.

We do this for every cell and add them all together to get our final test statistic. (Note: visual contributions are shown rounded to two decimals, but the true sum is roughly 8.33).

CHECK YOUR PROGRESS: RESIDUALS

Question: If observed = 20 and expected = 15, what does residual = +5 mean?

A. There were 5 fewer people than expected.
B. There were 5 more people than expected.
C. There were exactly 5 people in total.
D. The p-value is 5.

controls.label: A. There were 5 fewer people than expected.
B. There were 5 more people than expected.
C. There were exactly 5 people in total.

stages.title: The Reference Distribution
stages.text:
STAGE 05 · EVALUATE
The Reference Distribution

To evaluate our test statistic of 8.33, we map it onto a Chi-Square distribution. The curve's exact shape is determined by the Degrees of Freedom (df).

df = (Rows - 1) × (Cols - 1) = 1

If our statistic lands past the critical boundary (here, 3.84 for α = 0.05), the deviation is too large to be attributed to random chance.

stages.title: Reading the Output
stages.text:
STAGE 06 · EVALUATE
Reading the Output

Statistical software synthesizes these steps into a standard output summary. Here is how to read the final result:

ANALYSIS OUTPUT
Pearson's Chi-squared test
X-squared
8.33
df
1
p-value
0.0039
alpha (α)
0.05
Decision
Reject H₀
Effect Size (Phi)
0.41 (Moderate)
 Expected counts check
All expected counts ≥ 5
Understanding our p-value: The p-value is 0.0039. This means: if club choice and snack preference were truly unrelated, getting a pattern this strong or stronger would be very unlikely. So, we have strong evidence against the null hypothesis.
 Important: The p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. It is the probability of seeing a result this extreme or more extreme, assuming the null hypothesis were true.

Because the p-value (0.0039) is much smaller than our alpha threshold (0.05), we officially reject the null hypothesis. The Phi value of 0.41 confirms this is a moderate relationship.

WHAT KIND OF RELATIONSHIP IS IT?

The p-value tells us: “Something is going on.” (The variables are associated).
The residuals tell us: “What exactly is going on.” (The direction and pattern of the association).

GROUP	APPLE	CHIPS
Art	+5	-5
Sports	-5	+5

Let's break this down in human language:

Art students: The Art & Apple residual is +5 (more Art students liked apples than expected) and the Art & Chips residual is -5 (fewer Art students liked chips than expected). Therefore, Art students lean toward apples.
Sports students: The Sports & Apple residual is -5 (fewer Sports students liked apples than expected) and the Sports & Chips residual is +5 (more Sports students liked chips than expected). Therefore, Sports students lean toward chips.

Final Relationship Statement:

"There is a relationship between club choice and snack preference: Art students are more likely than expected to prefer apples, while Sports students are more likely than expected to prefer chips."

Caution: This is an association, not causation. We cannot say that joining Art causes students to like apples, or that joining Sports causes students to like chips.
CHECK YOUR PROGRESS: INTERPRETATION

Question: What does the p-value mainly tell us?

A. The exact cause of the relationship.
B. Whether there is evidence against the null hypothesis.
C. Which group caused the result.
D. The number of students surveyed.

B. Whether there is evidence against the null hypothesis.
C. Which group caused the result.
D. The number of students surveyed.

stages.title: Assumptions & Caveats
stages.text:
STAGE 07 · PREPARE
Assumptions & Caveats

Before closing the book on this relationship, we must acknowledge the strict assumptions required for a valid Chi-Square test.

REQUIRED CONDITIONS (ASSUMPTIONS)

Before trusting any Chi-Square test, you must ensure your study meets these three non-negotiable assumptions:

1
Count Data (Frequencies)

Beginner meaning: You must use actual counts of people or items falling into categories, not averages or scores.

 Bad: using average happiness ratings or continuous test scores.
 Good: counting how many students chose apples or chips.
2
Independence of Observations

Beginner meaning: Each person should only appear once in the table. They cannot belong to multiple cells.

 Bad: the same student is counted under both Art and Sports.
 Good: each student belongs to one club category and one snack category.
3
Expected Counts are Large Enough

Beginner meaning: The expected numbers computed under independence should not be too tiny.

 Bad: many expected cells are 1 or 2 (which invalidates our p-value).
 Good: all expected counts in this example are at least 5 (our cells are 15, 15, 10, and 10).

Tiny expected counts can make the Chi-Square approximation unreliable. Yates' continuity correction applies specifically to 2×2 tables and does not guarantee a reliable approximation for very sparse data. Fisher's Exact Test is mainly used for small or sparse 2×2 tables; larger sparse tables may need other exact or Monte Carlo alternatives.

INTERACTIVE: TEST YOUR INTERPRETATION

"There is evidence of a relationship between

club choice and snack preference
Art and Sports
.
Art students are more likely than expected to prefer 
-- select --
apples
chips

Sports students are more likely than expected to prefer 
-- select --

Check Answers
Show Answer
THE WHOLE STORY IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Let's connect all the dots we've covered on this page into one simple, logical narrative:

We counted students by club and snack: We started by putting students into categories based on two characteristics: their club (Art/Sports) and snack preference (Apples/Chips).
We assumed independence: We asked: "What would this table look like if club and snack preferences had absolutely nothing to do with each other?"
That gave us expected counts: Answering that question mathematically gave us our expected baseline counts (15, 15, 10, 10).
We compared observed counts to expected counts: We looked at how far our actual observed numbers (20, 10, 5, 15) fell from that independent baseline.
The differences were large enough: We squared and scaled these discrepancies, giving us a final test statistic of χ² = 8.33.
The p-value was small, so we rejected independence: A discrepancy at least this large would be unusual under independence (p = 0.0039), assuming the test conditions hold. The data provide evidence against independence; Cramér’s V and residuals describe magnitude and contributing cells.
The residuals showed the pattern: Looking closely at our cells, we saw the exact direction of this pattern—Art students lean apples, Sports students lean chips.
SYNTHESIS

We have strong statistical evidence that club choice and snack preference are connected. However, Chi-Square demonstrates association, not causation. We cannot declare that joining the Art club causes students to eat apples.

COMPLETE THE PICTURE
Effect size and small expected counts

A small p-value answers whether an association is detectable, not whether it is important. Add Cramér’s V to describe the strength of association.

When expected counts are too small, combine categories only when substantively justified or use an exact method such as Fisher’s exact test for a 2 × 2 table.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
Expected counts describe the table we would see under independence.
Large observed-minus-expected differences create larger χ² contributions.
Report χ², degrees of freedom, p-value, sample size, and an effect size such as Cramér’s V.

Practical method checklist

Before you finish
Assumptions

Independent counts and adequate expected cells for the approximation.

When the method fails

Sparse tables, repeated observations, structural zeros, and multiple cell inspection.

Validation and leakage

Confirm analysis choices without outcome-guided fishing.

Interpretation cautions

Evidence against independence does not identify causality or important cells.

What to report

Table, expected counts, statistic, df, p-value, Cramér’s V, and residuals.

stages.title: The Raw Data
stages.text:
STAGE 01 · OBSERVE
The Raw Data
BEFORE YOU START

A classification tree repeatedly divides the feature space into regions. Each terminal leaf predicts a class or class probability.

Every problem starts with data. We have measurements for fruit — Weight (x-axis) and Color Intensity (y-axis).

Each fruit is already labeled: an Apple or an Orange. The goal of our tree is to learn rules to sort them into cleaner groups.

 The Whole Idea of Classification Trees

A Classification Tree is a supervised machine-learning model that learns a sequence of simple yes/no flowchart-like questions to sort data into categories.

Raw Labeled Data → Root Node → Scan Best Question → Split Data → Repeat Recursively → Leaf Prediction → Evaluation
 Tiny Tree Dictionary
• Feature: A measurable property or input variable used to make predictions (e.g., Weight, Color Intensity).
• Label: The target outcome or true answer we want the model to predict (e.g., Apple, Orange).
• Class: One of the specific categorical outcomes (e.g., Apples vs. Oranges).
• Root Node: The very first top-level block containing 100% of the training data.
• Split: A division of a parent node into two child nodes based on a feature question.
• Child Node: The subgroups created after splitting a parent node.
• Leaf Node: A final terminal node that does not split further. It makes the final prediction.
• Impurity: A measure of how mixed or diverse the class labels are within a particular node.
• Gini Impurity: A mathematical metric used to calculate impurity (0.0 means perfectly pure; 0.5 is the maximum for a balanced binary node).
• Weighted Impurity: The combined impurity of child nodes, weighted by the proportion of samples that went into each child.
• Impurity Decrease: The difference between parent Gini and weighted child Gini. The tree maximizes this "gain".
• Decision Boundary: The geometric line(s) dividing different class zones on the coordinate map.
• Tree Depth: The length of the longest path from the root node down to any leaf node.
• Pruning: Cutting back branches to simplify the model and improve generalizability on unseen data.
• Overfitting: Memorizing noise in the training set, causing failure on unseen test data.
• Underfitting: Creating a model that is too simple (e.g. too shallow) to learn the real underlying patterns.

stages.text:
STAGE 02 · PREPARE
The Train / Test Split

To build a robust model, we never evaluate our tree on the exact same data it used for learning. Instead, we divide our original dataset into two parts:

 Data Partitioning
 Training Set

Used to scan thresholds, calculate Gini, and build rules.
Count: 28 fruits

 Test Set (Held out)

Kept completely hidden from the tree during training.
Count: 6 fruits

 Data Leakage Warning: Using test data to choose splits, tune tree depth, or pick stopping criteria is a cardinal sin of machine learning. The test set must ONLY be used for final generalizability assessment.

CHECK YOUR KNOWLEDGE

Why is a Train/Test split essential for decision trees?

It helps the tree grow deeper and generate more rules.
It allows us to detect overfitting by measuring performance on unseen samples.
It guarantees that Gini impurity reaches exactly 0.0.

It allows us to detect overfitting by measuring performance on unseen samples.

stages.title: The Root Node
stages.text:
STAGE 03 · UNDERSTAND
The Root Node

At the very beginning, a Classification Tree puts all the training data into one big group on the fruit map. We call this the Root Node.

This starting box is very "messy" because it contains a mix of both apples and oranges. The tree's job is to split this box into smaller, cleaner sub-groups.

Root Node Content
14
APPLES
14
ORANGES

stages.title: Measuring Messiness
stages.text:
STAGE 04 · UNDERSTAND
Measuring Messiness

To split effectively, the tree needs a way to measure how mixed a box is. We use a math rule called Gini Impurity.

A Gini score of 0.0 means the box is perfectly pure. For this binary example, 0.5 is the maximum at a 50/50 mix; multiclass maxima differ.

 Gini Impurity Formula

Gini = 1 - Σ pᵢ²

For two classes (Apple & Orange):
Gini = 1 - [ P(Apple)² + P(Orange)² ]
    
 Live Root Node Calculation
• Total training fruit (N): 28
• Apples (): 14
• Oranges (): 14

P(Apple) = 14 / 28 = 0.50
P(Orange) = 14 / 28 = 0.50

Gini = 1 - [ P(Apple)² + P(Orange)² ]
Gini = 1 - [ (0.50)² + (0.50)² ]
Gini = 1 - [ 0.25 + 0.25 ] = 0.50

 Meaning: This root node is very mixed because it contains equal numbers of Apples and Oranges.
 Gini Impurity vs. Entropy

While Gini is highly popular in CART (Classification and Regression Trees), another metric called Entropy is also widely used:

Entropy = - Σ pᵢ log₂(pᵢ)

Both metrics measure the same core property: disorder. A node with equal proportions of classes has a Gini score of 0.50 and an Entropy score of 1.0. Both reach 0.0 when a node is perfectly pure. In practice, Gini and entropy often choose very similar splits, but not always. This guide uses Gini because it is simple, common, and easy to compute.

CONCEPT QUIZ

What does a Gini Impurity of 0.0 indicate about a subset of fruit?

The subset contains exactly 50% Apples and 50% Oranges.
The subset is 100% pure (contains only one type of fruit).
The subset is empty.

controls.label: The subset contains exactly 50% Apples and 50% Oranges.
The subset is 100% pure (contains only one type of fruit).

stages.title: Testing Every Question
stages.text:
STAGE 05 · OBSERVE
Testing Every Question

How does the tree find the best split? It tries testing candidate split points between observed values across the map.

Because the tree asks one feature question at a time (e.g., "Is Weight < X?"), each possible split becomes a straight vertical or horizontal cut across the graph. Watch the sweeping line on the canvas analyze both features.

 The Candidate Search Strategy

How does a decision tree find the best threshold? It doesn't guess random decimals. Instead, it uses a deterministic mathematical process:

Sort values: For a given feature (like Weight), it sorts all observed training values in ascending order.
Compute Midpoints: It calculates the halfway points (midpoints) between every adjacent pair of unique values.
Evaluate Splits: It treats each midpoint as a candidate threshold (e.g., Weight < 5.40), splits the data, and evaluates the resulting weighted Gini impurity.
Live Search (Scanning...)

Testing Split: Weight < 5.0...

Average Gini: ~0.45

stages.title: How the Tree Scores One Split
stages.text:
STAGE 06 · BUILD
How the Tree Scores One Split

The tree found the single best question! By splitting the data at this specific threshold, it gets the lowest possible combined Gini impurity.

This first split is often very influential because it shapes the rest of the tree. It divides the fruit map cleanly into two distinct regions.

The Golden Question
Best Split: Color < 5.50
 How the Tree Scores This Split
 Chosen Split Question: Color < 5.50
Left Child (Yes):
• Total Samples: 13
• Apples (): 0 | Oranges (): 13
• Gini_left = 1 - [(0/13)² + (13/13)²] ≈ 0.000
Right Child (No):
• Total Samples: 15
• Apples (): 14 | Oranges (): 1
• Gini_right = 1 - [(14/15)² + (1/15)²] ≈ 0.124
 Weighted Gini Impurity:
Weighted Gini = (N_left / N) × Gini_left + (N_right / N) × Gini_right
Weighted Gini = (13/28 × 0.000) + (15/28 × 0.124) ≈ 0.067
 Impurity Decrease (Gini Gain):
Gini Decrease = Root Gini - Weighted Gini = 0.500 - 0.067 = 0.433
SPLIT CALCULATION QUIZ

What property makes a candidate split the absolute "winner" in a decision tree?

It always splits the dataset exactly 50/50 by quantity.
It yields the largest Gini impurity decrease (lowest weighted children impurity).
It guarantees that both left and right child nodes become 100% pure instantly.

controls.label: It always splits the dataset exactly 50/50 by quantity.
It yields the largest Gini impurity decrease (lowest weighted children impurity).
It guarantees that both left and right child nodes become 100% pure instantly.

stages.title: Recursive Splitting
stages.text:
STAGE 07 · BUILD
Recursive Splitting

The tree isn't done. It now treats each of the two new boxes as a separate problem, and asks again: "Can I perform another split to make these even cleaner?"

It repeats this process recursively, carving the map into smaller and smaller axis-aligned rectangles until a box becomes pure, gets too small, or reaches the depth limit.

 Tree Stopping Rules

To prevent the tree from growing infinitely, we define stopping constraints (hyperparameters in ML frameworks):

Node Purity: Stop if all items in a node belong to a single class (Gini = 0).
Max Depth (`max_depth`): Stop if the path length from the root matches our limit.
Min Samples Split (`min_samples_split`): Stop if a node contains too few samples to allow another split.
Min Samples Leaf (`min_samples_leaf`): Prevent splits that leave a child with too few samples.
Min Impurity Decrease (`min_impurity_decrease`): Stop if Gini gain is below a small threshold.
STOPPING RULES QUIZ

What is the main danger of growing a classification tree completely unchecked without any stopping rules?

The tree will underfit and fail to capture simple boundaries.
The tree will overfit by creating hyper-specific rules to capture training noise.
The root Gini impurity will increase beyond 0.50.

controls.label: The tree will underfit and fail to capture simple boundaries.
The tree will overfit by creating hyper-specific rules to capture training noise.
The root Gini impurity will increase beyond 0.50.

stages.title: The Decision Boundary
stages.text:
STAGE 08 · BUILD
The Decision Boundary

Once the tree stops growing, we fill in the colors. Each rectangular box becomes a "Leaf Node". The model assigns a prediction to the entire box based on the fruit type that appears most often in that box.

 Leaf Nodes: How Predictions Are Made

Every final sub-box is a terminal Leaf Node. It predicts the majority class contained within its boundary.

We can also calculate a Class Probability Estimate simply as the proportion of that class in the leaf box:

P(Apple) = Leaf_Apples / Total_Leaf_Samples

 Warning: These leaf-proportion probabilities can be overconfident, especially in deep trees with small sample sizes in leaf boxes (e.g. predicting 100% confidence because a leaf contains exactly 1 Apple).

stages.title: Depth Limiting vs. Post-Pruning
stages.text:
STAGE 09 · BUILD
Depth Limiting vs. Post-Pruning

Look closely at the tiny boxes the tree made just to capture one outlier fruit. The tree has started memorizing noise in the training dataset. This is called Overfitting.

If we give the tree new fruit, these hyper-specific rules will likely fail. We fix this by limiting the maximum depth of the tree (Pre-Pruning), so it learns general rules instead of tracking every detail.

Pre-Pruning vs. Post-Pruning
METHOD	HOW IT WORKS	PROS / CONS
Pre-Pruning	Stop tree growth early using rules like max_depth or min_samples_split.	Very fast to compute, but might stop too early before discovering complex interactions.
Post-Pruning	Grow the full complex tree first, then cut back nodes that do not add predictive value (e.g. cost-complexity pruning).	Often more systematic, but computationally heavier because you build the full tree first.

stages.title: Limitations & Model Choice
stages.text:
STAGE 15 · REFLECT
Limitations & Model Choice

Classification Trees are incredibly intuitive, but they are not always the best tool for every job. Understanding their trade-offs is crucial for a data scientist.

 Strengths vs.  Weaknesses
When they shine:
Explainability: Outputs simple rules that any non-expert can read and audit.
No Scaling Required: Features are evaluated independently, so feature magnitude does not matter.
Handles Mixed Types Conceptually: Trees can split numerical and categorical predictors, but raw categorical support depends on the software. Some libraries require encoded categories; others implement native categorical splits.
When they struggle:
High Variance: Extremely sensitive to tiny training set alterations, which can yield completely different splits.
Axis-Aligned Boundaries: Since splits are purely horizontal or vertical, diagonal patterns require jagged, inefficient steps.
Overfitting: Easily memorize noise if depth is unchecked.
Class Imbalance: If one class is much more common, the tree may favor that class unless class weights, resampling, or better evaluation metrics are used.
 Model Comparison Roadmap
MODEL	BOUNDARY TYPE	INTERPRETABILITY	BEST USED FOR...
Decision Tree	Axis-Aligned Boxes	High (Flowchart)	Rules-based audits, mixed categorical/numerical data.
Logistic Regression	Smooth Linear	Medium (Weights)	Linear associations with log-odds; estimated probabilities may need calibration.
K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)	Irregular / Local	Low (Instance-based)	Complex local shapes, feature manifolds.
Random Forest	Complex / Smooth	Low (Ensemble)	High-accuracy, non-linear tasks (reduces variance).

 The Upgrade Path: To overcome the instability and high variance of a single Classification Tree, we combine hundreds of trees into an ensemble. Models like Random Forests (voting trees) and Gradient Boosted Trees (sequential error correction) represent the state-of-the-art for tabular data!

COMPLETE THE PICTURE
Probabilities, leakage, and honest pruning

A leaf probability is the class proportion among training cases in that leaf. Small leaves can produce unstable probabilities, so minimum-leaf constraints and calibration may matter.

All pruning and hyperparameter choices must use training or validation data only. Letting the test set influence tree depth is data leakage wearing a respectable-looking branch costume.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
Each split should improve class purity enough to justify additional complexity.
Depth limits and pruning reduce overfitting.
Interpret both the decision path and out-of-sample metrics.

Practical method checklist

Before you finish
Assumptions

Representative observations and features available at prediction time.

When the method fails

Small leaves, unstable splits, conflicting labels, and distribution shift.

Validation and leakage

Choose depth and pruning through validation or cross-validation.

Interpretation cautions

Impurity, probabilities, and categorical support depend on context and software.

What to report

Tree constraints, pruning rule, class metrics with uncertainty, and final test result.

title: Confidence Intervals & Hypothesis Testing · StatML Academy

stages.title: The problem
stages.text:
STAGE 01

The problem
Inference connects a noisy sample to a population quantity. Confidence intervals show compatible effect sizes; tests quantify how surprising the data are under a specified null model.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.text:
STAGE 02

Intuition and objective
A p-value is computed assuming the null and asks about results at least as extreme. A confidence procedure is calibrated across repeated samples. Neither replaces effect size, assumptions, or practical meaning.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.text:
STAGE 03

Worked example
An estimated mean difference is 4 points with a 95% CI from 1 to 7 and p=.01. The data are inconsistent with zero under the test assumptions, while plausible effects range from small to substantial. The p-value is not a 1% probability that the null is true.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.text:
STAGE 04

Reasoning with the method

A p-value is a tail probability calculated under H₀ and every model assumption; the null is conditioned on, not assigned a probability. A compatible confidence interval often inverts a family of tests. Sample size affects precision, so tiny effects can be statistically clear and important effects can remain uncertain. Power is planned against a specific meaningful alternative and is not the probability that an observed finding is true. Type I error means rejecting a true null hypothesis; α controls its probability under the test assumptions. Type II error means failing to reject a false null; its probability β depends on the particular alternative. Power = 1 − β is the chance of detecting that alternative. All else equal, lowering α generally lowers power, while larger sample sizes or larger effect sizes generally raise it. Family-wise and false-discovery-rate procedures answer different multiplicity goals. Neither repairs optional stopping, outcome switching or selective reporting after results are known.

A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

stages.title: Interactive laboratory
stages.text:
STAGE 05

Interactive laboratory

Change sample size and effect size. See the standard error, confidence interval and approximate p-value change—without changing what a p-value means.

Larger n can make a small effect precise; it does not make the effect practically important.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.text:
STAGE 06

Assumptions and failure modes
Assumptions

The test, estimator, sampling design and dependence model must match. Pre-specified hypotheses protect the advertised error rate.

When the method fails

Optional stopping, many uncorrected tests, model misspecification, low power and selective reporting invalidate simple interpretations.

stages.title: Practical workflow
stages.text:
STAGE 07

Practical workflow
Define estimand, H₀ and H₁
Choose α and analysis before results
Check design and assumptions
Compute estimate, effect size, interval and p-value
Adjust for multiplicity when required
Interpret practical significance

stages.title: Interpretation and reporting
stages.text:
STAGE 08

Interpretation and reporting

What to report: Report estimate and compatible interval, exact p-value where useful, effect size, assumptions, multiplicity plan, sample size and practical consequences.

Common misuse: Calling p>.05 “no effect” or p<.05 “proof.”

stages.title: The Raw Data
stages.text:
STAGE 01 · OBSERVE
The Raw Data
BEFORE YOU START

Think of each observation as a matched pair: one X value and one Y value from the same case. A scatterplot should always come before the coefficient.

Correlation is a statistical technique used to answer one big question: When one thing changes, does another thing also change?

To find out, we need paired observations. For example, let's look at the relationship between hours studied and test scores for six students.

STUDENT	HOURS STUDIED (X)	TEST SCORE (Y)
A	1	52
B	2	57
C	3	63
D	4	68
E	5	74
F	6	79

By plotting these paired values on a scatterplot, we translate raw numbers into a visual pattern.

stages.title: Direction and Form
stages.text:
STAGE 02 · UNDERSTAND
Direction and Form

The first thing we look for in a scatterplot is the direction and form of the relationship.

If the dots rise from left to right, we have a Positive Correlation. As study hours go up, test scores also go up.

The "Walking Friends" metaphor: Think of two friends. If they both walk forward together, that's a positive correlation. If one walks forward while the other walks backward, that's negative.

We also check the form. Pearson correlation specifically measures linear relationships—meaning the dots tend to cluster around a straight line.

stages.title: Measuring Strength: r
stages.text:
STAGE 03 · UNDERSTAND
Measuring Strength: r

We quantify this relationship using Pearson's correlation coefficient, written as r.

The value of r always falls between -1.00 and +1.00.

r = +1.0 : Perfect positive correlation
r = -1.0 : Perfect negative correlation
r = 0.0 : No linear correlation

Interactive: Adjust the noise to see how r changes when the dots spread further from the perfect line.

Data Noise:
--
PEARSON'S R

stages.title: Formal Hypotheses
stages.text:
STAGE 04 · PREPARE
Formal Hypotheses

In statistics, we use a sample to make guesses about an entire population. To test if a correlation is "real", we set up formal hypotheses.

Null Hypothesis (H₀): ρ = 0

There is no linear correlation between the variables in the population. Any observed relationship is just random chance.

Alternative Hypothesis (H₁): ρ ≠ 0

There is a significant linear relationship between the two variables.

We use the Greek letter rho (ρ) for the population, and r for our sample.

stages.title: How it works: Covariability
stages.text:
STAGE 05 · UNDERSTAND
How it works: Covariability

How does the math actually figure out if they move together? It looks at the means.

r = 
Σ((X - X̄)(Y - Ȳ))
√[Σ(X - X̄)² × Σ(Y - Ȳ)²]

Translation: The sum of how they vary together, divided by the total of how they vary individually.

We draw a vertical line for the average of X, and a horizontal line for the average of Y. This creates four quadrants.

If points mostly fall in the Top-Right (both above average) and Bottom-Left (both below average), they are moving together. The formula multiplies their distances from the mean. Positive × Positive = Positive. Negative × Negative = Positive!

stages.title: Assumptions: Paired & Linear
stages.text:
STAGE 06 · PREPARE
Assumptions: Paired & Linear

Pearson's correlation is powerful, but you must check two critical assumptions before trusting the math:

Paired Numeric Data: Both variables must be numeric, and each X must belong to the exact same subject as Y.
Linearity: The relationship must be relatively straight.

Imagine a scenario where cramming too much causes sleep deprivation, hurting test performance. Scores rise initially, then fall.

--
CALCULATED R

The math yields an r near 0, suggesting "no relationship." But visually, there is a strong curvilinear relationship. Always inspect the scatterplot first.

stages.title: Robustness Check: Outliers
stages.text:
STAGE 07 · PREPARE
Robustness Check: Outliers

Extreme outliers are a robustness concern, not a formal assumption for calculating Pearson’s r.

Pearson’s r uses covariance—products of deviations from the two means—scaled by the standard deviations. Extreme deviations can strongly change these quantities; a distant point can have high leverage, pulling the apparent linear relationship and the r value toward itself.

Watch how a single anomalous student (who studied 12 hours but scored 30) pulls the trendline down, severely weakening our strong positive correlation.

stages.title: The Inferential Result
stages.text:
STAGE 08 · EVALUATE
The Inferential Result

Let's return to our original, clean data. We have calculated the sample statistic and must now make a formal decision.

--
SAMPLE SIZE (N)
--
OBSERVED R
--
P-VALUE
Statistical Decision:

Awaiting statistical computation...

A small p-value means a result at least this extreme would be unusual under H₀: ρ = 0, assuming independent pairs and the test model hold. It is not the probability that H₀ is true, the probability that chance caused the result, an effect size, or evidence of causality. Pair r with a confidence interval and practical interpretation.

stages.title: The Golden Rule: Causation
stages.text:
STAGE 09 · REFLECT
The Golden Rule: Causation

We found a statistically significant relationship. But how far can we stretch our interpretation?

Interpretation:

"There was a significant positive correlation between hours studied and test score, r = --, --. Students who studied more tended to score higher."

However, we cannot say that studying caused the score to increase.

Correlation does not equal causation. Two variables might move together because of a third, confounding variable (e.g., Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise together, but the sun causes both).

stages.title: Limitations & Summary
stages.text:
STAGE 10 · REFLECT
Limitations & Summary

To recap, correlation is an observational tool, not an experimental proof.

r measures linear tightness (from -1 to +1).
Check the plot: r is blind to curves and highly sensitive to outliers.
Significance vs. Size: A small p-value means the observed result would be unusual under H₀: ρ = 0, assuming the test assumptions hold. Report r, its confidence interval, sample size, and practical relevance.
Pearson versus Spearman: Pearson measures linear association; Spearman measures monotonic association through ranks. Spearman is not simply an outlier-proof Pearson, and neither fixes confounding, dependence, or a non-monotonic relationship.
Pearson vs. Spearman: Use Pearson for continuous data. Switch to Spearman if your data is ranked/ordinal or has a monotonic non-linear relationship.
No Causal Claims: It is only evidence of an association.

When you encounter a correlation, always ask: What does the scatterplot look like, and could a hidden variable be driving the pattern?

COMPLETE THE PICTURE
When Pearson correlation is not the best choice

Use Spearman rank correlation when the relationship is monotonic but not linear, the data are strongly skewed or ordinal, or extreme values make Pearson's r unstable.

Whichever coefficient you use, inspect the plot and report the sample size. A single number cannot reveal clusters, curves, or influential points.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
Correlation measures how two variables move together, not whether one causes the other.
Pearson’s r describes linear association and is sensitive to outliers.
Always pair the coefficient with a scatterplot and a contextual interpretation.

Practical method checklist

Before you finish
Assumptions

Paired independent observations and a relationship suited to the chosen coefficient.

When the method fails

Outliers, restriction of range, clusters, dependence, and non-monotonic form.

Validation and leakage

Use resampling that preserves groups or repeated observations.

Interpretation cautions

A small p-value is not the probability the null is true or proof of causality.

What to report

Plot, n, coefficient, confidence interval, assumptions, and practical meaning.

stages.title: The problem
stages.text:
STAGE 01

The problem
A model can appear excellent because information crossed the boundary between development and evaluation. Leakage estimates performance for a procedure that cannot exist in deployment.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.text:
STAGE 02

Intuition and objective
Treat the pipeline—not only the final algorithm—as the model. Anything that learns a mean, category frequency, component, selected feature, threshold, or synthetic observation must learn it inside each training fold.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.text:
STAGE 03

Worked example
Suppose missing ages are filled with the mean of all 1,000 rows and then five-fold CV is run. Every validation fold has influenced its own imputed values. The honest workflow fits five separate imputers, each on that fold’s 800 training rows, and applies it to the 200 held-out rows.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.text:
STAGE 04

Reasoning with the method

Leakage can enter through features, rows, groups, time or repeated comparison. A post-outcome billing code is feature leakage; duplicate images across folds are row leakage; tomorrow’s rolling average is time leakage; repeatedly checking the same test score creates selection leakage. Nested cross-validation separates inner model selection from outer evaluation. Target encoding, oversampling, outlier rules, feature selection, PCA and threshold selection are all estimators. Each must be re-learned within every training fold. The decisive audit question is whether a value, rule or analyst decision could have known anything about the held-out outcome.

A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

stages.title: Interactive laboratory
stages.text:
STAGE 05

Interactive laboratory

Classify each pipeline as safe or leaking. Feedback identifies exactly where information crosses the boundary.

Scale all rows → random CV
Grouped split → fold-fitted imputer → model
Oversample all rows → create folds
Chronological split → train-fitted features

Choose a pipeline.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.text:
STAGE 06

Assumptions and failure modes
Assumptions

The split must match the unit of independence and deployment timing. Features must exist at the moment a prediction is made.

When the method fails

Random CV fails for time order, repeated patients, households, organisations, duplicated rows, and target-derived features. Oversampling before CV creates near-duplicates across folds.

stages.title: Practical workflow
stages.text:
STAGE 07

Practical workflow
Define prediction time and independent unit
Reserve the final test set
Choose stratified, grouped, time-series, or nested resampling
Fit every learned transform inside training folds
Lock and evaluate once

stages.title: Interpretation and reporting
stages.text:
STAGE 08

Interpretation and reporting

What to report: Document split units, dates or groups, pipeline order, cross-validation variant, test isolation and every target-aware transformation.

Common misuse: Preprocessing the full dataset before splitting because “it is not the model.”
