stages.title: Within-Class Scatter
stages.text:
STAGE 06 · BUILD
Within-Class Scatter

Not all apples are identical. SW measures how much the points in each class wiggle around their own mean.

The covariance ellipses on the plot show the spread shape. Diagonal entries = how much each feature varies. Off-diagonal = how features vary together.

Within-Class Scatter Matrix SW
S_W = (n₁ − 1)·Σ_apple + (n₂ − 1)·Σ_orange

S_W = ⎡ 8.685  2.645 ⎤
      ⎣ 2.645  8.565 ⎦

Each class covariance is weighted by (n_k − 1) before summing. Diagonal: variance of each feature. Off-diagonal: how features co-vary within a class.

What does within-class scatter mean?

Within-class scatter tells us how messy or spread out each class is inside itself.
• If all apples are clustered tightly together, apple scatter is small.
• If apples are spread out all over the plot, apple scatter is large.

What is covariance?
Covariance tells us whether Sweetness and Color move together:
• Positive covariance: Sweetness goes up, and Color Score also tends to go up.
• Negative covariance: One goes up, while the other goes down.
• Near Zero: They do not move together in any pattern.

Understanding the Scatter Matrix:
• Diagonal entries: How much each feature varies by itself (variance).
• Off-diagonal entries: How much the two features move together (covariance).

Concept Check: Within-Class Scatter

What does within-class scatter measure?

A) The distance between the Apple center and Orange center.
B) How spread out or messy points are inside each class.
C) The accuracy of the final predictions on unseen data.
D) The total count of features we selected.

controls.label: A) The distance between the Apple center and Orange center.
B) How spread out or messy points are inside each class.
C) The accuracy of the final predictions on unseen data.
D) The total count of features we selected.

stages.title: The Shared Covariance Assumption
stages.text:
STAGE 07 · PREPARE
The Shared Covariance Assumption

Here's LDA's key assumption: all classes share the same covariance shape. The groups can have different centers, but their spread is assumed to be roughly the same.

So LDA pools the individual covariance matrices into one shared estimate. Watch the ellipses morph into a single shape.

Pooled Covariance Matrix Σ
Σ = S_W / (n − 2)

Σ = ⎡ 0.482  0.147 ⎤
    ⎣ 0.147  0.476 ⎦
Why does LDA pool covariance?

LDA assumes that the classes have similar spread shapes. Instead of keeping separate shapes for Apple and Orange, it combines them into one shared covariance estimate.

Simple meaning: Different centers, same general spread shape.

LDA vs. QDA Comparison:
• LDA (Linear): Assumes shared covariance → Draws a straight decision line.
• QDA (Quadratic): Allows different covariances per class → Can draw a curved decision line.

 Warning: If the class clouds actually have very different shapes, LDA's shared covariance assumption is violated. LDA may struggle, and QDA (Quadratic Discriminant Analysis) might fit the data much better.

Concept Check: Shared Covariance

What is LDA’s shared covariance assumption?

A) Every fruit in the dataset has the exact same sweetness value.
B) The test set must have the same size as the training set.
C) Classes can have different centers, but they are assumed to have similar spread shapes.
D) The decision boundary must always be curved.

controls.label: A) Every fruit in the dataset has the exact same sweetness value.
B) The test set must have the same size as the training set.
C) Classes can have different centers, but they are assumed to have similar spread shapes.
D) The decision boundary must always be curved.

stages.title: Between-Class Scatter
stages.text:
STAGE 08 · BUILD
Between-Class Scatter

SB measures how far apart the class centers are. The further apart, the easier it is for LDA to separate them.

LDA's goal is to maximize the ratio of between-class scatter to within-class scatter:

Between-class scatter = gap between class centers

Let's contrast the two scatter metrics:
• Within-class scatter asks: "How messy and spread out is each class inside itself?"
• Between-class scatter asks: "How far apart are the class centers (means)?"

LDA's Ultimate Goal: We want the gap between classes to be BIG, and the messiness inside each class to be SMALL!

J(w) = wᵀ S_B w / wᵀ S_W w

In simple terms, J(w) is maximized when:
1. Projected class means are far apart.
2. Projected class spreads are small.
Between-Class Scatter SB
S_B = (n₁·n₂/n) · (μ₁ − μ₂)(μ₁ − μ₂)ᵀ

S_B = ⎡ 77.224  107.485 ⎤
      ⎣ 107.485  149.604 ⎦

stages.title: The Optimal Direction
stages.text:
STAGE 09 · UNDERSTAND
The Optimal Direction

In this 2-class example, LDA gives one main discriminant direction w — the angle where classes appear most separated.

What is projection and why do we do it?

Projection means dropping every 2D point (Sweetness, Color) down onto a single 1D line or direction.

This turns a 2D pair of numbers into a single 1D score:

Fruit (Sweetness, Color) → [Project] → One LDA Score

Why project? If the projected Apple scores sit neatly on one side of the line and the projected Orange scores sit on the other side, LDA has found an excellent direction for separation!

w ∝ S_W⁻¹ (μ₁ − μ₂)

This isn't just the straight line between means.
It also tilts to avoid the direction of maximum within-class spread.
Optimal Direction w
w = S_W⁻¹ · (μ₁ − μ₂) → [ 0.4594, 0.8883 ]

This direction maximizes the Fisher criterion J(w). Points projected onto it show maximum class separation.

stages.title: The Decision Boundary
stages.text:
STAGE 10 · BUILD
The Decision Boundary

Because LDA is linear, the boundary between classes is a straight line (in 2D). Everything on one side is classified as Apple, the other as Orange.

Discriminant Scores: Highest Score Wins

LDA calculates a separate scoring function for each class, called the Discriminant Score (δ):

δ_apple(x) = Score indicating how much point x looks like an Apple
δ_orange(x) = Score indicating how much point x looks like an Orange

For any point, LDA compares the two scores: whichever score is higher is the predicted class!

Example Fruit Prediction:

(Simple illustrative example, not a live value from the current dataset)
• Apple Score (δ_apple) = 2.31
• Orange Score (δ_orange) = -1.44
 Since 2.31 is higher than -1.44, LDA predicts Apple!
What are priors (π_k)?

The prior probability (π_k) represents the class probability before observing its features. Priors may be estimated from training prevalence or specified externally.
• If apples and oranges are equally common, priors are equal (50% each).
• If we estimate priors from 90% apples in training, the apple score gets a prior boost, shifting the boundary slightly to favor Apple predictions.

δ_k(x) = xᵀ Σ⁻¹ μ_k − ½ μ_kᵀ Σ⁻¹ μ_k + log(π_k)

Predict class k with the highest δ_k(x)
Decision Rule
Prior π_apple = 0.50
Prior π_orange = 0.50

The boundary is where δ_apple(x) = δ_orange(x). Points on the apple side get a higher apple score.

Concept Check: Decision Rule

How does LDA decide the final predicted class of a point?

A) It checks which class is physically closer using plain Euclidean distance.
B) It calculates a discriminant score for each class and chooses the highest one.
C) It always predicts the class that has more training samples.
D) It uses random guessing when a point is near the boundary.

B) It calculates a discriminant score for each class and chooses the highest one.

stages.title: Assumptions & Limitations
stages.text:
STAGE 14 · PREPARE
Assumptions & Limitations

To use LDA effectively, you need to understand when it thrives and when it falls short.

LDA Works Best When:
Linearity: A straight-line boundary is a reasonable way to separate classes.
Normality: Each class looks like a symmetrical oval cloud (multivariate normal distribution).
Equal Spread: All classes share roughly the same spread/covariance shape.
Independence: Data samples are collected independently.
Data Volume: There are many more rows than features.
No Outliers: Extreme values are absent (outliers pull means away easily).
LDA Struggles When:
The true dividing boundary is highly curved.
Classes have very different shapes or spreads (e.g., one is a tight circle, the other is a giant flat ellipse).
There are severe outliers that skew centers.
You have too many features and not enough rows (overfitting).
Features are redundant or highly correlated (collinearity).
Alternative Methods

If LDA doesn't fit, consider these standard alternatives:

 QDA (Quadratic Discriminant Analysis): Excellent if class spreads are highly unequal.
 Logistic Regression: Also estimates class probabilities, but avoids LDA’s Gaussian class-conditional and shared-covariance assumptions.
 KNN or Decision Trees: Great for highly complex, non-linear boundaries.
COMPLETE THE PICTURE
Posterior probabilities and regularised LDA

The discriminant scores can be converted into posterior class probabilities. These probabilities are useful for ranking and threshold decisions, not merely producing a hard label.

When the covariance estimate is unstable because there are many features or limited data, shrinkage or regularised LDA can trade a little bias for much lower variance.

stages.title: It Starts with Data
stages.text:
STAGE 01 · UNDERSTAND
It Starts with Data 
BEFORE YOU START

Logistic regression predicts the probability of a class. The final class label is produced only after applying a decision threshold to that probability.

Imagine you run an ice-cream shop. Every day you note the temperature, whether it was sunny, and whether someone bought ice cream.

The plot shows each day as a dot: temperature on the x-axis, outcome (bought or didn't) on the y-axis.

Legend

● Bought (y = 1)   ● Didn't buy (y = 0)

What is probability? 

Probability means "how likely something is to happen." It is always written as a number between 0 and 1:

0 means impossible (0% chance).
0.5 means 50-50 (50% chance).
1 means certain (100% chance).

In this guide, probability means: "How likely is someone to buy ice cream?"

Bought = 1 and Didn't buy = 0 are just category labels. They do not mean someone bought one ice cream or zero ice creams. They simply mark the two possible outcomes for the model.

Notice how higher temperatures tend to cluster near y = 1? That's the signal our model will learn to capture.

 This is a small toy dataset with 20 rows designed for teaching. Real datasets have hundreds or thousands of rows.

stages.title: Why Lines Break
stages.text:
STAGE 02 · UNDERSTAND
Why Lines Break 

Your first instinct might be to draw a straight line through the data — that's linear regression.

But watch what happens: the line predicts values above 1 and below 0. Those aren't valid probabilities!

ŷ = b₀ + b₁ · Temperature
Can give 1.5 or −0.3 … not a probability!
Why Bounds Matter 

A probability cannot be below 0 or above 1:

Below 0 would mean “less than impossible.”
Above 1 would mean “more than certain.”

So a prediction like 1.5 means 150%, which makes no real-world sense. We need a curve that stays strictly between 0 and 1.

We need a function that squishes any number into the 0–1 range. Enter the sigmoid.

stages.title: From a Raw Score to a Probability
stages.text:
STAGE 03 · BUILD
From a Raw Score to a Probability 

First, logistic regression starts the same way linear regression does. For each data point, one linear equation combines that point's features with the model's learned weights and produces one raw number, called z.

z = b₀ + b₁x₁ + b₂x₂ + ···

one data point → one raw score z

z is not a z-score or a standard score. It is not learned separately for each point. It is simply the model's raw opinion before that opinion becomes a probability. z can be any number from negative infinity to positive infinity. If z = 0, the model is exactly at 50/50.

Only after that do we apply the sigmoid function to turn z into a probability between 0 and 1.

p = 1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ)

Large positive z → probability near 1
Large negative z → probability near 0
z = 0 → probability exactly 0.5
See the Sigmoid Respond
Raw score z =
0.0
0.500
PROBABILITY
Where Does z Come From? 

For this interactive slider: yes, you are choosing the raw score z manually so you can see how the sigmoid responds.

In a real machine learning model: no, you do not choose z manually. The model runs its linear equation on each data point's features and learned weights.

Features + Weights → raw score z
raw score z → Sigmoid → Probability

“The z slider is only a teaching demo. In real logistic regression, the model calculates a separate raw score z for each row, then the sigmoid turns it into a probability.”

 Concept Check Quiz 1

In real logistic regression, where does the raw score z come from?

A. The model's linear equation combines each row's features with learned weights.
B. The user chooses a new z for every row.
C. The sigmoid chooses z after calculating the probability.
D. z is the same as the decision threshold.

 The sigmoid on the canvas is a 2D slice — it plots probability vs. temperature while holding Sunny and Weekend fixed at a neutral 0.5. The real model uses all three features simultaneously.

stages.title: Weighted Clues
stages.text:
STAGE 04 · UNDERSTAND
Weighted Clues 

How do we construct the score z? Think of our features (Temperature, Sunny, Weekend) as clues. Each weight describes the change in log-odds for a one-unit increase in that feature, holding the other modeled predictors fixed:

• A positive weight pushes the score toward "Buy" (y = 1).
• A negative weight pushes the score toward "Don't Buy" (y = 0).
• The final raw score z is the total combined push from all clues. The Sigmoid then turns this raw score into a clean final probability.

These sliders are a sandbox. You are manually changing the weights only to see how the mathematical curve reacts. In real training, the model learns these weights automatically by reducing log loss.

Stage 04 (Sandbox):

You adjust weights manually to see the shapes of the decision curve.

Stage 05 (Machine Learning):

The model adjusts weights automatically using gradient descent.

z = b₀ + b₁·standardized Temp + b₂·Sunny + b₃·Weekend

b₀ = bias (baseline push) · b₁, b₂, b₃ = individual clue pushes

Standardized temperature means we convert raw temperature values into a scaled version with a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1. Scaling mainly helps optimisation run smoothly and makes regularisation penalties more comparable across features. Large raw values do not inherently overpower the final fitted model: coefficients account for feature units.

Live Score Builder 

Let's test our current weights on an example day: a hot 30°C day (Raw Temperature) that is sunny (1) and a weekend (1).

• Baseline Bias Push (b₀): 0.00
• Temperature Push (b₁ × std temp 0.44): 1.50 × 0.44 = 0.66
• Sunny Push (b₂ × 1): 0.80 × 1.0 = 0.80
• Weekend Push (b₃ × 1): 0.50 × 1.0 = 0.50
Total Score (z) = 1.96
Probability = Sigmoid(z) = 87.6%
Who decides what? 
ITEM	WHO DETERMINES IT?	BEGINNER MEANING
Features	Data / user	Inputs like temperature, sunny weather, weekend status
Weights	Model learns them	How strongly each clue pushes the prediction
Raw score z	Model calculates it	Total push from all weighted clues combined
Probability	Sigmoid calculates it	Converts score z into a 0 to 1 probability (0% to 100%)
Threshold	Human chooses it	Cutoff boundary for Yes/No decision (often 0.50)
Final prediction	Decision rule applies it	Probability ≥ threshold means Yes (Predict Buy)

stages.title: Learning from Mistakes
stages.text:
STAGE 05 · BUILD
Learning from Mistakes 

The model starts with initial weights, makes predictions, measures how wrong it was using log loss, then nudges the weights to improve. This is gradient descent.

Training does not directly choose z. Training learns better weights. Once the weights improve, the model calculates better z values for each row of data automatically:

Training updates weights → weights calculate z → sigmoid turns z into probability → threshold turns probability into Yes/No
L = −[ y·log(p) + (1−y)·log(1−p) ]

The model is punished more when it's
very confident but very wrong.
How Log Loss Thinks 

Log loss measures the penalty of wrong answers. If the actual answer is 1 (Bought):

REAL ANSWER	PREDICTED PROB	MEANING	LOSS PENALTY
1 (Bought)	0.95	Confident & correct	Small Loss (0.05)
1 (Bought)	0.55	Unsure but leaning right	Medium Loss (0.60)
1 (Bought)	0.05	Confident & wrong!	Huge Loss (3.00)

* Note: These loss values are examples for one single prediction. The training loss shown below is the average loss across all training rows.

Gradient descent is like adjusting a recipe little by little. If the model is wrong, it changes the weights in the direction that reduces loss. The learning rate controls how big each adjustment step is. Gradient descent is one teaching-friendly optimiser, not the definition of logistic regression: Newton, quasi-Newton, coordinate-descent and other solvers are also common. Feature scaling often improves numerical optimisation and is especially relevant with regularisation; fit scaling inside training folds.

 Warning on Learning Rate:
• Too small: Learning is very slow, requiring thousands of steps.
• Too large: The model may jump right over the best values and fail to settle.

B. Better weights that reduce log loss.

stages.title: Drawing the Line
stages.text:
STAGE 06 · UNDERSTAND
Drawing the Line 

The sigmoid gives a probability. But we need a decision: Yes or No. We pick a threshold.

If p ≥ threshold → predict Yes (1)
If p < threshold → predict No (0)

The model only gives probabilities. The threshold is a decision rule chosen by humans. We choose it based on what kind of mistake is worse or more costly for our specific situation:

Threshold vs. Probability 

The threshold does not change the probability itself. It only changes how we convert that probability into a final Yes/No decision.

Example: If the model predicts a probability of 0.62:
• At threshold 0.50 → predict Yes (since 0.62 ≥ 0.50)
• At threshold 0.70 → predict No (since 0.62 < 0.70)

The probability stayed exactly 0.62. Only the decision rule changed.

Lowering the Threshold (e.g., 0.30):

Predicts "Yes" more easily. You catch more real buyers (high recall), but you also create more false alarms (false positives).

Raising the Threshold (e.g., 0.70):

Predicts "Yes" only when highly confident. You reduce false alarms (high precision), but you might miss many real buyers (false negatives).

Set Threshold
Threshold
0.50

Select this threshold on validation data, never the final test set. Use error costs, prevalence, capacity, and the real objective. Lock the threshold with all preprocessing and calibration choices, then report final test performance once. Probability calibration and classification accuracy answer different questions.

 Concept Check Quiz 3

Who chooses the decision threshold?

A. Usually the human/researcher, based on the problem.
B. The sigmoid function.
C. The raw temperature column.
D. The y-axis.

 A medical test might use 0.3 (catch more sick people), while a spam filter might use 0.7 (avoid false alarms).

controls.label: A. Usually the human/researcher, based on the problem.

stages.title: Select the Decision Rule on Validation Data
stages.text:
STAGE 07 · UNDERSTAND
Select the Decision Rule on Validation Data 

Use the validation set to explore threshold-dependent trade-offs. The final test set remains hidden while the threshold, metrics and model choices are still changing.

Every validation prediction falls into one of four boxes:

• TP (True Positive): Predicted Bought, and they really bought. Correct prediction!
• TN (True Negative): Predicted Didn't buy, and they did not buy. Correct prediction!
• FP (False Positive): Predicted Bought, but they did not buy. (False alarm!).
• FN (False Negative): Predicted Didn't buy, but they actually bought. (Missed buyer!).

Validation Confusion Matrix

 Click on any grid cell below to show its plain-English explanation.

Pred Yes (≥ t)
Pred No (< t)
Real Yes

True Positive (TP): The model predicted Bought, and the customer actually bought ice cream. Correct prediction!

● Dim dots = training set     ● Vivid dots = validation set

 Threshold Dependencies: Changing the decision threshold changes the validation TP, TN, FP, and FN counts. Use these development results to select and lock the rule; do not repeatedly inspect the test set.

Validation Metrics
Overall Accuracy
100%
Formula: (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)

Meaning: How often was the model correct overall? Best used when mistakes are equally costly.

Precision (Reliability of Yes Predictions)
100%
Formula: TP / (TP + FP)

Meaning: When the model predicts Bought, how often is it right? Critical when false alarms (FP) are expensive.

Recall (Sensitivity / Detection Rate)
100%
Formula: TP / (TP + FN)

Meaning: Out of all real positive buyers, how many did the model catch? Critical when missing a real positive (FN) is costly.

F1-Score
1.000
Formula: 2 × (Precision × Recall) / (Precision + Recall)

Meaning: F1 is a balance score between precision and recall. It is not a normal average; it gives a low score if either precision or recall is weak. Perfect when you want to look at general model balance.

Final untouched test evaluation

Hidden until the model and validation-selected threshold are locked. Reveal this result once, after development is complete.

stages.title: The Validation ROC Curve
stages.text:
STAGE 08 · UNDERSTAND
The Validation ROC Curve 

The validation ROC curve shows: at every possible threshold, how does recall trade off against false-alarm rate? It is a development visual and never reads the final test set.

Think of a smoke alarm: too sensitive and it goes off when you cook toast; too lenient and it misses an actual fire.

Accuracy vs. ROC / AUC:

• Accuracy shows model performance at a single chosen threshold (like 0.50).

• ROC shows performance trade-offs across all possible thresholds.

• AUC (Area Under Curve) is not the same as accuracy. AUC summarizes how well the model separates/ranks positive cases from negative cases across all thresholds.

Key ROC Metrics Explained

An ROC curve plots two key metrics against each other at all possible thresholds from 0.0 to 1.0:

True Positive Rate (TPR / Recall): TP / (TP + FN)
Meaning: Out of all real buyers, what percentage did we catch? (Higher is better!)
False Positive Rate (FPR / False Alarm Rate): FP / (FP + TN)
Meaning: Out of all non-buyers, what percentage did we wrongly predict as buyers? (Lower is better!)

The ROC curve checks many possible thresholds, not just 0.5. Each point on the curve comes from a specific threshold value. Moving the threshold changes TPR and FPR.

—
AUC (AREA UNDER CURVE)

• AUC = 1.0: Perfect separation on this dataset.
• AUC = 0.5: Random guessing. The model has no predictive strength.

Note: AUC does not mean the model is perfect forever. It only summarizes separation performance on the data being evaluated.

 Note: Because this teaching example has a very small validation set, the ROC curve looks coarse and jumpy. With a larger validation sample, the curve would usually be smoother.

stages.title: What the Numbers Mean
stages.text:
STAGE 09 · REFLECT
What the Numbers Mean 

We often want to know how the model estimates each feature (temperature, sunny day, weekend status) is associated with higher or lower predicted odds, while holding other features constant. Logistic regression gives us weights that can be converted into Odds Ratios.

Probability vs. Odds 

Probability and Odds are related but express likelihood differently:

• Probability (p) asks: "Out of all outcomes, how likely is Yes?" (Varies between 0 and 1).
• Odds asks: "How much does the chance of Yes beat No?" (Varies from 0 to infinity). Formula: Odds = p / (1 - p)

PROBABILITY (P)	ODDS FORMULA	ODDS VALUE	MEANING
0.50 (50%)	0.50 / 0.50	1 to 1 (1.0)	Yes and No are equally likely
0.75 (75%)	0.75 / 0.25	3 to 1 (3.0)	Yes is three times as likely as No
0.80 (80%)	0.80 / 0.20	4 to 1 (4.0)	Yes is four times as likely as No

Taking the exponent of a weight (eweight) gives us the Odds Ratio (OR). This ratio tells us how the odds of buying are multiplied for each unit increase in that feature.

 Beginner Warning:
Odds are not the same as probability. An odds ratio of 2 does not mean the probability doubles! It means the odds ratio doubles (e.g. from 1:1 odds to 2:1 odds).

 Coefficient ≠ proof of cause:
A positive coefficient means the feature is associated with higher predicted probability in this model. It does not prove that modifying the feature directly causes buying behavior.

Our Weights & Odds Ratios

Positive Weight (OR > 1): Feature is associated with pushing probability and odds up.
Negative Weight (OR < 1): Feature is associated with pushing probability and odds down.
Near Zero Weight (OR ≈ 1): Feature has little to no association with predicted odds.

stages.title: The Full Picture
stages.text:
STAGE 10 · REFLECT
The Full Picture 

You've walked through the entire logistic regression pipeline! Let's review the whole story in plain English:

The Story of Logistic Regression 
We collect historical raw data: temperature, sunny weather, weekends, and whether someone bought ice cream.
A straight linear regression line is not suitable because it predicts impossible values (below 0 and above 1) for probabilities.
Instead, logistic regression builds an intermediate score called z by adding up weighted features (clues).
The mathematical sigmoid function gracefully "squishes" this score z into a valid probability between 0% and 100%.
A decision threshold translates probabilities into labels. Select it on validation data from error costs, prevalence and objectives; 0.50 is only a convention.
During training, the model starts with baseline weights and iteratively adjusts them using gradient descent to minimize average log loss.
A validation confusion matrix is used to compare threshold choices without touching the final test set.
Performance is summarized using descriptive metrics: Accuracy (overall correctness), Precision (purity of Yes calls), Recall (capture rate of actual positives), and F1-score (their balanced harmony).
The validation ROC curve and AUC summarize ranking trade-offs across thresholds during development.
After the model and threshold are locked, the test set is revealed once for the final performance estimate.
By analyzing coefficients and odds ratios, we can interpret how the model estimates each feature is associated with higher or lower odds of a purchase.
Concept Checklist

 Collected and plotted raw data

 Saw why linear regression can't predict probabilities

 Met the sigmoid that squishes scores into 0–1

 Built the score z from weighted features

 Trained with gradient descent to minimize log loss

 Chose a threshold to turn probabilities into decisions

 Evaluated with confusion matrix and metrics

 Explored the ROC curve for threshold trade-offs

 Interpreted coefficients and odds ratios

↑ Back to top
COMPLETE THE PICTURE
Thresholds, imbalance, and calibration

The default threshold of 0.50 is a convention, not a law. Choose a threshold based on the relative cost of false positives and false negatives.

With imbalanced classes, accuracy may look impressive while the model misses the minority class. Inspect precision, recall, ROC or precision–recall curves, and whether predicted probabilities are well calibrated.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
The sigmoid maps a linear score to a probability between 0 and 1.
Coefficients act on log-odds; exponentiated coefficients are odds ratios.
Evaluation and threshold choice should reflect the real cost of classification errors.

Practical method checklist

Before you finish
Assumptions

Appropriate link, independent observations, and a suitable linear predictor.

When the method fails

Separation, omitted nonlinearity, imbalance, poor calibration, and drift.

Validation and leakage

Tune regularisation, calibration, and threshold on validation data.

Interpretation cautions

A 0.5 threshold is a convention; coefficients are conditional associations.

What to report

Solver, scaling, odds ratios with intervals, calibration, threshold, and metrics.

stages.title: The problem
stages.text:
STAGE 01

The problem
Missing values and categories carry structure. A convenient fill value or numeric code can change the estimand, introduce false order, or leak outcome information.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.text:
STAGE 02

Intuition and objective
Imputation predicts or substitutes missing values; encoding represents categories numerically. Both are learned transformations and belong inside the pipeline.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.text:
STAGE 03

Worked example
Income is missing more often for high earners. Mean imputation pulls their values toward the centre and understates variation. A missingness indicator may help prediction, but it does not make the missing-at-random assumption true for inference.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.text:
STAGE 04

Reasoning with the method

MCAR, MAR and MNAR are assumptions about the missingness process, not labels that a plot can prove. Complete-case analysis is valid for limited targets under restrictive conditions. Single imputation treats filled values as known and usually understates inferential uncertainty; multiple imputation combines within- and between-imputation variation. Encoding defines geometry: one-hot separates unordered levels, ordinal encoding asserts order, and target encoding borrows outcome information. Target and frequency encoders need fold-safe fitting and an unseen-level policy. Raw columns and a data dictionary should be retained so every transformation remains auditable.

A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.text:
STAGE 06

Assumptions and failure modes
Assumptions

Missing-data methods rely on assumptions about why values are absent. Category encodings assume a structure—unordered, ordinal, or target-related—that must be defensible.

When the method fails

Single imputation understates inferential uncertainty; ordinal codes create fake distances; target encoding leaks without cross-fitting; unseen categories can break deployment.

stages.text:
STAGE 07

Practical workflow
Profile missingness and category levels
Separate structural from accidental missingness
Split data before fitting transforms
Choose imputation for the analysis goal
Encode with explicit reference and unknown-level policy
Run sensitivity analyses

stages.title: Interpretation and reporting
stages.text:
STAGE 08

Interpretation and reporting

What to report: Report missingness rates, mechanism assumptions, imputation model, number of imputations, encoding, reference levels, unknown-category policy and sensitivity.

Common misuse: Using zero as “missing” when zero has a real scientific meaning.

stages.title: The Overfitting Trap
stages.text:
STAGE 01 · BUILD
The Overfitting Trap
BEFORE YOU START

Model selection is part of model fitting. Every candidate comparison must be contained inside the training or cross-validation process.

Building a predictive model is tricky. It is tempting to include every available piece of data. We often assume that more clues guarantee better answers.

However, adding too many variables introduces massive noise. This noise obscures the true relationship. The model ends up memorizing random accidents in the training data rather than learning the actual signal.

The Illusion of Accuracy: A highly complex model performs flawlessly on its "homework" (the training data). But it collapses in the real world on unseen data. This failure is called overfitting.

stages.title: The n-p Puzzle
stages.text:
STAGE 02 · UNDERSTAND
The n-p Puzzle

To build a reliable model, we must balance two things. First is the number of samples (
𝑛
). Second is the number of variables or clues (
𝑝
).

Think of this in three simple steps:

Step 1: You need enough examples to prove a real pattern exists.
Step 2: Every new variable adds a whole new dimension for the model to search.
Step 3: When 
𝑝
>
𝑛
, ordinary least squares has no unique coefficient solution unless constraints are imposed. Ridge, Lasso, or other regularisation can still support useful prediction, although instability and overfitting are serious concerns.

At this point, the design matrix is rank deficient. Without additional constraints, many coefficient vectors may fit the training data equally well. This makes coefficient interpretation unstable and creates a high risk of overfitting. Useful prediction may still be possible with appropriate regularisation, feature structure and honest validation.

Keep the ideas separate: non-unique coefficients concern identifiability; interpolation means matching the observed training outcomes; overfitting is poor generalisation caused by learning sample-specific patterns; predictive performance must be measured on unseen data. Ridge, Lasso and Elastic Net impose different constraints that can produce estimable predictors, but they are not automatic cures.

stages.title: Picking the Best Team
stages.text:
STAGE 03 · UNDERSTAND
Picking the Best Team

One way to fix this is Subset Selection. This means literally picking a specific group of variables and throwing the rest out.

FORWARD Start empty. Add the single best predictor. Then add the next one that helps the most. Keep going.

BACKWARD Start with all variables. Find the weakest predictor and bench them. Repeat until only the best are left.

HYBRID Add the best predictors one by one. But constantly re-evaluate. If an old predictor becomes redundant, remove it.

MINI-CHECK

Why don't we just test every single combination of variables?

It decreases accuracy.
It is computationally impossible. Just 40 predictors creates over a billion models.

stages.title: The Shrinking Trick
stages.text:
STAGE 05 · UNDERSTAND
The Shrinking Trick

Subset selection is an "all-or-nothing" approach. A variable is either in or out. But what if we just made a weak variable's influence smaller?

This is called Regularization. Imagine a soundboard where each slider controls a variable. Regularization turns down the volume on loud, messy variables. It shrinks their coefficients (
𝛽

𝜆

Crucial Step: Variables should be centered first, and usually standardized when their scales differ, to create a level playing field. Otherwise, a variable measured in huge numbers (like dollars) would face unfair shrinkage compared to a variable measured in small numbers (like years).

What is the main goal of Regularization?

To delete all the variables and start over.
To turn down the volume (shrink the coefficients) of noisy or less useful variables.

STAGE 08 · UNDERSTAND
Finding the Sweet Spot

How do we know the right amount of shrinkage? We use K-Fold Cross-Validation to find the optimal

Choose CV from the data structure. Use stratified folds for imbalanced classes, grouped folds for repeated subjects or organisations, time-series CV for ordered observations, repeated CV for stability, and nested CV when model selection and unbiased evaluation must both occur. Imputation, scaling, encoding, feature selection, PCA, outlier rules, oversampling and threshold tuning all belong inside the training folds.

Why average them? Averaging prevents a "lucky split." It stops us from accidentally choosing a model that just happened to get easy data during validation.

stages.title: The "Super-Variable" Secret
stages.text:
STAGE 09 · UNDERSTAND
The "Super-Variable" Secret

If we have 100 highly correlated variables, they provide redundant information. Dimension Reduction allows us to "squish" them into a few super-variables called Principal Components.

PCR

Compress first, predict later. It squishes variables together without looking at what you are trying to predict.

PLS

Compress while paying attention. It squishes variables together by finding directions that best explain the target you want to predict.

Think of PCR as combining 100 photos of a dog into a single "Super-Photo" of the whole dog. PLS knows you are trying to predict happiness, so it squishes the photos specifically to highlight the wagging tail.

STAGE 10 · UNDERSTAND
Decision Helper

I have highly correlated variables

Best match: Lasso & Best Subset Selection
You prioritize explaining 'why' and keeping models simple.

RECOMMENDED
Lasso & Best Subset Selection

Best for Interpretability & Simplicity. These methods drop variables entirely, leaving a clean, short list of the most important drivers. Essential in healthcare or finance where explaining the "why" matters.

Ridge & PCR

Best for Pure Prediction & Correlated Data. When you have many overlapping clues and prediction accuracy matters more than a simple explanation, keeping all variables with smaller, stable weights helps minimize error on new data.

stages.title: Common Mistakes
stages.text:
STAGE 11 · REFLECT
Common Mistakes

Even advanced statistical methods are not magic. Here is how to avoid common traps.

MISTAKE 1

Choosing a model based on training accuracy.

CORRECT PRACTICE

Always compare and judge models based on cross-validation error. Training accuracy is always overly optimistic.

MISTAKE 2

Testing on the final test set multiple times.

CORRECT PRACTICE

Lock the final test set in a vault. Use it only once at the very end to check your final model. If you use it to tweak parameters, it is no longer an honest test.

COMPLETE THE PICTURE
Prefer the simplest near-best model

Validation scores contain noise. The one-standard-error rule chooses the simplest model whose performance is within one standard error of the best observed score.

When comparing many pipelines, use nested cross-validation or a final untouched test set. Otherwise the “best” model may simply be the one that benefited most from repeated checking.

stages.title: Final Synthesis
stages.text:
STAGE 12 · REFLECT
Final Synthesis

We do not want a model that is too simple (underfitting). We do not want a model that is too dramatic (overfitting).

By using Cross-Validation, we compare and validate models fairly. By applying Regularization or Subset Selection, we penalize messiness and force the model to focus only on what matters.

The ultimate goal is Generalization. We want to build a model that stays trustworthy and useful when reality shows up and starts ruining everyone's assumptions.

FINAL CHECK

What is the ultimate goal of model selection and regularization?

To achieve 0% error on the training data.
Generalization: performing well on unseen real-world data.
KEY TAKEAWAYS
Regularisation controls variance by shrinking coefficients.
Ridge keeps all predictors; Lasso can set some coefficients to zero.
Tune the full modelling pipeline and favour stable, defensible complexity.

When the method fails

Repeated comparison, unstable selection, rank deficiency, and correlated predictors.

Validation and leakage

Use nested CV or a final untouched test for unbiased evaluation.

Interpretation cautions

Lasso selection is neither uniquely important nor causal.

What to report

Candidate set, full pipeline, selection rule, uncertainty, stability, and final performance.

stages.title: The Multi-Variable World
stages.text:
STAGE 01 · OBSERVE
The Multi-Variable World
BEFORE YOU START

Multiple regression extends simple regression by adding predictors. Each coefficient is conditional on the other variables included in the model.

Life is messy. If we want to predict a student's Test Score, knowing how many hours they studied is helpful, but it's rarely the full story.

What about how much sleep they got? What about the number of practice papers they completed? Multiple Linear Regression allows us to use several clues together to predict one number.

Our Data Universe

To the right, we plot a dataset of students in 3D space:

X-Axis: Hours Studied
Z-Axis: Hours Slept
Y-Axis (Height): Test Score

stages.title: The Secret Recipe
stages.text:
STAGE 02 · UNDERSTAND
The Secret Recipe

In simple regression, we draw a line. But with three predictors—Study, Sleep, and Practice—we technically need a 4D space! Since we can't see 4D, we'll draw a 3D plane as a visual stepping stone.

We'll plot Study and Sleep on the axes, and hold Practice temporarily constant at its average to visualize one slice of the full model. Think of the full equation like a cake recipe with multiple ingredients:

y = β0 + β1x1 + β2x2 + β3x3 + ε
THE TARGET (Y)
Test Score
THE PREDICTORS (X)
Study, Sleep, Practice
THE BOOSTERS (Β)
Coefficients
THE MESSINESS (Ε)
Unexplained Error

stages.title: Finding the Fit
stages.text:
STAGE 03 · BUILD
Finding the Fit

We want our model to pass as closely to the actual student scores as possible. The distance between our prediction and the actual score is called a Residual (the red dashed lines).

Try adjusting the full set of coefficients manually. The indigo surface is the average-practice slice, while the hollow red markers show the full three-variable prediction used for the residuals and SSE.

Base Score (β0)
0.0
Study Boost (β1)
0.0
Sleep Boost (β2)
0.0
Practice Boost (β3)
0.0
SUM OF SQUARED ERRORS (SSE)
55897

stages.title: The Least Squares Method
stages.text:
STAGE 04 · BUILD
The Least Squares Method

Instead of guessing, the computer uses matrix algebra to instantly derive the absolute lowest possible Sum of Squared Errors directly from the dataset.

By minimizing the squared residuals across all 3 dimensions simultaneously, it settles perfectly into the optimal fit.

Snap to Optimal Fit
Why Square the Errors?
1. It stops positive (+4) and negative (-4) misses from canceling out to zero.
2. It heavily punishes huge misses (a miss of 10 costs 100 points), forcing the model to compromise evenly across all variables.

stages.title: The Superpower: Holding Constant
stages.text:
STAGE 05 · UNDERSTAND
The Superpower: Holding Constant

This is the most critical concept in multiple regression. What does a Study Boost (β1) actually mean when we have an optimal fit?

It means: If a student studies one extra hour, their score increases by exactly that boost amount—assuming their sleep and practice papers stay exactly the same.

This logic applies to each predictor's coefficient: β1 is the estimated association with Study while Sleep and Practice are held fixed, β2 is the estimated association with Sleep while Study and Practice are held fixed, and β3 is the estimated association with Practice while Study and Sleep are held fixed. These are not automatically causal effects.

The model does not literally freeze variables in real life—rather, it does this mathematically to estimate each variable's conditional association holding other modeled predictors fixed.

Notice the highlighted slice on the plane. We've locked "Sleep" at 6 hours (and Practice at its average). As we move purely along the Study axis, the score rises in a perfect straight line determined solely by β1.

Score = 0.0 + 0.0(Study) + 0.0 (Sleep = 6.0, Practice = avg 2.3)

stages.title: Building the Prediction
stages.text:
STAGE 06 · UNDERSTAND
Building the Prediction

Now we transition away from the 3D plane. In multiple regression, the prediction is built from a base intercept plus separate contributions from each predictor.

Each predictor adds or subtracts its own specific amount. The final score is simply the sum of all these individual parts. Because of how the model fits the data, each of these contributions is added while the other predictors are treated as fixed.

PREDICTING A SPECIFIC STUDENT
Study
4.0 hrs
Sleep
7.5 hrs
Practice
2 pps
How it stacks up:
• Base Score = Starting point
• Study Boost = β1 × Study hours
• Sleep Boost = β2 × Sleep hours
• Practice Boost = β3 × Practice papers
Final Score = Sum of all parts

stages.title: The Spurious Trap
stages.text:
STAGE 07 · UNDERSTAND
The Spurious Trap

If multiple variables just stack, why not run a simple regression for each variable separately? Because of Spurious Correlations.

Imagine we want to predict Shark Attacks. If we run a simple model using Ice Cream Sales, the correlation is huge! It looks like ice cream causes shark attacks.

But the true driver is a lurking variable: High Temperature. Hot days cause both ice cream sales and beach visits (which lead to shark attacks).

The Power of "Holding Constant"
Multiple regression estimates a variable's conditional association holding other modeled predictors fixed, which can reveal when a variable only looked important because it moved together with another predictor. If we put both Ice Cream and Temperature into the model, the model essentially compares days with the same temperature. Holding temperature constant, ice cream sales have almost zero conditional association with shark attacks in this example.

If a coefficient shrinks close to zero after the other predictors are included, that suggests it has little conditional association with the predicted outcome (y) after accounting for the others. This does not prove the variable has no real-world effect at all, only that its estimated conditional association is small within this specific model.

Note: A larger coefficient doesn't always mean a "more important" predictor, as they depend on the unit of measurement.

stages.title: The Adjusted R² Penalty
stages.text:
STAGE 08 · REFLECT
The Adjusted R² Penalty

How do we know if our team of variables is actually good? R² tells us what percentage of the variance we explained.

For least-squares models with an intercept fitted to the same training observations, adding predictors makes training R² stay the same or increase. Even "Student's Shoe Size" may increase it, without improving predictions on new data.

Adj R² = 1 - [ (1 - R²)(n - 1) / (n - p - 1) ]

Adjusted R² corrects for this by penalizing model complexity. In the formula, n is the number of observations and p is the number of predictors.

Every new predictor (p) uses up flexibility and increases the penalty. Adjusted R² can rise or fall, even for an irrelevant variable in a particular sample. It is a descriptive aid, not an automatic feature-retention rule: consider validation performance, the modeling goal, and subject knowledge.

stages.title: Reading the Model Output
stages.text:
STAGE 09 · EVALUATE
Reading the Model Output

When a data analyst fits a multiple linear regression, they don't look at a 3D plot—they look at a summary table to evaluate the results.

Estimate:
The coefficient (β). How much the prediction changes for a one-unit increase in this predictor, holding all other predictors constant.
Std. Error:
The uncertainty around the estimate. A smaller standard error means we are more confident in the coefficient.
t value:
The estimate divided by its standard error. A larger absolute value (typically > 2) indicates strong statistical evidence that the true effect is not zero.

Note: Each coefficient should be read as "the change in predicted y for a one-unit increase in this predictor, holding the others constant." Because predictors can be measured in entirely different units, coefficients cannot be compared as pure "importance scores" unless the predictors are on comparable scales.

Diagnostics belong with the output. Inspect residual-versus-fitted, Q–Q, scale-location, leverage and influence plots. Use VIFs and coefficient intervals to diagnose multicollinearity; document categorical reference levels and interactions. Report confidence intervals for mean responses and wider prediction intervals for new observations. These coefficients are adjusted associations, not causal effects without a causal design.
Multiple linear regression is a powerful detective. It models additive effects, isolates individual drivers, and finds the mathematically optimal fit by minimizing squared errors.
COMPLETE THE PICTURE
Diagnostics the fitted equation cannot show

Before trusting coefficient estimates, inspect residual plots and influential observations. Check multicollinearity because strongly overlapping predictors can make individual coefficients unstable even when overall prediction remains good.

Interactions are needed when the association with one predictor changes across levels of another. Add them deliberately and interpret the combined terms rather than reading each coefficient in isolation.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
Each coefficient describes a partial relationship while the other predictors are held constant.
Adjusted R² penalises adding predictors that do not provide enough improvement.
Prediction quality, residual diagnostics, collinearity, and subject-matter logic all matter.

Practical method checklist

Before you finish
Assumptions

Correct form, independent errors, stable variance, and a defensible adjustment set.

When the method fails

Omitted variables, collinearity, interactions, nonlinearity, and influential cases.

Validation and leakage

Choose features and transformations within training folds.

Interpretation cautions

Coefficients are adjusted associations unless a causal design justifies more.

What to report

Reference levels, interactions, VIFs, intervals, diagnostics, and validation error.

stages.title: Start with a pile of labeled emails.
stages.text:
01
Observe the case

Start with a pile of labeled emails.

Naive Bayes learns from examples where the answer is already known. In this miniature dataset, each row is an email, three clues are recorded, and the final column says whether the message was spam.

The model does not understand the sentence the way a person does. It sees a structured record: free? winner? meeting? and a class label.

A
Start with the past. The model’s evidence comes from what happened in earlier examples.

stages.title: Separate the target from the clues.
stages.text:
02
Frame the question

Separate the target from the clues.

The thing we want to predict is the target variable, Y. Everything else becomes a feature, X—a measurable clue the model can use.

For text, the original sentence is transformed into a vector of usable values. A word being present can become 1; absent can become 0.

X₁ = contains “free”
→
[1, 0, 1, 0]

stages.title: Keep the final exam hidden.
stages.text:
03
Protect the test

Keep the final exam hidden.

Before learning anything, divide the dataset. The training set teaches the model. The test set stays untouched until the end, so the final score tells us how the model handles examples it has not memorised.

A common starting point is around 80% training and 20% test. Peeking at the test set early gives an overly optimistic picture.

train = learn
test = untouched

stages.title: Choose the version that fits the feature.
stages.text:
04
Match the evidence

Choose the version that fits the feature.

“Naive Bayes” is a family of models. The prediction logic stays recognisable, but the likelihood calculation changes with the kind of feature you have.

Tap a model type to see what it expects.

Bernoulli
Multinomial
Categorical
Gaussian
Selected
Bernoulli
yes / no features

stages.title: Count what each class tends to contain.
stages.text:
05
Learn the starting belief

Count what each class tends to contain.

Training is mostly about learning probabilities from the training data. First comes the prior: how common is each class before we inspect the new email?

Scale note:
the six-email ledger was a tiny pattern-finding example. The board below imagines a larger training set of 100 emails, so its 40/60 prior is a separate, clearly labelled example.

Then come the likelihoods: inside each class, how often did each clue appear? In a count-based model, this is a probability table made from the data.

P(Spam) = 40 / 100 = 0.40
P(Free | Spam) = 30 / 40 = 0.75

stages.title: Pretend the clues can speak separately.
stages.text:
06
Make the naive move

Pretend the clues can speak separately.

Real words can be related. “Free” and “winner” may travel together. Naive Bayes deliberately ignores that relationship once the class is known.

This conditional-independence assumption is the shortcut: each feature contributes a separate piece of evidence, so the pieces can be multiplied together. When this assumption is strongly violated, posterior probabilities may be overconfident or poorly calibrated.

Show what the shortcut ignores ↗

stages.title: Prior × evidence = a class score.
stages.text:
07
Score a new observation

Prior × evidence = a class score.

Our new email contains “free” and “winner”. The model asks the same question twice: how well would this evidence fit Spam? How well would it fit Not Spam?

Tap the clues on the diagram to include or ignore them. The class scores and normalised posterior update immediately; ignoring a clue is different from observing that it is absent.

Current prediction
Spam
98.4% posterior
Reset evidence

stages.title: Numbers need a different likelihood.
stages.text:
08
Change the kind of feature

Numbers need a different likelihood.

For a height, age, or temperature, counting exact matches is not useful. Nobody may be exactly 169 cm, but that height can still be typical of a class.

Gaussian Naive Bayes learns a mean and a spread for each class, then asks how normal the new number looks under each bell-shaped distribution.

Observation height:
169 cm
Class A ≈ 168 cm
Class B ≈ 181 cm

stages.title: Two small engineering fixes.
stages.text:
09
Keep the arithmetic stable

Two small engineering fixes.

If a feature was never seen in a class, its count can produce a likelihood of zero. One zero would erase the whole product. Laplace smoothing adds a small artificial count so “unseen” does not mean “impossible”. This applies to discrete/count variants, not Gaussian Naive Bayes.

With hundreds of features, multiplying tiny numbers can underflow. Implementations use log probabilities: multiplication becomes addition, while the class ranking stays the same.

Smoothing
Log space

stages.title: Use folds while you build.
stages.text:
10
Develop honestly

Use folds while you build.

Do not keep checking the final test set while tuning the model. Instead, rotate through the training set with 5-fold cross-validation: four folds train, one fold validates, then the validating fold moves.

After choosing the model, train once more on all training data. Only then do you test on the untouched 20%.

Round 1 · Fold 1 validates

2

stages.title: A prediction is a decision with consequences.
stages.text:
11
Read the result

A prediction is a decision with consequences.

Accuracy is not the only question. Precision asks whether predicted spam really was spam. Recall asks how much of the real spam the model caught. F1 balances the two.

In a spam filter, a false positive can bury an important email. The metric that matters most depends on the cost of being wrong.

Protect inbox
Catch more spam
Precision focus · keep false positives visible.

stages.title: Prior → likelihoods → posterior.
stages.text:
12
Keep the mental model

Prior → likelihoods → posterior.

Naive Bayes is a detective with a disciplined shortcut: start with what was common, score how each clue fits each class, combine the evidence, then choose the most probable explanation.

Remember four words: prior, likelihood, naive assumption, and posterior.

What I believed before + what the evidence says = what I believe now.

stages.title: The whole idea: learn patterns from examples
stages.text:
STAGE 01
The whole idea: learn patterns from examples

A neural network is a model made of small calculation units called neurons. Each neuron receives numbers, gives some of them more importance than others, combines them, and passes a new number forward.

Imagine teaching a child to recognize cats. You do not write every possible cat rule. You show many examples labeled cat or not cat. The child gradually notices patterns. A neural network does something similar with numbers.

→

Plain-English translation: examples go in, a prediction comes out, mistakes are measured, and the internal settings are adjusted so the next prediction is less wrong.

Normal programming versus machine learning

Normal programming: a human writes the rules, the computer applies them, and an answer comes out. Machine learning: a human supplies examples and correct outcomes, then the model learns useful rules from those examples. Neural networks are valuable when the rules are too numerous or complicated to write by hand.

BEFORE YOU CONTINUE

You only need basic comfort with multiplication, averages, and percentages. Every specialist word is defined before it is used.

stages.title: Data becomes features and labels
stages.text:
STAGE 02
Data becomes features and labels

Data is the collection of examples the model learns from. In our toy problem, each row describes one student.

STUDY HOURS	SLEEP HOURS	ATTENDANCE	PASSED?
8	7	90%	Yes
2	4	40%	No
5	6	70%	Yes
Features

The clues the model receives: study hours, sleep hours, and attendance.

Label

The correct answer it must learn to predict: passed or failed.

Supervised learning means the training examples already contain the correct answers. Features are the clues; the label is the answer key.

stages.title: Clean, encode, scale, then split
stages.text:
STAGE 03
Clean, encode, scale, then split

Real data is rarely ready to train on. Missing values, duplicates, impossible values, inconsistent labels, and suspicious outliers must be investigated before the model sees them.

1. Clean

Fix or remove records that are missing, duplicated, impossible, or inconsistent.

2. Encode

Turn words and categories into numbers because the network performs mathematics.

3. Scale

Put numerical features on comparable ranges so a large unit does not look important merely because its number is bigger.

4. Split

Keep separate training, validation, and test sets so memorization cannot impersonate learning.

Training set   ≈ 70%  → teaches the model
Validation set ≈ 15%  → tunes choices during development
Test set       ≈ 15%  → final, untouched exam

Keep the final exam separate: the test examples must not be used to teach or tune the model. Otherwise the final score no longer shows how well the model handles genuinely unseen data.

ACADEMIC PRECISION

Why scaling is useful
What it prevents

A feature measured in thousands can dominate numerical updates even when it is not more meaningful.

What it does not mean

Scaling does not automatically decide which feature matters. The network still learns weights from the data.

stages.title: A network is layers of tiny calculators
stages.text:
STAGE 04
A network is layers of tiny calculators

The input layer receives study, sleep, and attendance. Each hidden neuron receives its own weighted mixture of those inputs. Across training, different mixtures become sensitive to different combinations—perhaps high study with low sleep, or strong attendance with moderate study. These are emergent feature detectors: useful sensitivities discovered from data, not roles assigned to neurons by a person.

Student pass/fail architecture: 3 → 8 → 4 → 1
3 inputs → hidden patterns → 1 pass-score neuron
WHAT YOU CHOOSE
Design decisions before training
How many hidden layers
How many neurons per layer
Hidden and output activations
Optimizer and learning rate
WHAT THE MODEL LEARNS
Parameters discovered from examples
Every connection weight
Every neuron bias
Useful internal sensitivities
Representations that reduce loss
?

Why not something simpler? A linear model may be enough when one straight boundary captures the pattern. Hidden layers are justified only when interactions and reusable intermediate patterns improve performance on new data.

The visual begins with the skeleton you designed, then animates the connection strengths that training learns. A larger network is not automatically better: more depth and width need more data, computation, and protection against overfitting.

stages.title: One feature has a different weight into every hidden neuron
stages.text:
STAGE 05
One feature has a different weight into every hidden neuron

There is not one universal “sleep weight.” Sleep connects to every neuron in the next layer, and each connection learns a separate value. One neuron may respond strongly to sleep, another weakly, and another negatively because it combines sleep with different evidence.

CONNECTION EXPLORER

Choose an input to reveal its four independently learned connections.

Study
Sleep
Attendance
hidden neuron j score = study × wstudy,j + sleep × wsleep,j + attendance × wattendance,j + biasj
w

What: weights control sensitivity and biases shift activation. How: training changes all of them to reduce loss. Why: separate weights let neurons specialize in different combinations. Why not assign roles? Human labels would constrain the model before the data reveals which combinations are useful.

Interpretability note: you can inspect every weight, but raw numbers rarely translate into one clean human rule. A neuron usually participates in a distributed pattern with many other neurons.

stages.title: Non-linearity lets stacked layers learn bends
stages.text:
STAGE 06
Non-linearity lets stacked layers learn bends

First ask why an activation is needed. If every layer performs only a linear weighted sum, stacking ten layers still collapses into one linear transformation. The network gains more arithmetic, but not a more flexible decision boundary.

inputs → weighted sum + bias → raw score → activation function → output signal
BOUNDARY EXPERIMENT
Linear only
ReLU on

Use the buttons to focus either path; both remain visible for a direct comparison. Hidden layers use ReLU by default here. The output activation changes with the task:

Binary sigmoid
Multiclass softmax
Regression linear
↳

ReLU is a learned-pattern gate. A positive raw score passes as evidence that one learned pattern is present; zero means that neuron does not pass evidence for that pattern. It is misleading to say the network simply “throws away negative information”: other neurons—with different weights and biases—can represent opposing or complementary evidence.

Hidden layers: ReLU

ReLU(2.5) = 2.5 passes positive evidence; ReLU(-3) = 0 gates that detector off.

Binary output: sigmoid

One raw output becomes a score from 0 to 1, such as a pass score of 0.82.

Multiclass output: softmax

Several class scores are converted together into probabilities that total 100%.

Regression output: linear

The output remains a direct number because a probability constraint would be inappropriate.

Design decision: humans choose activations before training. Training learns the weights and biases that determine which patterns produce positive or non-positive raw scores.

stages.title: Forward propagation makes one pass-score prediction
stages.text:
STAGE 07
Forward propagation makes one pass-score prediction

Forward propagation means information moves from the three inputs, through every hidden layer, to the single output neuron used by this binary task.

study + sleep + attendance
→ hidden-layer calculations and ReLU activations
→ one raw output score
→ sigmoid
→ pass score between 0 and 1

For one student, the output neuron might produce 0.82. We read that as an 82% model score for “pass.” The corresponding fail score is 1 − 0.82 = 0.18.

The output neuron does not yet make the final Pass/Fail decision. Stage 14 will apply a separate decision threshold, such as 0.50, to turn this continuous score into a class label.

stages.title: Loss measures how wrong the prediction was
stages.text:
STAGE 08
Loss measures how wrong the prediction was

A loss function converts prediction error into a number. Smaller loss is better. Larger loss tells the training process that the current weights need more correction.

Regression

When predicting a number, mean squared error is common. It squares mistakes, so large errors receive extra punishment.

Classification

When predicting a class, cross-entropy loss is common. It strongly penalizes a model that is confidently wrong.

!

Loss is the teacher's marking pen. It does not merely say “wrong.” It gives the optimizer a numerical signal showing how much improvement is needed.

DO NOT CONFUSE THESE

Loss versus metric
Loss

The quantity optimized during training. It guides weight updates.

Metric

A human-readable measure such as accuracy, precision, recall, MAE, or RMSE.

stages.title: Backpropagation computes gradients—only gradients
stages.text:
STAGE 09
Backpropagation computes gradients—only gradients

A gradient is a collection of slopes: for each weight, it answers “if this weight increased a tiny amount, how would the loss change?” The sign gives a direction and the magnitude describes local sensitivity.

forward pass → prediction
prediction + truth → loss
backpropagation → gradient for every weight and bias
weights are still unchanged

Backpropagation applies the chain rule from the loss backward through the network. It calculates how local changes connect to the final error. It does not choose a learning rate and it never updates a parameter.

Plain distinction: backprop computes gradients only. The optimizer later uses those gradients to update weights.

stages.title: The optimizer takes iterative, local steps
stages.text:
STAGE 10
The optimizer takes iterative, local steps

Gradient descent applies the update. It combines the local gradient with a learning rate: next weight = current weight − learning rate × gradient. Because the gradient describes only the slope near the current point, optimization must repeat rather than jump directly to the answer.

WATCH IT WALK DOWNHILL
Tiny steps
Medium steps
Too large
Pause

Small steps need many updates. Medium steps descend efficiently. Large steps can overshoot and bounce away. Drag the current point on the curve to inspect a different local slope.

∇

What: a gradient is local slope. Why: it tells the optimizer which nearby direction lowers loss. How: multiply it by the learning rate and update. Why not one giant step? the landscape bends, and the local slope does not reveal the whole terrain.

Why local does not guarantee global

controls.label: Why local does not guarantee globalA low point reached from the current start may be a local minimum, while a lower global minimum exists el

stages.title: One update has a strict causal order
stages.text:
STAGE 11
One update has a strict causal order

The model usually learns from a small batch. Each update follows the same sequence; confusing these steps hides what actually causes learning.

1. take data
2. forward pass makes predictions
3. loss measures error
4. backpropagation computes gradients
5. optimizer applies parameter updates
6. updated weights change the next prediction
7. repeat
Batch
EXAMPLES PER UPDATE
Iteration
ONE UPDATE STEP
Epoch
ONE FULL PASS THROUGH TRAINING DATA
1,000 examples ÷ batch size 100 = 10 iterations per epoch
↻

The forward pass supplies a prediction; loss supplies an objective; backprop supplies gradients; the optimizer supplies the update. Repetition turns many local corrections into learned behavior.

stages.title: Choose the model before validation gets worse
stages.text:
STAGE 12
Choose the model before validation gets worse

Training loss can keep falling while validation loss eventually rises. That is the causal signature of overfitting: the model is improving on examples it trains on while becoming less useful on unseen data. Keep the checkpoint near the lowest validation loss, not the final training step.

Local is not global: an optimizer follows nearby slopes and may settle in one valley even if a lower valley exists elsewhere. Validation asks a different question: whichever valley training reaches, does that model generalize?

!

Why can dependence be bad? A neuron might learn a brittle shortcut such as “attendance decides everything.” If later neurons rely heavily on that one pathway, the network may fail when the shortcut does not hold for new students.

REGULARIZATION CONTROL
Dropout rate during training: 20%

Decrease the rate and more hidden neurons stay active on the right. Increase it and more paths switch off, which can reduce shortcut dependence but may underfit; at 100%, this simplified visual switches off every hidden neuron.

During training

Different hidden neurons are temporarily switched off on different updates.

Validation and real use

Dropout is switched off, the full network is used, and the framework handles the required scaling.

Decrease dropout

More paths stay active, but the model may overfit by leaning on shortcuts.

Increase dropout

More paths switch off in the visual, spreading reliance until excessive dropout starts to underfit.

Keep this model: save the checkpoint at the validation minimum. Dropout is one possible regularizer, not an automatic requirement; its value depends on the architecture, data, and observed overfitting.

stages.title: Humans choose the architecture and hyperparameters
stages.text:
STAGE 13
Humans choose the architecture and hyperparameters

Parameters are learned by the model: every weight and bias. Hyperparameters are design decisions made before or around training.

DESIGN DECISIONS

Why each choice exists
Depth and width

Control representational capacity. Too little can underfit; too much can waste data and computation or overfit.

Activations

Add non-linearity and match output constraints. Hidden layers remain ReLU here.

Optimizer

Defines how gradients are converted into parameter updates.

Learning rate

Sets update scale: small is slow; large can overshoot.

OUTPUT-LAYER EXPLORER
Binary class
Multi-class
Regression
Binary classification

Hidden layers: ReLU. Output: one neuron with sigmoid.

Multi-class classification

Hidden layers: ReLU. Output: one score per class with softmax.

Regression

Hidden layers: ReLU. Output: usually one linear numerical value.

Feature engineering

Structured problems may improve when raw fields are turned into more useful clues, such as date of birth → age.

There is no universal “best” architecture. A design must match the task, data quantity, noise, complexity, and cost of mistakes.

stages.title: The test set evaluates both scores and decisions
stages.text:
STAGE 14
The test set evaluates both scores and decisions

After training and tuning are finished, the model is evaluated once on the untouched test set. For our binary task, sigmoid first produces a pass score. A separate classification decision threshold then converts that score into Pass or Fail.

model pass score = 0.72
decision threshold = 0.50
0.72 ≥ 0.50
prediction = Pass

This threshold is not the school’s exam passing mark. It is the model’s cutoff for turning a score between 0 and 1 into a predicted class.

DECISION CONTROL
Classification decision threshold: 0.50

Lowering the threshold predicts Pass more easily: recall usually rises, but false positives may increase. Raising it is stricter: false positives may fall, but more actual passes can be missed.

0.75
PRECISION
0.75
RECALL
0.75
F1-SCORE
	ACTUALLY PASSED	ACTUALLY FAILED
PREDICTED PASS	True positive: 3	False positive: 1
PREDICTED FAIL	False negative: 1	True negative: 3

Accuracy alone can mislead. Precision asks whether predicted passes were usually correct. Recall asks how many actual passes the model successfully found.

stages.title: Error analysis starts with individual students
stages.text:
STAGE 15
Error analysis starts with individual students

Overall scores hide which people are affected. Move the threshold, inspect the highlighted false positives and false negatives, and connect each case to the metric that represents its cost.

CASE-LEVEL THRESHOLD EXPLORER
Classification threshold: 0.50
Sort by score
Sort by distance to threshold

Noor, score 0.68, actually failed: at the starting 0.50 threshold this is a false positive. If wrongly predicting success is costly, prioritize precision.

Sam, score 0.43, actually passed: at the starting 0.50 threshold this is a false negative. If missing a student who would pass is costly, prioritize recall.

Ana, score 0.57, actually passed: at the starting threshold this is a borderline true positive that flips when the threshold rises past 0.57. F1 is useful when both false positives and false negatives matter and one balanced summary is needed.

FROM CASE TO ACTION

Threshold changes only the decision rule; it does not repair weak features, biased labels, or poor calibration. Inspect concrete errors, diagnose the cause, change the appropriate part, then evaluate again by relevant groups.

stages.title: Saving, deployment, and monitoring finish the lifecycle
stages.text:
STAGE 16
Saving, deployment, and monitoring finish the lifecycle

Once performance is acceptable, the final model is saved. The saved package includes the architecture, learned weights and biases, and often the preprocessing rules needed to reproduce training-time inputs.

new user input
→ same preprocessing used during training
→ saved model
→ prediction
→ application response

Deployment puts the model into a website, mobile app, server API, edge device, or business system. A model sitting in a notebook is an experiment, not a working service.

AFTER LAUNCH

Monitor accuracy, error types, input-data changes, speed, complaints, fairness, and security. When the world changes and performance falls, the model is experiencing drift.

stages.title: Different network families organize information differently
stages.text:
STAGE 17
Different network families organize information differently
Feedforward network

Information moves from input to hidden layers to output. This is the structure used throughout this lesson.

Convolutional network (CNN)

Common for images. Early layers notice edges; later layers combine them into shapes and object parts.

Recurrent network (RNN)

Designed for sequences and previous context, such as text, audio, and time series.

Transformer

Uses attention to connect relevant parts of data, allowing many relationships to be considered at once.

This layered transformation is called representation learning. Raw inputs become increasingly useful internal patterns: pixels → edges → shapes → objects, or word pieces → phrases → context.

Interpretability: weights are visible, but a representation is usually distributed across many parameters. Inspecting one large weight rarely yields a faithful human rule; use case-level explanations, sensitivity analyses, and validation evidence together.

Neural networks are powerful because they can learn complex representations. They are used for images, speech, text, translation, recommendations, medical scans, fraud detection, forecasting, game playing, and large language models. They are not magic: they still depend on good data, sensible design, testing, monitoring, and human judgment.

stages.title: Try the tiny student-pass network
stages.text:
STAGE 18
Try the tiny student-pass network

Move the inputs and watch the same network update. This is an illustrative toy, not a trained admissions or education model.

Study hours: 6
Sleep hours: 7
Attendance: 75%
0.77
TOY PASS SCORE
Pass
AT CURRENT THRESHOLD
High
DISTANCE FROM THRESHOLD

A score is not a guarantee and does not explain causation. This toy only demonstrates how changed inputs can flow through a fixed set of weights.

stages.title: One full training cycle
stages.text:
FINAL SYNTHESIS
One full training cycle
THE CAUSAL CHAIN
You choose the architecture, activations, optimizer, and learning rate.
Data enters and a forward pass produces predictions.
Loss converts prediction error into an objective.
Backpropagation computes gradients only.
The optimizer updates every weight and bias.
Updated parameters change the next forward pass.
Validation identifies the checkpoint that generalizes best.
Testing, deployment, monitoring, and error analysis keep the model accountable after training.
data → forward pass → loss → backprop gradients
→ optimizer step → updated weights → repeat
↻

What: a parameterized function. Why: to learn patterns too complex to specify cleanly. How: repeated local updates reduce loss. Why not something simpler? use a simpler model whenever it generalizes well enough and is easier to maintain or explain.

Final check

Which dataset should stay untouched until training and tuning are complete?

Training set
Validation set
Test set
