stages.title: What problem is One-R solving?
stages.text:
STAGE 01 · OBSERVE
What problem is One-R solving?

Classification predicts a category, such as Yes or No. A feature is an input column. The target is the category we want to predict.

Our teaching sample records 14 days. Each row contains outlook, humidity, wind, temperature, and whether someone carried an umbrella.

THE CENTRAL QUESTION

“If I may inspect only one column, which column should I choose, and what should I predict for each of its values?”

14 rows
4 candidate features
Yes target
No target

stages.title: First, make the lazy prediction.
stages.text:
STAGE 02 · BASELINE
First, make the lazy prediction.

Before building a model, count the target classes. There are 8 Yes rows and 6 No rows, so the majority classifier predicts Yes for every case.

majority accuracy = largest class count ÷ all rows
8 ÷ 14 = 57.1%

This baseline is intentionally dull. That is its job. A new classifier that cannot beat it has not earned its electricity.

Class imbalance warning. If 95% of rows are No, always predicting No scores 95% accuracy while learning nothing about Yes. Accuracy needs company.

If a dataset has 70 Yes rows and 30 No rows, what does the majority classifier predict?

Yes for every row, producing 70% training accuracy.

stages.title: Make a rule from one categorical feature.
stages.text:
STAGE 03 · BUILD
Make a rule from one categorical feature.

Choose a candidate feature, such as Outlook. Handle each distinct value separately and predict its local majority class.

1
Collect all rows where Outlook is Sunny.
2
Count Yes and No among those rows.
3
Use the local majority as the prediction for Sunny.
4
Repeat for Cloudy and Rainy.
EXAMPLE RULEBOOK
IF Outlook = Sunny THEN Umbrella = No
IF Outlook = Cloudy THEN Umbrella = Yes
IF Outlook = Rainy THEN Umbrella = Yes
error for a feature value = rows that disagree with that value’s majority class

stages.title: Test every feature. Keep the lowest-error rule.
stages.text:
STAGE 04 · COMPARE
Test every feature. Keep the lowest-error rule.

One-R repeats the same construction for every candidate feature. Each feature gets a rulebook and a total error count.

FEATURE	TRAINING ERRORS	ERROR RATE	RESULT
Outlook	3 / 14	21.4%	Selected
Humidity	4 / 14	28.6%	Runner-up
Wind	5 / 14	35.7%	Rejected
Temperature*	5 / 14	35.7%	After buckets
selected feature = arg min(feature training errors)
Inspect a rulebook
Outlook
Humidity
Wind
Ties are allowed. Declare a policy in advance: prefer fewer values, use a fixed feature order, or choose the winner under cross-validation. Do not improvise after seeing the result.

*Temperature uses the fixed teaching intervals introduced next. Exact bucketing procedures vary by implementation.

stages.title: Turn numeric values into intervals.
stages.text:
STAGE 05 · PREPARE
Turn numeric values into intervals.

A rule for every exact temperature would memorise the training sample and fail on a new value such as 23.6°C. One-R therefore discretises numeric values into intervals.

1
Sort rows by the numeric feature.
2
Group neighbouring values into sufficiently reliable buckets.
3
Assign each bucket its majority class.
4
Merge or adjust unstable neighbours according to the chosen implementation.
ONE POSSIBLE TRAINING-ONLY DISCRETISATION
Temperature ≤ 22.5 → Yes
22.5 < Temperature ≤ 27.5 → Yes
Temperature > 27.5 → No
Exact values
Stable intervals
Leakage alert. Fit cut-points using training data only. Choosing intervals after inspecting test labels is answer-shopping in a lab coat.

stages.title: Missing values and unseen categories are part of the model.
stages.text:
STAGE 06 · SAFEGUARD
Missing values and unseen categories are part of the model.

Real inputs are rarely as cooperative as textbook tables. Decide what happens when the selected feature is missing, a category never appeared during training, classes tie, or a number falls outside the observed range.

?
MISSING INPUT
New
UNSEEN CATEGORY
4–4
LOCAL TIE
REASONABLE FALLBACK

Use the overall training-set majority class or estimated class prior. Another option is to learn “Missing” as its own category when enough training rows contain missing values.

The fitted rule uses Outlook, but a future row has Outlook = “Hazy”. What happens?

Use the declared fallback. Do not invent a rule from the test row.

stages.title: Prediction is deliberately cheap.
stages.text:
STAGE 07 · PREDICT
Prediction is deliberately cheap.

Read the selected feature, find its stored value or interval, return the class, and use the fallback if nothing matches.

Outlook
Sunny
Cloudy
Rainy
Hazy
Humidity
Low
High
Wind
Calm
Breezy
Strong
Run the one-rule prediction
Prediction: Outlook = Cloudy → Umbrella = Yes. Humidity and wind are ignored because Outlook won training selection.

The model is saying Outlook is the strongest standalone predictor in this sample. It is not saying the other features have no relationship with umbrella use.

stages.title: One feature cannot express an interaction.
stages.text:
STAGE 08 · UNDERSTAND
One feature cannot express an interaction.

Suppose people carry umbrellas only when it is both cloudy and very humid. Neither feature alone may be strongly predictive, but their combination is.

useful pattern: Outlook = Cloudy AND Humidity = High
1
FEATURE USED
0
INTERACTIONS
INSPECTABILITY
ONE-R SEES

One column and one lookup table.

ONE-R MISSES

Interactions, gradual multi-feature effects, and alternative routes to the same class.

Interpretability is not innocence. A selected feature may be a proxy, unfair, operationally inappropriate, or merely associated rather than causal.

stages.title: Validate the whole learning process
stages.text:
STAGE 09 · EVALUATE
Validate the whole learning process

Don’t judge the model only on the final prediction. Any choice the model makes—like selecting the best feature or building rules—must be done inside the training fold, then checked on data it has not seen.

1
Split the data into folds
2
Use the training fold to learn
Build buckets, test candidate rules, and choose the best option here.
3
Freeze the rule
Stop changing it. No more label peeking.
4
Test on the held-out fold
Predict unseen rows and record the error.
5
Repeat and average
Run this across all folds, then average the results.
Grouped data: If several rows belong to the same person, device, or organisation, keep the whole group in one fold. Otherwise the model may recognise the group instead of learning a pattern that generalizes.

stages.title: Evaluate each fold. Decide what to do next.
stages.text:
STAGE 10 · MEASURE
Evaluate each fold. Decide what to do next.

Cross-validation gives multiple views of performance. Use the right metric for your goal, check stability across folds, and decide whether to proceed, tune, or collect more data.

1
CHOOSE THE RIGHT METRIC

Pick the metric that matches the problem and the cost of mistakes.

Overall
Precision
Recall
Overall accuracy

Focus when classes are balanced and both types of errors matter similarly.

Best for: General performance check, balanced datasets.

Precision

Focus when false positives are costly (predicting Yes when it’s actually No).

Best for: Spam detection, fraud alerts, medical testing.

Recall

Focus when false negatives are costly (missing actual Yes cases).

Best for: Disease screening, churn prevention, safety monitoring.

2
MEASURE STABILITY ACROSS FOLDS

Compute the chosen metric for each fold. Then summarize the stability.

FOLD-SCORE DISTRIBUTION

Report individual fold scores and, when useful, repeat cross-validation with different splits.

fold_scores = scores
mean = scores.mean()
sd = scores.std(ddof=1)
range_ = (scores.min(), scores.max())

Fold scores share overlapping training data; their spread is not a confidence interval for generalisation performance.

REPORT ALL THREE (RECOMMENDED)

Always look at these together for the full picture.

Mean (μ): average performance across folds
Sample SD: spread of performance
Score distribution: individual fold or repeated-CV scores

Also check the min–max range across folds.

3
INTERPRET STABILITY IN CONTEXT

There are no universal percentage bands or automatic proceed/stop rules. Consider dataset size, class balance, the metric, domain, and the impact of errors.

REPORT	INTERPRETATION	WHAT IT MEANS
Fold scores	Distribution	Inspect the full spread, including unusually low scores.
Mean	Average	Compare with a relevant baseline on the same splits.
SD and range	Spread	Judge variation against the metric and consequences of errors.
Repeated CV	Split sensitivity	Report scores across repeats; investigate changes across splits.
Intervals	Uncertainty	State the method and account for dependence between CV scores.
Read together: Mean, SD, range, and the score distribution describe these splits. Consistency alone does not establish useful performance or justify deployment.

stages.title: Use simple models as diagnostic instruments.
stages.text:
STAGE 11 · REFLECT
Use simple models as diagnostic instruments.
MODEL	USES	TYPICAL PURPOSE
Majority	No features	Absolute minimum baseline
One-R	One feature, many value rules	Transparent signal baseline
Decision stump	One tree split	Single partition baseline
Full tree	Sequential splits	Interactions and complexity

One-R and a decision stump are related, but not identical. Categorical One-R can assign a separate class to every value of one feature; a stump is usually described as one split with leaf predictions.

Suspiciously strong simplicity. If One-R nearly matches a complex model, one feature may dominate the task, or the evaluation may contain leakage. Investigate both before celebrating.
USEFUL WHEN
interpretable benchmark
small data
cheap deployment
strongest standalone feature
WEAK WHEN
interactions matter
signals must combine
feature drift
unequal error costs

stages.title: Build the rule, then explain what it means.
stages.text:
STAGE 12 · PRACTICE
Build the rule, then explain what it means.

Choose a candidate feature and a new case. The visual updates the value-level rulebook, training error, and prediction. The point is not merely to obtain a label, but to explain exactly how that label appeared.

Candidate feature
Outlook
Humidity
Wind
New value
Sunny
Cloudy
Rainy
Apply this rulebook
3
TRAINING ERRORS
3
VALUE RULES
No
NEW PREDICTION

One-R selected Outlook. Humidity also relates strongly to the target. Is “humidity is useless” the correct conclusion?

No. Outlook produced the best single-feature rule under this procedure. Humidity may still add useful information in a multi-feature model.

KEY TAKEAWAYS

One-R creates a majority-class rule for every value or interval of each candidate feature.

It selects the lowest training error, but performance belongs on held-out data.

Numeric buckets, fallbacks, ties, and missing values are fitted-model decisions.

Its value is transparent baseline reasoning, not pretending one feature explains the universe.

stages.title: The Unsupervised Explorer
stages.text:
STAGE 01 · OBSERVE
The Unsupervised Explorer
BEFORE YOU START

PCA is unsupervised: it uses the predictors without consulting an outcome label. It preserves variance, not necessarily predictive usefulness.

In traditional "supervised" machine learning, we act like students with an answer key. We know what we want to predict (e.g., house prices) and use features to find the answer.

Principal Components Analysis (PCA) belongs to unsupervised learning. Here, we are explorers. There is no answer key. We are handed a messy box of variables and asked to find the hidden structure.

Imagine measuring students on a full performance sheet instead of only two numbers:

Speed (m/s)
Strength (kg)
Endurance (min)
Agility (score)
Balance (score)
Jump (cm)

60 rows x 6 columns

The canvas will still use a 2D Speed-vs-Strength slice to build intuition, but the loadings, scores, and scree plot later on will come from the full generated dataset.

stages.title: The "Too Much Information" Problem
stages.text:
STAGE 02 · UNDERSTAND
The "Too Much Information" Problem

Why can't we just look at the variables one by one?

Because dimensionality explodes fast. With 6 variables you already have 15 pairwise plots, and with 10 variables you jump to 45. No single view tells the whole story.

If we only look at Speed (squashing the data to the horizontal axis), we lose all information about strength. The points overlap and hide the true shape of our students.

If we only look at Strength (vertical axis), we lose speed. Neither axis alone captures the main "soul" of the dataset, because athletic students tend to be both fast and strong.

When variables are correlated (moving together), keeping them separate is redundant. We need a way to combine them.

stages.title: Finding the First Principal Component
stages.text:
STAGE 03 · BUILD
Finding the First Principal Component

PCA looks for a brand new direction—a line sliced straight through the cloud of data.

It rotates this line until the data points, when projected onto the line, spread out as much as possible.

1.88
CURRENT SPREAD (VARIANCE)

The direction that creates the largest spread is called Principal Component 1 (PC1). By maximizing the spread, this line stays closest to the entire data cloud, giving us the clearest single summary.

stages.title: The Secret Sauce: Loadings
stages.text:
STAGE 04 · BUILD
The Secret Sauce: Loadings

How does PCA actually draw this line? It acts like a "dimmer knob", mixing the original variables together using weights.

These weights are called Loadings. They tell us how much each original variable contributes to the new component.

PC1 Score =
+0.49 x Speed
+0.43 x Strength
+0.33 x Endurance
+0.44 x Agility
+0.32 x Balance
+0.42 x Jump

For this generated dataset, the PC1 loadings are computed directly from the same PCA fit used for the scores and scree plot:

Speed
+0.49
Strength
+0.43
Endurance
+0.33
Agility
+0.44
Balance
+0.32
Jump
+0.42

All of these weights come from the same standardized PCA fit. Speed contributes most strongly here, but PC1 stays broad because several columns are moving together.

stages.title: When Scaling Is Appropriate
stages.text:
STAGE 05 · PREPARE
When Scaling Is Appropriate

There is a massive trap in PCA. Because it hunts for maximum variance, it can be bullied by units.

Even in this generated dataset, Strength naturally varies much more than Speed in raw units. Without scaling, PCA leans toward the higher-variance column; after Standardization, both columns get a fair vote.

Step 1: Mean (μ) = Average of column
Step 2: Center = X - μ
Step 3: Variance (σ²) = Average of (X - μ)²
Step 4: Std Dev (σ) = √Variance

Step 5: Scaled (Z) = (X - μ) / σ

Result: After scaling, every variable has a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. Units disappear, and no single variable dominates just because it has bigger raw numbers.

Scaling is a modelling choice, not a universal rule. It is normally appropriate for variables in unlike units—such as height in centimetres and income in dollars—or when raw scale should not determine the components. If measurements share the same units and their variance differences are scientifically meaningful, scaling may be undesirable. Fit the scaler on training data only.

1.18 / 11.79
RAW STD DEVS (SPEED / STRENGTH)
1.00 / 1.00
AFTER STANDARDIZATION

stages.title: Capturing the Leftovers: PC2
stages.text:
STAGE 06 · UNDERSTAND
Capturing the Leftovers: PC2

PC1 captured the main trend (overall athleticism). But there is still some "thickness" left over in the cloud.

To capture this, PCA finds a Second Principal Component (PC2). It follows the exact same logic, but with one non-negotiable rule:

It must be exactly 90 degrees (perpendicular) to PC1.

Because it is perpendicular, PC2 is completely uncorrelated with PC1. It captures the contrasts—for example, students who are stronger than expected for their speed.

stages.title: The Transformation (Scores)
stages.text:
STAGE 07 · BUILD
The Transformation (Scores)

Here is where the magic happens. We don't just draw lines on the old graph. We rotate the entire coordinate system.

PCA finds the directions that capture the greatest sample variance. These directions are not automatically the most scientifically important or most predictive.

Original matrix: 60 x 6
PCA scores kept here: 60 x 2

The same observations are represented in a new coordinate system. When all principal components are retained, the centred data can be reconstructed up to numerical precision. When components are discarded, some sample variance and potentially useful information are lost. A few rows from the original matrix become PC scores side by side:

stages.title: Proportion of Variance Explained
stages.text:
STAGE 08 · UNDERSTAND
Proportion of Variance Explained

How do we know if our components are actually useful? We look at the Proportion of Variance Explained (PVE) using a Scree Plot.

Think of the total sample variance as a pizza. PC1 takes the biggest slice and PC2 takes the next. The cumulative line approaches 100% of sample variance—not 100% of general information, scientific importance, or predictive signal.

60%
PC1 VARIANCE
89%
CUMULATIVE (PC1+PC2)

Look for the "Elbow" in the plot. In datasets with 100 columns, you might find that just 2 or 3 components explain 95% of the variance. That's the "Magic Shrink Ray" at work.

PCA is unsupervised and ignores the target. A low-variance component may still contain important predictive or scientific information. Discarding low-variance components reduces noise only when noise mainly occupies those directions; this is not guaranteed.

stages.title: Interactive Playground
stages.text:
STAGE 09 · EXPLORE
Interactive Playground

Now you are the algorithm. Use the slider to rotate the projection line through the original data space.

Watch how the spread (variance) changes based on the angle. Your goal is to find the angle that maximizes the variance.

Projection Angle
45°
1.88
PC1 VARIANCE
0.12
PC2 LEFTOVER VARIANCE

PC2 is locked to stay 90° from PC1, so it always shows the next-biggest leftover spread instead of being chosen freely.

The angle with the highest variance is exactly where the math places Principal Component 1.

stages.title: The Best Summary
stages.text:
STAGE 10 · REFLECT
The Best Summary

PCA represents centred observations along directions of greatest sample variance. Those directions need not be the most scientifically meaningful or predictive.

PCA may reduce noise when discarded directions mainly contain noise, but this is not guaranteed. Low-variance components can still contain meaningful structure or predictive signal.

Remember:

Decide whether scaling is appropriate based on the variables’ units and whether raw variance differences should influence the components.
Loadings are the weights.
Scores are the new coordinates.
Stop when the "pizza slices" of variance get too small.
COMPLETE THE PICTURE
Avoid preprocessing leakage

In a predictive pipeline, estimate means, standard deviations, and principal components using the training data only. Then apply those learned transformations to validation and test data.

The sign of a principal component is arbitrary: multiplying all loadings and scores by −1 describes the same component. Interpret relative direction and magnitude rather than treating the sign as sacred scripture.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
PCA rotates the feature space into uncorrelated directions ordered by variance.
Loadings describe directions; scores are observations expressed in the new coordinates.
Scale features when appropriate and fit PCA inside the training pipeline.

Practical method checklist

Before you finish
Assumptions

Numeric features, meaningful covariance geometry, and a justified scaling choice.

When the method fails

Target signal in low-variance directions, outliers, drift, or uninterpretable components.

Validation and leakage

Fit scaling and PCA inside training folds only.

Interpretation cautions

Explained variance is not general information or predictive usefulness.

What to report

Scaling decision, loadings, explained sample variance, components retained, and stability.

stages.title: Inspect the Raw Data
stages.text:
STAGE 01 · OBSERVE
Inspect the Raw Data
BEFORE YOU START

Polynomial regression is still linear in its coefficients. The curve appears because the model includes transformed features such as x² and x³.

WHAT WE DO
Plot the raw input against the response.
WHY WE DO IT
To visually check the shape. A straight line will naturally fail to capture a curved dataset.
WHAT THIS MEANS
If the data forms a hill, a valley, or an S-curve, simple math won't be enough.

Let's see what happens if we force a straight line anyway.

Look at the black dots on the chart. Notice how they structurally form a curved shape rather than a straight path.

stages.title: Fit a Straight Line
stages.text:
STAGE 02 · BUILD
Fit a Straight Line
WHAT WE DO
Fit a basic, flat or sloped straight line.
WHY WE DO IT
To set a baseline and prove that standard linear regression fails on curves.
WHAT THIS MEANS
The line completely ignores the true shape of our data. This failure is called underfitting.

We need to give the math the flexibility to bend.

See the rigid blue line on the chart and the simple equation in the dashboard.

stages.title: Expand the Features
stages.text:
STAGE 03 · UNDERSTAND
Expand the Features
WHAT WE DO
Create new columns by squaring and cubing the input data.
WHY WE DO IT
Adding powers of the input gives the underlying formula the ability to curve.
WHAT THIS MEANS
First, we shrink the input numbers so squaring them doesn't create huge, unstable values. Then we build our Design Matrix.

Now the model has more ingredients to build with.

Check the Design Matrix overlay. The model now sees the squared input as just another normal feature to learn from.

stages.title: Fit the Weights
stages.text:
STAGE 04 · BUILD
Fit the Weights
WHAT WE DO
The algorithm calculates the best weights for each column in our matrix.
WHY WE DO IT
To find the exact mathematical combination that fits the dots.
WHAT THIS MEANS
The weights act like knobs that tell the curve how strongly to bend and in what direction.

Let's check how close our curve actually gets to the data.

Look at the Weights overlay and the new equation in the dashboard. The curve now gracefully follows the data points.

stages.title: Compute Errors
stages.text:
STAGE 05 · BUILD
Compute Errors
WHAT WE DO
Measure the vertical distance between the true dots and our curve.
WHY WE DO IT
To see exactly where the model is still wrong.
WHAT THIS MEANS
Small random misses are normal, but a clear pattern in the misses means the model is still failing.

Let's see what happens if we add too many curves.

See the dashed red lines and the Residual Plot. The Train MSE above scores how well the model fits the data it saw.

stages.title: Check for Overfitting
stages.text:
STAGE 06 · BUILD
Check for Overfitting
WHAT WE DO
Push the model to extreme complexity and test it on hidden data.
WHY WE DO IT
To catch overfitting before we use the model in the real world.
WHAT THIS MEANS
Training error can look amazing while validation error gets much worse, which is the warning sign of overfitting.

We need to find the balance between too simple and too complex.

Look at the validation curve. Training error drops, but validation error rises. The gold dots are validation observations used to choose degree; the final test set remains untouched.

stages.title: Find the Sweet Spot
stages.text:
STAGE 07 · REFLECT
Find the Sweet Spot
WHAT WE DO
Compare candidate complexities using validation or cross-validation error.
WHY WE DO IT
The best shape changes depending on the data.
WHAT THIS MEANS
We want the simplest curve that generalizes well to new situations.

Play with the controls until you find the perfect balance.

Change the dataset shape, then use the slider to explore. Find the simplest near-best point on the validation curve before validation error rises.
Candidate Degree
2
Show Point Residuals
Regenerate Noise Split

stages.title: Lock in the Model
stages.text:
STAGE 08 · REFLECT
Lock in the Model
WHAT WE DO
Select the final model and lock in the formula.
WHY WE DO IT
We only deploy a model after validation proves it works.
WHAT THIS MEANS
We choose the simplest model that performs almost as well as the absolute best one.

This final equation is now ready for the real world.

Review the Model Deployed card below the chart for your final, validated results.

Final workflow: fit candidate degrees on training data, choose the degree by validation or cross-validation error, lock the basis and preprocessing, refit using the chosen setup, and evaluate once on the untouched test set. Inspect residual form, unequal variance and influential points. High-degree polynomials can oscillate near boundaries and are especially unsafe for extrapolation; centring and scaling polynomial features often improve numerical stability and make regularisation penalties more comparable, but are not mathematically required. Orthogonal bases can also improve numerical stability.

COMPLETE THE PICTURE
Respect hierarchy and avoid wild extrapolation

If a model includes x³, normally retain x and x² as well. This hierarchy principle keeps the model interpretable and stable.

Polynomial curves can behave wildly outside the observed range. Use them mainly for interpolation, centre or scale X when helpful, and validate the degree using held-out data or cross-validation.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
Higher degree increases flexibility but also variance.
Select the degree using validation performance, not training error alone.
Polynomial predictions beyond the observed range can become implausible very quickly.

Practical method checklist

Before you finish
Assumptions

Correct functional family and observations that support the fitted range.

When the method fails

Boundary oscillation, high-degree instability, influence, and extrapolation.

Validation and leakage

Select degree by validation or cross-validation; use test data once.

Interpretation cautions

Nonlinear in x does not mean nonlinear in coefficients.

What to report

Degree-selection procedure, scaling or basis, uncertainty, and final test result.

stages.title: The problem
stages.text:
STAGE 01

The problem
Observed statistics vary from sample to sample. Probability provides a language for that uncertainty and sampling distributions describe how an estimator behaves under repeated study designs.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.text:
STAGE 02

Intuition and objective
Conditional probability P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B), for P(B) > 0, means the chance of A given B. Independence means P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B): knowing one event occurred does not change the chance of the other. Expectation E[X] is the probability-weighted average of a random variable; variance Var(X) = E[(X − E[X])²] measures its spread, when these quantities exist. A population distribution describes individual values. A sampling distribution describes a statistic—such as a mean—across repeated samples. Its standard deviation is the standard error.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.text:
STAGE 03

Worked example
If individual scores have standard deviation 12, the mean of n=36 independent observations has standard error about 12/√36=2. Doubling n does not halve uncertainty; roughly quadrupling n does.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.text:
STAGE 04

Reasoning with the method

Discrete probability masses add directly, whereas continuous density integrates to probability over an interval. Density height is not itself point probability and may exceed one. A statistic is a random variable before data are observed, and its sampling distribution depends on the population, statistic and design. The central limit theorem supports many normal approximations but does not make every small or heavy-tailed sample normal. Standard deviation describes individual variation; standard error describes estimator variation. Clustering, unequal weights and finite-population sampling change the familiar independent-sample formula and the effective amount of information.

A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.text:
STAGE 06

Assumptions and failure modes
Assumptions

Repeated-sampling claims presume the same population and design. The usual √n improvement requires independent or appropriately modelled observations.

When the method fails

Density height is not point probability; dependence reduces effective sample size; skew and heavy tails can slow normal approximations; convenience samples do not become representative by growing.

stages.title: Practical workflow
stages.text:
STAGE 07

Practical workflow
Define population and random variable
Identify discrete or continuous support
Specify the sampling design
Choose a statistic
Study or approximate its sampling distribution
Quantify standard error

stages.text:
STAGE 08

Interpretation and reporting

What to report: Name the population, sample mechanism, statistic, sample size, dependence structure, estimated standard error and approximation used.

Common misuse: Confusing the spread of individual observations with the uncertainty of their mean.

STAGE 01 · OBSERVE
The Raw Data Cloud
BEFORE YOU START

QDA extends LDA by estimating a separate covariance matrix for each class. That extra freedom requires more data.

Imagine sorting fruit into APPLES and PEARS based on two measurements: Sweetness (

In generative modeling, we look at where each class cluster sits and how the points are distributed across the features.

The Whole Idea of QDA

Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA) is a supervised classification method. It models each class as its own independent multi-dimensional probability cloud.

Simple intuition: QDA asks: "Which of these distinct class clouds does this new coordinate fit into best?"

Unlike LDA (which forces every class to share the exact same shape), QDA allows each class to have its own unique spread, stretch, and tilt. This mathematical flexibility is what creates curved boundaries.

QDA Pipeline: Labeled data → Split Train/Test → Fit class-specific shapes → Score new test coordinates → Make prediction → Evaluate performance

stages.text:
STAGE 02 · PREPARE
Train / Test Split

To perform proper Machine Learning, we cannot estimate our model and test its performance on the same data points. This is known as Data Leakage.

The Rules of the Split:

Training Set (80%): Used exclusively to calculate Class Priors, Means, and Covariance Matrices.
Test Set (20%): Hidden away completely during the learning phase. Used only for final model evaluation.
Warning: Including testing data in your mean or covariance calculations will falsely inflate performance metrics, making you think your model generalizes better than it actually does!

stages.title: Testing with Shape-Aware Distance
stages.text:
STAGE 05 · BUILD
Testing with Shape-Aware Distance

Euclidean distance only measures straight-line distance. It assumes classes are perfect, un-tilted circles.

QDA uses Mahalanobis Distance, which measures distance in units of class-specific standard deviations, aligning with the class's natural stretch and tilt.

Try it: Tap and drag on the canvas to reposition the test probe. Look at the contour lines of equal distance wrapping around each class mean.

The posteriors are calculated assuming the features are strictly normally (Gaussian) distributed. If your real-world data is heavily skewed or multimodal, the model's confidence scores will be poorly calibrated!

When QDA Thrives:

 Classes have completely different shapes and orientations.

When QDA Struggles:

 Extremely small datasets (leads to overfitting and singular matrices).
 Datasets with many features (parameter explosion).

Alternatives to QDA:

 LDA: If dataset is small or class spreads are similar.
 Logistic Regression: If you prefer to model class boundaries without making Gaussian distribution assumptions.

COMPLETE THE PICTURE
When full QDA is too unstable

Separate covariance matrices contain many parameters. With few observations or many features, estimates can become unstable or singular.

Regularised discriminant analysis provides a continuum between LDA and QDA by shrinking class covariance estimates toward a shared structure. Cross-validation should choose the amount of flexibility.

QDA uses class-specific covariance matrices and can form curved boundaries.
Its flexibility can outperform LDA when class shapes genuinely differ.
That flexibility costs data and may require regularisation.

stages.title: The problem
stages.text:
STAGE 01

The problem
A single tree is interpretable but unstable. Random forests average many deliberately varied trees so individual split noise cancels while shared predictive structure remains.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.text:
STAGE 02

Intuition and objective
Each tree sees a bootstrap sample and a random subset of candidate features at each split. Averaging mainly reduces variance when trees make partly independent errors.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.text:
STAGE 03

Worked example
One tree classifies 82% of validation cases, but across resamples it ranges from 74% to 87%. A 300-tree forest reaches 86% with a much narrower range. The gain comes from averaging; 300 trees are not 300 independent datasets.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.text:
STAGE 04

Reasoning with the method

Bootstrap samples vary observations and random feature subsets vary candidate splits. Diversity matters because averaging highly correlated trees removes less variance. Out-of-bag predictions provide a development estimate, but extensive optimisation against that estimate still needs outer evaluation. More trees reduce Monte Carlo noise; they do not cure leakage, biased sampling or drift. Permutation importance measures predictive reliance under disruption, not causality. Correlated predictors can substitute for one another, and partial dependence can average over unrealistic combinations. Leaf size and weighting also affect the smoothness and calibration of predicted probabilities.

A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

stages.title: The problem
stages.text:
STAGE 01

The problem
A fitted equation always returns numbers; diagnostics ask whether the functional form, error behaviour, and individual observations make those numbers defensible.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.text:
STAGE 02

Intuition and objective
Residuals should fluctuate without systematic shape around zero. Curvature signals missing functional form, a funnel signals changing variance, a Q–Q departure challenges normal-error inference, and an isolated high-leverage point can rotate the fitted line.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.text:
STAGE 03

Worked example
A salary model has residual spread of ±5k for junior staff and ±40k for senior staff. The fan pattern violates constant variance. Coefficients may still describe a mean pattern, but ordinary standard errors and a single-width prediction band are unreliable; robust errors or a variance model may be needed.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.text:
STAGE 04

Reasoning with the method

Residual-versus-fitted plots examine mean form and variance structure. Q–Q plots compare ordered residuals with a reference distribution and matter for inference that relies on that reference; predictors and outcomes need not themselves be normal. Leverage describes unusual predictor combinations. Influence describes how fitted results change, so Cook’s distance is a screening tool rather than a deletion command. VIF shows how strongly a predictor overlaps the others and can explain wide coefficient intervals without proving bias. Diagnostics should prompt a scientific response: correct errors, represent nonlinearity, model variance or dependence, and report justified sensitivity analyses.

A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

stages.title: The Raw Target
stages.text:
STAGE 01 · OBSERVE
The Raw Target
BEFORE YOU START

A regression tree predicts a number by averaging training outcomes within a terminal leaf. The fitted function is therefore piecewise constant.

A regression tree is a model that helps us predict a number. Not a category like "cat or dog", but a continuous value like an exam score, temperature, or a house price.

Let's look at a small dataset of houses. We want to predict the Price (in thousands) based entirely on the Size of the house (in square meters).

Look at the canvas. The horizontal axis is Size (m²), and the vertical axis is Price (in thousands of dollars, or $k). Hover over the canvas to see active tooltips.

stages.title: From Dataset to Model
stages.text:
STAGE 02 · UNDERSTAND
From Dataset to Model

Before teaching an algorithm, we need a disciplined plan. A standard Machine Learning workflow protects us from creating models that look perfect on paper but fail in the real world.

The ML Pipeline:
Target y
The number we want to predict (e.g., Price).
Features X
The inputs we use (e.g., Size).
Data Split
Divide points into Training and Validation sets.
Tune & Predict
Limit tree growth to generalize and make unseen predictions.
Look at the canvas: The data has been split. We use the 16 training houses to grow our tree, keeping 6 validation houses hidden to test general performance.

stages.title: The Clumsy Guess
stages.text:
STAGE 03 · UNDERSTAND
The Clumsy Guess

At the very start, the tree puts all houses in one big group (the Root Node). Before asking any questions, it asks: "If I had to guess one price for all houses, what should I use?"

The standard answer is the average. If we take all 16 training house prices and average them, we get exactly $483.1k.

Root Prediction = Average(y) = 483.1

This is a clumsy guess. The red lines on the canvas show the Residuals—the mathematical distance (errors) between our flat guess and reality.

stages.title: The First Split
stages.text:
STAGE 04 · BUILD
The First Split

Now the tree asks a question to divide the data: "Can I split the houses into 2 groups so the prices inside each group become more similar?"

It checks a "cut point". Based on the math, the best first rule is: Is Size ≤ 100?

If Yes, go Left. If No, go Right.

Now, instead of one average for everything, we have two averages. A lower average ($363.3k) for smaller houses, and a higher average ($637.1k) for bigger houses.

stages.title: The Error Engine (RSS)
stages.text:
STAGE 05 · UNDERSTAND
The Error Engine (RSS)

How did it know to split exactly at 100? The algorithm is "Greedy". It tests candidate split points between sorted training values and chooses the one that leaves the least amount of mess.

It measures "mess" using the Residual Sum of Squares (RSS). It squares all the red error lines and adds them up. Lower RSS is always better.

stages.title: Real Trees Check Many Questions
stages.text:
STAGE 06 · OBSERVE
Real Trees Check Many Questions

In real machine learning, a regression tree is not limited to checking just one feature. It considers multiple input variables simultaneously, checking every possible partition point across size, age, rooms, and locations.

The tree runs a "Greedy Search": it picks the single feature and threshold that yields the largest drop in RSS.

Winning Split: Size wins because partitioning by Size ≤ 100 m² leaves the least error (lowest post-split RSS) among all candidate features.

stages.title: Recursive Splitting
stages.text:
STAGE 07 · BUILD
Recursive Splitting

After finding the best first split, the tree does the exact same thing inside each new group. It splits, then splits inside the split. Like cutting a cake into pieces, then cutting those pieces again.

This is called Recursive Binary Splitting. With every split, the prediction line stops looking flat and starts looking like a set of stairs.

Play: Grow Tree Sequentially

Watch the regions split and slide to form deeper nodes.

stages.title: The Anatomy of a Tree
stages.text:
STAGE 08 · UNDERSTAND
The Anatomy of a Tree

Even though we call it a tree, data scientists draw them upside down.

Root Node: The top, where all data starts.
Internal Node: A fork in the road where a decision is checked (e.g., Size ≤ 100).
Terminal Node (Leaf): The final box that gives the prediction number.
Interactive: Move your mouse over the canvas right now. The tree diagram will light up to trace the exact decision path for the region your cursor is in.

stages.title: The Overfitting Trap
stages.text:
STAGE 09 · BUILD
The Overfitting Trap

What happens if we never tell the tree to stop? It will keep splitting until every single data point is alone in its own leaf, creating a zero-error fit on training data.

This creates a massive risk of Overfitting—the model memorizes the random noise in our training set and fails to generalize to unseen houses.

Bias-Variance Tradeoff
TREE DEPTH	BIAS	VARIANCE	DESCRIPTION
Too Shallow	High	Low	Underfits (Misses pattern)
Balanced	Medium	Medium	Best fit (Generalizes)
Too Deep	Low	High	Overfits (Memorizes noise)
Overfit Comparison

stages.title: Stopping Rules
stages.text:
STAGE 10 · UNDERSTAND
Stopping Rules

To prevent overfitting, we enforce Stopping Rules (also known as pre-pruning). We restrict depth and control minimum partition requirements before splits can occur.

Validation Metric:
RSS (Error Sum)
MAE (Mean Error)
RMSE (Typical Error)
Metric Decoder
Error Actual price − predicted price.
RSS Σ(actual − predicted)²

Add up all squared errors. Excellent for comparing model error, though numbers become quite large due to squaring.

MAE average(|actual − predicted|)

Average absolute mistake. Easiest to explain because it matches the original unit ($k).

RMSE √average((actual − predicted)²)

Square root of average squared error. Expressed in original units ($k), but heavily punishes larger individual mistakes.

 Example: If MAE = $30.0k, the model is off by about $30,000 on average. If RMSE = $33.0k, the typical error is about $33,000, with bigger mistakes punished more strongly.
Why compare Train vs Validation?
• Training Error tells us how well the tree fits the data it learned from.
• Validation Error tells us how well it performs on unseen, hidden houses.
• A deep tree can drive training error down to zero by memorizing noise, but will perform poorly on validation data.
• Rule of thumb: Always choose settings that minimize validation error. If two trees perform similarly, choose the simpler one!
Max Depth: 2
Min Samples per Leaf: 1
TOTAL LEAF NODES
4
...
TRAIN RSS
...
VALIDATION RSS
CURRENT DECISION ANALYSIS

Evaluating current parameters...

The tuning curve changes max depth while holding leaf size fixed; the heatmap compares depth and leaf size together.

 How to Choose Stopping Rules
Do not choose the model based solely on the lowest training error.
Use validation error to estimate performance on unseen, real-world data.
Prefer lower validation error. Minimize this value to find the sweet spot.
If two settings perform similarly, always pick the simpler tree (Occam's razor).
Use both rules together: max_depth limits levels, while min_samples_leaf prevents tiny leaves that isolate individual outliers.

Notice that making the tree deeper eventually makes training error drop to 0, but the validation error starts increasing. That turning point is the sweet spot.

stages.title: Pruning: Let It Grow, Then Cut It Back
stages.text:
STAGE 11 · BUILD
Pruning: Let It Grow, Then Cut It Back

Sometimes stopping early (pre-pruning) can be too short-sighted. It might stop before discovering splits that become useful in combination with other splits.

The alternative is Post-Pruning: We allow the tree to grow deep first, and then collapse weak, low-utility sub-branches back into parent leaf nodes using a complexity penalty called ccp_alpha.

Prune Weak Branches

Look at the canvas to see the overgrown staircase collapse into a cleaner, stable staircase when pruned.

stages.title: Trees vs. Lines
stages.text:
STAGE 12 · UNDERSTAND
Trees vs. Lines

Linear regression fits a smooth, straight line. It assumes a constant rate of change. Regression trees carve the world into intervals and assign a flat average to each.

Show Tree Model (Indigo)
Show Linear Model (Green)
Show Tree Errors
Show Linear Errors

If the data has sudden thresholds or "if/then" behaviors, trees capture it naturally. If it's a smooth trend, lines win.

stages.text:
STAGE 14 · UNDERSTAND
Sample Output: Reading the Tree Result

After training the regression tree, we do not just look at the final prediction. We read the rules, follow the decision path, and check the validation metrics to see whether the model generalizes.

Model Output Settings:
Model: Regression Tree
Target: Price ($k)
Feature used: Size (m²)
Max depth: 3
Min samples per leaf: 1
Leaf prediction rule: Average price of training houses inside that leaf
TRAINED REGRESSION TREE OUTPUT
1. If Size ≤ 100:
      If Size ≤ 71.5:
          If Size ≤ 52.5 → Predict $290.0k
          Else → Predict $320.0k
      Else:
          If Size ≤ 84.0 → Predict $405.0k
          Else → Predict $460.0k

2. If Size > 100:
      If Size ≤ 124.0:
          If Size ≤ 117.5 → Predict $565.0k
          Else → Predict $620.0k
      Else:
          If Size ≤ 140.0 → Predict $645.0k
          Else → Predict $710.0k
Interpretation Walkthrough
Example house: Size = 112 m²
Step 1: Is Size ≤ 100? No → go right.
Step 2: Is Size ≤ 124? Yes → go left.
Step 3: Is Size ≤ 117.5? Yes → go left.
Final leaf prediction: $565.0k

 Plain-English interpretation: The model predicts about $565,000 because the 112 m² house lands in a leaf containing similar-sized training houses. The prediction is the average price of that leaf, not a guaranteed exact price.

Metric Interpretation
Training
Train RSS: 1,750
Train MAE: $9.4k
Train RMSE: $10.5k
Validation
Val RSS: 6,550
Val MAE: $30.0k
Val RMSE: $33.0k
• RSS: total squared error. Lower is better.
• MAE: average absolute mistake.
• RMSE: typical prediction mistake, with larger errors punished more heavily.
Interpretation: Validation RMSE = $33.0k means that on unseen validation houses, the model is typically off by around $33,000. This is more realistic than the training error because the validation houses were not used to grow the tree.
 Common Mistake:
“Do not say: The model is always correct.”
Correct Interpretation:
“Say: The model gives an estimate based on the average price of similar training houses in the same leaf.”

stages.title: Reality Check: Limitations
stages.text:
STAGE 15 · REFLECT
Reality Check: Limitations

While extremely powerful and explainable, single regression trees have key engineering limitations that you must look out for in practice.

 Poor Extrapolation
Trend Fail

Trees predict flat averages. If a house size is larger than any seen in training (e.g., 220 m²), the tree cannot continue a trend upward; it flatlines at the average of the largest leaf.

 Jagged Step Predictions
Staircase

Real-world factors often rise smoothly. Trees build staircases with sudden step jumps, struggling to cleanly represent smooth curves without huge depths.

 High Instability (Variance)
High Variance

A tiny shift in data (e.g., swapping one point's price) can completely re-arrange the root split boundary, producing a highly unstable prediction layout.

 Axis-Aligned Splits
Orthogonal

Basic trees split one feature at a time at right angles, making it difficult to capture diagonal correlations (like price dropping when size decreases and age increases simultaneously).

 Easy to Overfit
High Complexity

Without strict stopping rules or pruning, deep trees will easily grow until they isolate every single point, memorizing individual training points instead of discovering generalizable patterns.

Interactive Demo: Click any card above to see a live visual simulation of that limitation on the right canvas.

stages.title: Synthesis
stages.text:
STAGE 16 · REFLECT
Synthesis

Let's review the final sequence to build and use a regression tree:

1.
Put all training data in the Root Node.
2.
Test possible splits (greedy thresholds) across all available features.
3.
Pick the feature/split that results in the lowest RSS.
4.
Repeat the process recursively inside each new branch.
5.
Use validation error to choose stopping rules or pruning, instead of trusting training error alone.
6.
Each final leaf predicts the average target value inside that leaf.

While a single regression tree can be unstable on its own, this recursive logic is the fundamental building block for advanced modern algorithms like Random Forests and Gradient Boosting.

Ensemble Learning: Ensembles improve single trees by combining hundreds of them, smoothing out jagged steps and yielding highly stable predictions.
COMPLETE THE PICTURE
Extrapolation and uncertainty

A regression tree cannot naturally extrapolate a trend beyond the training range. New extreme values usually inherit the prediction of the outermost leaf.

Single-tree predictions can be unstable. Ensembles such as random forests or gradient boosting reduce variance, while conformal or bootstrap methods can add uncertainty estimates when required.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
Splits are chosen to reduce within-node squared error.
Pruning trades a little training fit for better generalisation.
Trees capture interactions and nonlinearities but predict in steps and extrapolate poorly.

STAGE 01 · UNDERSTAND
The Editable Reality
BEFORE YOU START

A regression line predicts a numerical outcome Y from a numerical predictor X. The fitted line summarises a trend; it does not force every point to sit on the line.

Data science begins with observation. We collect pairs of information to see if one thing can predict another.

Below is our dataset: Hours Studied (x) vs Test Score (y). Try changing the numbers! Watch the canvas update live.

stages.title: The Penalty for Being Wrong
stages.text:
STAGE 04 · UNDERSTAND
The Penalty for Being Wrong

If we just add up the errors, positive and negative errors cancel out. To prevent this, we square the errors.

Squaring turns all negatives positive, and heavily punishes massive mistakes (an error of 10 explodes into 100).

YOUR LINE'S TOTAL SUM OF SQUARED ERRORS (SSE)
51.0

On the right, the red boxes represent these squared errors. To find the best line, we need to shrink this SSE number to the absolute minimum.

stages.title: The Least Squares Engine
stages.text:
STAGE 05 · BUILD
The Least Squares Engine

Instead of guessing, calculus gives us the exact formulas to minimize the squares. Watch the math compute live based on your data:

1. Find Means: x̄ = 3.00, ȳ = 60.00
2. Numerator = Σ(x - x̄)(y - ȳ) = 49.00
3. Denominator = Σ(x - x̄)² = 10.00
4. Slope (b₁) = Num ÷ Den = 4.900
5. Intercept (b₀) = ȳ - b₁x̄ = 45.30

Notice the green dot on the canvas? That is the mean point (x̄, ȳ). The least-squares fitted line with an intercept always passes exactly through the average of x and the average of y.

stages.title: The Model Scorecard
stages.text:
STAGE 07 · EVALUATE
The Model Scorecard

How much can we trust this line? We grade the model using your live data:

R² (Proportion of Variation Accounted For): 0.992
R² tells us what proportion of the observed variation in test scores is accounted for by the fitted model using study hours; it does not establish causation. 1.0 means zero residual error on these data. We compare our line's errors (SSE) against the errors of just guessing the flat average (SST).

R² = 1 - (SSE / SST)
What SST actually is

SST = Total variation in your data

It measures: "How spread out are the actual scores from the average score?"

SST = Σ(y - ȳ)²
TRANSLATE THAT INTO ENGLISH
y = actual value (like a student's score)
ȳ = average of all scores
y - ȳ = distance from the mean
square it → so negatives don't cancel positives
sum everything (Σ) → total spread
Step-by-step example

Using your live data! The current average score (ȳ) is 60.0.

SCORE (Y)	DISTANCE (Y - Ȳ)	SQUARED (Y - Ȳ)²
50	-10.0	100.0
55	-5.0	25.0
61	+1.0	1.0
64	+4.0	16.0
70	+10.0	100.0
SST Total = 242.0
Why SST matters in R²
SST is the "baseline total spread" (if we just guessed the average).
SSE is how much error our fitted model still has.

R² tells us what proportion of the original variation (SST) our fitted model accounts for. 1.0 means zero residual error on these data.

RSE (Residual Standard Error): 0.80
This is the typical size of our miss. When we predict a score, we are typically off by this many points.

Can we trust the line?

Inspect residual-versus-fitted values for curvature and changing spread, a Q–Q plot when classical inference requires residual normality, and leverage/Cook’s distance for influential observations. Independence comes from the study design.

Intervals answer different questions: a confidence interval describes uncertainty in the estimated mean response; a wider prediction interval describes uncertainty for one new observation. A high R² does not prove that the model is correct, causal, or useful on new data.

COMPLETE THE PICTURE
Assumptions and prediction intervals

Check whether the relationship is roughly linear, residual spread is reasonably constant, observations are independent, and no single point dominates the fit.

A confidence interval estimates the mean response at a chosen X. A prediction interval is wider because it predicts one new individual outcome. Avoid extrapolating far beyond the observed X range.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
Least squares chooses the line with the smallest sum of squared residuals.
The slope describes the expected change in Y for a one-unit increase in X.
A strong fit does not establish causation, and predictions are safest inside the observed range.

Practical method checklist

Before you finish
Assumptions

Linear form, independent errors, and stable residual spread.

When the method fails

Curvature, influential observations, extrapolation, or changing variance.

Validation and leakage

Validate predictive performance on unseen data.

Interpretation cautions

R² is not correctness, causality, or guaranteed usefulness.

What to report

Slope with units, interval, residual error, diagnostics, and prediction interval.

title: Support Vector Machines — Separate classes with breathing room

stages.title: Points, labels, and a decision boundary
stages.text:
STAGE 01 · OBSERVE
Points, labels, and a decision boundary

Each point is one labelled training row with two features. Colour marks the class. A classifier needs a rule that places a future point on one side or the other.

f(x) > 0  →  Class +1
f(x) < 0  →  Class −1

In two dimensions the boundary is a line. In three dimensions it is a plane. Beyond that, it becomes a hyperplane, a dramatic name for the same separating idea.

The plot uses two features because humans remain tragically dependent on visible space. The model itself can work with many features.

stages.title: Why not choose any separating line?
stages.text:
STAGE 02 · QUESTION
Why not choose any separating line?

When the classes are separable, several lines can classify every training point correctly. Training accuracy alone cannot tell us which line is safer.

Narrow clearance

Fits the training rows, but a small measurement change can flip a prediction.

Wide clearance

Leaves more room before the nearest point crosses the boundary.

A linear SVM adds a preference: choose the separator with the greatest distance to the closest points from either class.

Quick check: what extra criterion does SVM use?

controls.label: Quick check: what extra criterion does SVM use?It chooses the separating line with the largest margin, subject to the model’s allowance for

stages.title: The margin is protected space
stages.text:
STAGE 03 · UNDERSTAND
The margin is protected space

The margin is the gap between two parallel support planes touching the closest training points on each side.

Boundary: wᵀx + b = 0
Margin boundaries: wᵀx + b = +1 and −1
Geometric margin width = 2 / ‖w‖

Maximising the margin is equivalent to keeping the weight vector small while still satisfying the classification constraints.

A wide margin can make the separator less sensitive. It cannot rescue biased data, leakage, poor labels, or a mismatched kernel. Geometry is useful, not divine intervention.

stages.title: Support vectors are the points that matter most
stages.text:
STAGE 04 · FOCUS
Support vectors are the points that matter most

Support vectors lie on or inside the margin. They directly constrain the fitted boundary.

f(x) = Σᵢ αᵢ yᵢ K(xᵢ, x) + b
Only rows with αᵢ > 0 are support vectors.

Move a distant, safely classified point a little and the boundary may not change. Move a support vector and the solution can shift immediately.

Important distinction: “support vector” means the row constrains this fitted margin. It does not mean the row is causally or commercially important in every possible sense.

stages.title: Hard margins break when reality overlaps
stages.text:
STAGE 05 · RELAX
Hard margins break when reality overlaps

A hard-margin SVM demands perfect separation with every row outside the margin. Real classes overlap, labels contain errors, and outliers appear because datasets enjoy sabotage.

A soft-margin SVM introduces slack variables ξᵢ so violations are allowed but penalised.

yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) ≥ 1 − ξᵢ,  with ξᵢ ≥ 0
SLACK	MEANING
ξ = 0	Correct and on or beyond the margin
0 < ξ ≤ 1	Correct side, but inside the margin
ξ > 1	Misclassified

stages.title: C decides how expensive violations are
stages.text:
STAGE 06 · TUNE
C decides how expensive violations are
minimise  ½‖w‖² + C Σᵢ ξᵢ
Small C

Violations are cheaper. The model accepts more errors to preserve a wider, smoother margin.

Large C

Violations are expensive. The model fits training rows more aggressively, often with a narrower margin.

C is an inverse regularisation parameter: larger C means less regularisation.

A huge C does not mean “more accurate”. It means “punish training violations more”, which can also mean “memorise the noise with confidence”.

stages.title: Scale features before comparing distances
stages.text:
STAGE 07 · PREPARE
Scale features before comparing distances

SVM geometry uses dot products and distances. A feature ranging from 0 to 100,000 can dominate another ranging from 0 to 1, even when the smaller-scale feature is genuinely informative.

standardised value = (value − training mean) ÷ training standard deviation

Fit the scaler inside each training fold, then apply that fitted transformation to validation, test, and production rows.

Two distinct failures: scaling before the split leaks information; scaling the test set separately changes the coordinate system. Both are wrong in impressively different ways.

stages.title: Hinge loss ignores easy correct points
stages.text:
STAGE 08 · FORMALISE
Hinge loss ignores easy correct points
hinge loss = max(0, 1 − y × f(x))
SIGNED MARGIN Y F(X)	LOSS	INTERPRETATION
≥ 1	0	Correct and safely beyond the margin
0 to 1	positive	Correct but inside the margin
≤ 0	≥ 1	Misclassified

Once a point is correctly beyond the margin, its hinge loss is zero. Distant easy points stop pulling the boundary.

Quick check: y f(x) = 1.7. What is the loss?

controls.label: Quick check: y f(x) = 1.7. What is the loss?max(0, 1 − 1.7) = 0.

stages.title: The decision score is not automatically a probability
stages.text:
STAGE 09 · INTERPRET
The decision score is not automatically a probability

The decision function reports which side of the boundary a row occupies and how strongly it lies in that direction.

larger positive f(x) → stronger Class +1 decision
larger negative f(x) → stronger Class −1 decision

For a linear SVM, the score relates to signed distance after accounting for ‖w‖. For a kernel SVM, treat it as a boundary score rather than literal distance in the original plot.

f(x) = 2 does not mean 200%, nor twice the probability of f(x) = 1. Probability estimates require a separate calibration model fitted with held-out predictions.

stages.title: A straight boundary cannot solve every pattern
stages.text:
STAGE 10 · EXTEND
A straight boundary cannot solve every pattern

Imagine one class forming an inner cluster and another forming an outer ring. No straight line can separate them in the original two-feature space.

A transformed feature such as squared radius can reveal the structure:

r² = x₁² + x₂²

In transformed space, a simple threshold on r² can separate inner from outer points. A curved boundary in the original plot can still correspond to a linear rule elsewhere.

stages.title: The kernel trick avoids explicit feature explosion
stages.text:
STAGE 11 · KERNELISE
The kernel trick avoids explicit feature explosion

A kernel computes similarities that behave like inner products in a richer feature space, without explicitly constructing every transformed coordinate.

K(x, z) = φ(x)ᵀφ(z)

RBF: K(x,z) = exp(−γ ‖x − z‖²)
Small gamma

Each point has broad influence. The decision surface changes slowly.

Large gamma

Influence becomes local. The boundary can wrap tightly around training points.

Large gamma plus large C can create an intricate boundary that remembers noise instead of learning structure.

stages.title: Tune the whole pipeline inside cross-validation
stages.text:
STAGE 12 · VALIDATE
Tune the whole pipeline inside cross-validation

Kernel, C, gamma, class weights, and preprocessing are hyperparameters. Choose them using validation folds inside the development data.

Pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC())
GridSearchCV(C, gamma, kernel, scoring)
Create an untouched final test set when the dataset is large enough.
Fit scaling and feature processing inside each training fold.
Score candidate settings using a metric aligned with the task.
Refit on all development data, then evaluate once on the test set.
Search C and gamma on logarithmic scales. If the winner sits at the edge, extend the range rather than declaring the boundary divinely optimal.

stages.title: Measure the errors the problem actually cares about
stages.text:
STAGE 13 · EVALUATE
Measure the errors the problem actually cares about

Accuracy alone can hide minority-class failures. Use confusion matrices, per-class recall, and precision–recall analysis when the positive class is rare.

Class imbalance

Consider class weights when minority-class mistakes deserve a larger penalty.

Operational thresholds

Tune the decision threshold on validation data when the default boundary is unsuitable.

Calibration

Map held-out SVM scores to probabilities using sigmoid, isotonic, or another calibration method.

Multiclass

Combine binary models using one-vs-rest or one-vs-one decisions.

One-vs-one classifiers: K(K−1)/2
One-vs-rest classifiers: K
A calibrated 0.8 has a frequency meaning: among cases assigned about 0.8, roughly 80% should belong to that class. Raw margin scores make no such promise.

stages.title: Change the knobs and watch the boundary answer back
stages.text:
STAGE 14 · SYNTHESIS
Change the knobs and watch the boundary answer back

The playground fits a small SVM directly in your browser. Change the dataset, kernel, C, and gamma. Click the plot to add a labelled point. Support vectors are ringed.

scale within a pipeline
start linear when appropriate
cross-validate C and kernel
inspect support-vector count
measure class-specific errors
calibrate only when needed
Strengths

Effective in high dimensions, flexible kernels, margin regularisation, sparse dependence on support vectors.

Limits

Kernel training can scale poorly, tuning matters greatly, probabilities are not native, nonlinear models are hard to interpret globally.

Final concept check: extremely large RBF gamma?

stages.title: The Raw Data & The Question
stages.text:
STAGE 01 · OBSERVE
The Raw Data & The Question
BEFORE YOU START

Time is part of the data structure. Rows cannot be shuffled freely because later observations may depend on earlier ones.

Before any complex math, a time series begins as a sequence of observations. Imagine a company asking: "What will product demand look like over the next two years?"

In standard data analysis, you can shuffle rows without losing meaning. In time series, order matters. Because today affects tomorrow, shuffling the dates destroys the story.

DATA GENERATION PARAMETERS
Trend Strength
1.0
Seasonality
15
Noise Level
10
MONTH (T)	OBSERVED DEMAND (Y)
Month 1	45.69
Month 2	43.55
Month 3	45.38
Month 4	48.70
Month 5	64.66

Displaying first 5 of 120 observations.

stages.title: The Time Plot
stages.text:
STAGE 02 · UNDERSTAND
The Time Plot

The very first step in analysis is visual. A Time Plot connects our raw observations chronologically.

By mapping time on the x-axis and our measured value on the y-axis, human intuition can instantly spot behaviors that spreadsheets hide. Does the sequence climb steadily? Does it repeat in a wave? Are there violent spikes?

Hover over the canvas to inspect the exact values at any point in time.

stages.title: Decomposing the Pattern
stages.text:
STAGE 03 · UNDERSTAND
Decomposing the Pattern

A time series is rarely a single, simple movement. We can typically decompose it into three underlying structural components:

Trend Seasonality Noise / Residual
ADDITIVE DECOMPOSITION MODEL
Yt = Tt + St + Rt

Observed Data = Long-term Trend + Repeating Seasonality + Remainder (Noise)

Note: The lines displayed on the canvas represent the exact, known components used to generate our simulation, rather than an estimated decomposition. In practice, models must infer these hidden components from the raw data.

stages.title: The Assumption of Stationarity
stages.text:
STAGE 04 · PREPARE
The Assumption of Stationarity

Many advanced statistical models require a series to be stationary before forecasting. For weak stationarity, the mean and finite variance are constant, and autocovariance depends only on lag, not calendar time.

STATIONARITY CONDITIONS
Constant Mean: The average does not drift up or down.
Constant Variance: The spread (volatility) stays consistent.
Lag-dependent Autocovariance: Covariance between observations depends on how far apart they are, not when they occur.

Watch the rolling moving average on the plot. If it climbs or falls significantly, the mean is not constant. This series violates the assumptions of basic autoregressive modeling and requires transformation.

stages.title: Fixing It: Differencing
stages.text:
STAGE 05 · BUILD
Fixing It: Differencing

To stabilize the mean of a trending series, we apply differencing. Instead of looking at raw values, we analyze the change between consecutive months.

Apply 1st-Order Differencing
Y't = Yt - Yt-1

Differencing can remove or reduce certain trends and help achieve stationarity. Check the transformed series: one difference does not guarantee stationarity.

99.33
MEAN (RAW SERIES)
0.96
MEAN (DIFFERENCED)

stages.title: Looking to the Past (Lags & ACF)
stages.text:
STAGE 06 · BUILD
Looking to the Past (Lags & ACF)

A massive concept here is a lag—looking backward in time. Today's demand might be highly correlated with demand from exactly 12 months ago.

The Autocorrelation Function (ACF) mathematically measures how strongly a series is related to its own past values across different lags.

Max Lags to Compute
24

How to read this genuinely computed ACF: Bars outside the approximate confidence bounds suggest autocorrelation at those lags, but interpret the pattern collectively and in the context of the fitted model. Repeating spikes may suggest seasonality; confirm with residual ACF and model diagnostics.

Use the PACF to examine the additional association at a lag after shorter lags are accounted for. After fitting, inspect the residual ACF and use a Ljung–Box test as an omnibus diagnostic. Seasonal or non-stationary series can make individual lag bars misleading.

stages.title: Forecasting the Future
stages.text:
STAGE 07 · BUILD
Forecasting the Future

Validation must move forward in time. Never randomly shuffle observations. Use a chronological holdout, expanding-window evaluation, or rolling-window evaluation, and state whether forecasts are one-step or multi-step. Compare against naïve, seasonal-naïve, drift and moving-average baselines before treating a complex forecast as useful.

Since this is an interactive environment, we project the future using a structural simulation forecast built from our known trend and seasonal generators, rather than estimating an ARIMA model from scratch.

Forecast Horizon (Months)
24
PREDICTION INTERVALS

A forecast is an estimate, not a prophecy. The shaded area represents the 95% prediction interval.

Note: The expanding fan shown here is a simplified heuristic to illustrate how uncertainty accumulates over time, rather than a mathematically derived forecast variance.

stages.title: Diagnostics: Evaluating Residuals
stages.text:
STAGE 08 · UNDERSTAND
Diagnostics: Evaluating Residuals

How do we know if a real-world forecasting model is adequate? We subtract the model's historical predictions from the actual raw data to check the residuals.

Residualt = Actual Yt - Predicted Yt
WHAT GOOD RESIDUALS LOOK LIKE
Centered around zero: No overall drift up or down.
Constant spread: Variance shouldn't wildly fan out.
No waves or patterns: All seasonality and trend should be captured by the model.
Occasional outliers: Random spikes are normal, but they shouldn't cluster.
Simulate a "Bad" Model (Leftover Pattern)

Toggle the switch to see what happens when a model fails to capture the underlying seasonality. A robust model leaves residuals that closely resemble pure random noise.

stages.title: Reading the Output
stages.text:
STAGE 09 · EVALUATE
Reading the Output

A statistical analysis translates a visual chart into actionable business metrics. Below is a simulated summary of what we learned from our generated data.

SIMULATED ANALYSIS REPORT
Underlying Trend	Positive (+1.00/mo)
Seasonal Peak	Month 4
Mean MoM Change	0.96
Key Pattern Identified	Seasonal (12m cycle)
Next Period Forecast	160.00
95% Prediction Bounds	[145.0, 175.0]

stages.title: Limitations & Caveats
stages.text:
STAGE 10 · REFLECT
Limitations & Caveats

Time series models fundamentally rely on the assumption that the future will structurally resemble the past. It is crucial not to overclaim the certainty of any forecast.

WHAT MODELS CAN'T DO
Black Swan Events: Standard models cannot predict unprecedented external shocks (pandemics, sudden market crashes).
Structural Breaks: If a company pivots its business model at month 100, data from month 1 is no longer highly relevant.
Infinite Horizons: Prediction intervals eventually grow so wide that long-term forecasts become practically useless.
COMPLETE THE PICTURE
Validate forecasts in time order

Random train/test splitting leaks future information into the past. Use a chronological holdout or rolling-origin evaluation so every forecast is tested only on observations that occur later.

Always compare a complex model with a simple baseline, such as the last observed value or the value from the same season one cycle earlier. Sophistication is not a metric, despite software marketing departments trying their best.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
Plot the series before modelling it.
Use time-aware validation and compare against a baseline forecast.
Good residuals should be patternless, centred near zero, and reasonably stable in spread.

Practical method checklist

Before you finish
Assumptions

Stable features or explicit modelling of change and seasonality.

When the method fails

Structural breaks, non-stationarity, long horizons, and changing measurement.

Validation and leakage

Use chronological, expanding-window, or rolling-window evaluation—never random shuffling.

Interpretation cautions

ACF bounds are approximate and lag patterns must be interpreted collectively.

What to report

Forecast horizon, split, baselines, errors with uncertainty, intervals, and residual diagnostics.

stages.title: The Raw Data
stages.text:
STAGE 01 · OBSERVE
The Raw Data
BEFORE YOU START

You only need a basic understanding of means and variance. ANOVA asks whether differences among group means are large compared with the variation inside the groups.

Imagine we are comparing test scores across three different teaching methods (Group A, B, and C).

If you look at the raw data in the visual panel, you'll notice that not everyone in Group A scored exactly the same. There is a natural spread, or noise, within every group. This is everyday biological, psychological, or measurement variation.

stages.title: The Research Question
stages.text:
STAGE 02 · OBSERVE
The Research Question

Our question isn't about individuals; it's about the group averages (the black lines).

Are the gaps between these group means large enough to confidently say the teaching methods have different effects? Or are the means just slightly off from each other by pure chance, drowning in the natural noise of the students?

Teaching Interaction: Shape the Data

Within-Group Spread (Noise)
Low
High
Group Differences (Signal)
Distinct
Equal

stages.title: The Rules of the Game
stages.text:
STAGE 03 · PREPARE
The Rules of the Game

Before we build an ANOVA model, we must check our assumptions. If the data breaks the rules, standard ANOVA might mislead us.

Normality

Technically, ANOVA assumes the residuals (the error or distance of each point from its group mean) are normally distributed. In practice, researchers often check if the data within each group resembles a bell curve.

Homogeneity of Variance

The spread (variance) of scores should be roughly equal across all groups. ANOVA is robust to minor violations, provided sample sizes are equal.

Independence

Data points must not influence each other. If the same student is tested multiple times, you must use a Repeated-Measures ANOVA instead.

stages.title: Variance Decomposition
stages.text:
STAGE 04 · BUILD
Variance Decomposition

ANOVA answers our question by splitting the total variation in the data into two components. Look at the canvas to see these distances visualized.

Between-Group Variance (Signal)
The systematic variance associated with the independent variable. Measured by how far each group mean (black line) deviates from the Grand Mean (dashed line).
Within-Group Variance (Noise)
The unsystematic variance or error. Measured by how much individual dots deviate from their own group mean.

stages.title: The F-Statistic
stages.text:
STAGE 05 · UNDERSTAND
The F-Statistic

ANOVA summarizes this decomposition into a single ratio, the F-statistic. It compares the size of the treatment effect to the size of the error.

𝐹
=
Between-Group Variance
Within-Group Variance
F=
Within-Group Variance
Between-Group Variance
	​

stages.title: Degrees of Freedom
stages.text:
STAGE 06 · UNDERSTAND
Degrees of Freedom

Before we can calculate our variance estimates (Mean Squares) for the F-statistic, we need to divide our Sum of Squares by our Degrees of Freedom (df).

In statistics, df simply means how many values are still free to vary once a constraint has been imposed. Imagine picking 3 numbers that must average to 10. You can freely choose the first two (say, 8 and 15), but the third is locked (-13). You have 2 degrees of freedom.

In our specific teaching example, we have N = 36 total students spread across k = 3 groups:

dfbetween = k - 1 = 3 - 1 = 2
Once the overall Grand Mean is set, only 2 of our 3 group means are free to vary.
dfwithin = N - k = 36 - 3 = 33
Within each group, the students' scores must average out to their respective group mean. We lose 1 degree of freedom per group constraint.
dftotal = N - 1 = 36 - 1 = 35
If we only knew the Grand Mean, 35 out of the 36 students' scores would be free to vary.

stages.title: A Worked Example
stages.text:
STAGE 07 · UNDERSTAND
A Worked Example

Let’s bring this together using the data currently on display. We divide our sums of squared deviations (Sum of Squares, SS) by our degrees of freedom to get the Mean Squares (MS), which are variance quantities used in F = MS_between / MS_within. Under the null hypothesis and standard ANOVA assumptions, both estimate the same error variance.

FROM THE DISPLAYED SCORES

Group means: A = 80, B = 68, C = 56. Grand mean = 68. Each group has n = 12, so N = 36.

BETWEEN-GROUP SIGNAL

SSbetween = 12[(80 - 68)2 + (68 - 68)2 + (56 - 68)2] = 3456

WITHIN-GROUP NOISE

SSwithin = 132 + 132 + 132 = 396

APPLYING DEGREES OF FREEDOM

dfbetween = 2; dfwithin = 33.
MSbetween = 3456 / 2 = 1728.
MSwithin = 396 / 33 = 12.
F = 1728 / 12 = 144.

Scroll down to see these quantities organized into the universal language of statisticians: the ANOVA table.

stages.title: Reading the ANOVA Table
stages.text:
STAGE 08 · UNDERSTAND
Reading the ANOVA Table

When you run ANOVA in software like R, SPSS, or Python, the output is standardized into this table format.

Interact with the table in the visual panel: Tap or hover over the column headers (SS, df, MS, F, p) and the rows to understand exactly what each number represents and how they mathematically connect.

The Conclusion:

Because our p-value (< 0.001) is less than our threshold (0.05), we reject the null hypothesis. We conclude that at least one teaching method has a significantly different mean score.

stages.title: How Big Is The Effect?
stages.text:
STAGE 09 · UNDERSTAND
How Big Is The Effect?

A small p-value indicates that the observed result would be unusual under the null hypothesis, assuming the model assumptions hold. It is not the probability that the null is true or a measure of practical importance, so report an effect size and confidence intervals too.
