stages.title: Depth builds features
stages.text:
06

STACK USEFUL TRANSFORMATIONS

Depth builds features

A deep network turns the same example into a sequence of increasingly useful descriptions. Each layer receives the previous layer’s features and composes them into larger ideas.

WHY IT MATTERS

Raw pixels are a poor language for “dog.” Edges are more useful; groups of edges can describe fur or curves; those patterns can form ears, eyes, and snouts. Hierarchy lets the model reuse simple discoveries to build complex ones.

HOW IT WORKS
1

Early layers respond to local changes such as edges, colour transitions, or short sound patterns.

2

Middle layers combine repeated local clues into textures, shapes, or meaningful phrase fragments.

3

Later layers gather evidence across a wider area and make features useful for the final task.

Picture it: It is like looking through a stack of tracing sheets. Each sheet redraws the scene using the patterns that matter at its level.

The feature names are a helpful simplification, not rules written by a programmer. Training discovers the filters that reduce the loss.

stages.title: How learning happens
stages.text:
07

THE CORRECTION CYCLE

How learning happens

Learning is a repeated correction loop. Forward pass → loss → backpropagation computes gradients → optimiser updates weights. The network makes predictions, measures error, computes how the loss changes with each weight, and uses those gradients to adjust the weights.

WHY IT MATTERS

A loss number alone says only “this was wrong.” Backpropagation turns that complaint into useful directions for millions of parameters, so an optimiser can use the loss gradients to update the weights.

HOW IT WORKS
1

Forward propagation moves a batch through the layers and produces predictions.

2

A loss function compares predictions with the correct answers; backpropagation calculates gradients from output to input.

3

An optimiser uses those gradients to update the weights. The learning rate controls how large each step is.

Picture it: Imagine descending a foggy hill. The gradient tells you which way slopes downward; the learning rate decides whether you take careful steps or dangerous leaps.

One update teaches very little. Useful behaviour emerges from many batches of examples providing many small, partly noisy corrections.

Run one learning step
→
LEARNING RATE
0.5

stages.title: Learn patterns, not the answer sheet
stages.text:
08

TRAIN WITH DISCIPLINE

Learn patterns, not the answer sheet

Training must continue long enough to discover stable patterns, but not so blindly that the model memorises quirks of the training set.

WHY IT MATTERS

Training loss almost always rewards more training. Validation data asks the more important question: are these improvements useful on examples that did not update the weights?

HOW IT WORKS
1

Train on small batches; one pass through every training example is an epoch. Switch to evaluation mode before validation.

2

Plot training and validation curves together. High values for both suggest underfitting; a widening gap suggests overfitting.

3

Use augmentation, weight decay, dropout, a simpler model, or early stopping—and save the best validation checkpoint.

Picture it: One coach watches practice; another watches an unseen match. If practice keeps improving while match performance worsens, the player is learning the drill rather than the game.

Hyperparameters such as learning rate, batch size, depth, and dropout are chosen with validation evidence. They are not learned like ordinary weights.

MOVE THROUGH TRAINING
EPOCH 12
UNDERFIT
USEFUL FIT
OVERFIT

stages.title: Choose an architecture
stages.text:
09

MATCH SHAPE TO PROBLEM

Choose an architecture

An architecture is a set of useful assumptions about how information is organised. The right design makes important patterns easier and cheaper to learn.

WHY IT MATTERS

Images contain many local patterns, not one universal feature. Sequences need memory or direct links across time. Architecture decides how information is shared, how far context can travel, and what the model can compute efficiently.

HOW IT WORKS
1

A CNN layer learns many filters. Every filter scans every image, producing its own feature map. Training changes the filter values; testing reuses the learned filters without inventing new ones.

2

An RNN reads one item at a time and updates a hidden state—a fixed-length vector that compresses what it has seen. That state can produce scores for the next word or another sequence output.

3

A Transformer creates a query, key, and value for every token. Query–key matches become attention weights, which gather useful values into context. Training rewards links that help reduce prediction error.

Picture it: Choose a tool shaped like the material: a movable stencil for space, a notebook passed through time, or a web of spotlights for attention.

Choose with evidence, not fashion. CNNs remain natural for spatial data. RNNs can suit compact streaming systems. Transformers usually handle long context and parallel training better, but standard attention can require much more memory as a sequence grows.

CNN
space
RNN
sequence
TRANSFORMER
attention
CNN · A BANK OF REUSABLE SPATIAL DETECTORS
1

A layer learns many filters—not only one. Early filters may respond to different edges, colours, or textures.

2

Every learned filter scans every training image and every test image. One filter produces one feature map showing where its pattern responded.

3

Training adjusts all filter values. At test time those values are frozen and reused; the model does not design a special filter for each new picture.

4

Later layers combine the stack of feature maps into more complex evidence such as curves, parts, or whole objects.

Picture it: Picture a case of many reusable stencils. Every stencil is swept across every picture, producing its own map of matches.

When to choose it: Choose a CNN when locality and spatial reuse matter—images, video frames, grids, or compact vision systems. CNN ideas are also often combined with attention.

stages.title: Start from a pretrained model
stages.text:
10

REUSE USEFUL EXPERIENCE

Start from a pretrained model

Transfer learning starts from a model that has already learned general patterns from a large dataset, then adapts that knowledge to your narrower task.

WHY IT MATTERS

Training a large network from random weights can require enormous amounts of labelled data and computation. Useful early features—edges, textures, shapes, language patterns—often transfer between related tasks.

HOW IT WORKS
1

Replace the old output head with one that matches the new classes or target.

2

First freeze the pretrained backbone and train only the new head; this tests the existing features cheaply.

3

If needed, unfreeze some layers and fine-tune gently with a smaller learning rate so useful knowledge is not destroyed.

Picture it: A trained carpenter does not relearn how to measure and cut wood for every new table. They reuse general craft and learn the new design.

Transfer works best when the earlier data and new task share useful structure. A model can also transfer unwanted biases, so evaluation still matters.

stages.title: Make an honest judgement
stages.text:
11

EARN CONFIDENCE

Make an honest judgement

Evaluation asks not only “how often is it right?” but “where, for whom, and with what confidence does it fail?” The final test set estimates performance on genuinely unseen data.

WHY IT MATTERS

A model can reach 95% accuracy by always predicting the common class in an imbalanced dataset. In medicine, fraud, or safety, one missed positive can matter far more than one false alarm.

HOW IT WORKS
1

Evaluate the selected checkpoint once on the untouched test set and report class-level precision, recall, F1, and support.

2

Read the confusion matrix and inspect individual errors for bad labels, rare conditions, occlusion, or shortcut patterns.

3

Check calibration, uncertainty, and subgroup performance. Choose decision thresholds on validation data using real-world costs.

Picture it: Accuracy is the final grade; the confusion matrix is the marked paper showing which questions were misunderstood.

Lower thresholds usually find more true positives but create more false alarms. Higher thresholds usually do the opposite.

DECISION THRESHOLD
0.50
FIND MORE
BALANCE
FEWER ALARMS

stages.title: Ship the whole pipeline
stages.text:
12

MOVE BEYOND THE NOTEBOOK

Ship the whole pipeline

A deployed model is not only a weights file. It is a complete, repeatable route from raw input to a decision that behaves the same way outside the training notebook.

WHY IT MATTERS

A brilliant model can produce nonsense if the live system resizes differently, swaps class order, forgets normalisation, or leaves dropout active. Most production failures happen at the seams around the network.

HOW IT WORKS
1

Save the architecture, weights, class order, dimensions, normalisation, tokeniser, threshold, software versions, and configuration.

2

Validate the input, apply the same preprocessing, switch to evaluation mode, disable gradients, predict, and decode the result.

3

Test the complete pipeline in its target environment for latency, memory, privacy, energy use, throughput, and failure handling.

Picture it: Treat deployment like sealing a recipe with its ingredients, measurements, oven settings, and serving rule—not saving only the cake tin.

The same pipeline may run on a phone, API, browser, hospital system, edge device, or cloud GPU. The constraints can change which model is best.

stages.title: The problem
stages.text:
STAGE 01

The problem
A model produces many kinds of errors. A metric turns those errors into a comparison, but only after the real decision defines what matters. A hospital triage model and a spam filter should not inherit the same priorities by convenience.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.text:
STAGE 02

Intuition and objective
MAE counts absolute regression misses in outcome units; RMSE gives large misses extra weight. Accuracy counts correct labels, precision asks how many predicted positives were right, and recall asks how many actual positives were found. F1-score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall: F1 = 2 × precision × recall / (precision + recall), when the denominator is positive. It is useful when both matter, but ignores true negatives and is not automatically the best metric. Log loss and Brier score evaluate probabilities, while calibration compares predicted risks with observed frequencies.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.text:
STAGE 03

Worked example
A screening model sees 1,000 people: 100 have disease. It finds 80 of them and falsely flags 90 healthy people. TP=80, FN=20, FP=90, TN=810. Accuracy is 89%, recall is 80%, and precision is 47%. The apparently healthy accuracy hides that more than half of alerts are false.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.text:
STAGE 04

Reasoning with the method

MAE targets absolute error in outcome units, while squared-error optimisation gives large misses extra weight. Accuracy summarises a thresholded confusion matrix; precision, recall and specificity condition on different denominators. ROC-AUC measures ranking across thresholds, whereas PR-AUC emphasises positive retrieval and depends on prevalence. Log loss and Brier score evaluate probabilities, and calibration asks whether predicted risks match observed frequencies. Out-of-sample R² compares with a mean-prediction baseline and may be negative. With asymmetric consequences, write expected cost explicitly and choose the threshold that supports the actual decision and operational capacity.

A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.text:
STAGE 06

Assumptions and failure modes
Assumptions

The evaluation sample must represent the deployment population, labels must be trustworthy, and each metric must be calculated on genuinely held-out predictions.

When the method fails

Accuracy fails under imbalance or unequal costs. MAPE behaves badly near zero. ROC-AUC can obscure performance at the operating region, and a strong ranking score does not guarantee calibrated probabilities.

stages.text:
STAGE 07

Practical workflow

Choose primary and secondary metrics before model comparison
Tune model and threshold on validation data
Lock the full pipeline
Report final test metrics with bootstrap or repeated-sample intervals

stages.title: Interpretation and reporting
stages.text:
STAGE 08

Interpretation and reporting

What to report: State the metric definition, threshold, prevalence or outcome scale, baseline, point estimate, uncertainty interval and real-world costs.

Common misuse: Selecting whichever metric makes a preferred model look best after seeing the results.

stages.title: The problem
stages.text:
STAGE 01

The problem
Causal conclusions depend more on assignment, measurement and follow-up than on a sophisticated final test. Design defines what comparison the data can identify.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.text:
STAGE 02

Intuition and objective
Random assignment balances confounders in expectation. Blocking improves balance on known prognostic variables; clustering changes the independent unit; blinding protects measurement and behaviour.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.text:
STAGE 03

Worked example
Twenty schools—not 600 students—are randomised to a teaching programme. Student outcomes remain clustered within schools. Treating 600 rows as independent exaggerates precision; analysis and power must account for 20 randomisation units and intraclass correlation.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.text:
STAGE 04

Reasoning with the method

An estimand specifies population, treatment strategies, comparator, outcome, time and summary contrast. Allocation concealment protects enrolment; blinding protects behaviour and measurement. Blocking randomises within prognostic strata. Cluster randomisation assigns groups and reduces effective sample size through intraclass correlation, so power and analysis must use the randomisation unit. Intention-to-treat preserves the randomised contrast; per-protocol analysis answers a different, more selection-sensitive question. Noncompliance, attrition and interference should be anticipated in the protocol. Power planning must include meaningful effect, variance, allocation, clustering, multiplicity and attrition.

A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

Assumptions

Assignment is implemented as planned, outcomes are measured consistently, interference is limited or modelled, and attrition does not destroy exchangeability.

When the method fails

Noncompliance, differential attrition, spillovers, outcome switching, hidden multiplicity and analysing below the randomisation unit can bias results or uncertainty.

stages.title: The problem
stages.text:
STAGE 01

The problem
Instead of averaging independent trees, boosting builds a sequence in which each new weak learner targets the current model’s loss gradient.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.text:
STAGE 02

Intuition and objective
Learning rate controls how much each tree contributes; tree count controls how many correction steps occur. Small learning rates often need more trees, so these settings must be tuned together.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.text:
STAGE 03

Worked example
At learning rate .3, validation loss falls quickly then rises after 60 trees. At .05 it improves more slowly and reaches a better minimum near 300 trees. Early stopping chooses the round from validation data, not the test set.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.text:
STAGE 04

Reasoning with the method

Boosting creates an additive predictor by fitting each learner to a negative loss gradient. For squared error this resembles residual fitting, but other losses create different pseudo-residuals. Learning rate scales contributions, tree depth limits interactions, and row or feature subsampling regularises. These settings interact, so learning rate and round count must be tuned together. Training loss normally keeps falling and cannot select stopping. Validation-based early stopping is a hyperparameter choice. Class weighting changes the objective and can damage calibration. Gain importance and attribution methods explain the fitted model, not a causal mechanism.

A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

Assumptions and failure modes
Assumptions

The loss must match the target and decision; validation must reflect deployment; preprocessing and early stopping must stay inside development data.

When the method fails

Too many rounds chase noise, poor tuning overfits, probabilities may be miscalibrated, and importance is unstable under correlated predictors.

stages.title: The Uncharted Planet
stages.text:
STAGE 01 · OBSERVE
The Uncharted Planet
BEFORE YOU START

Hierarchical clustering requires a distance measure and a linkage rule. Both choices define what it means for groups to be close.

Imagine landing on a distant planet with no map or guidebook. Your goal isn't to reach a destination; it's simply to see what is there. This is the essence of Unsupervised Learning.

Unlike supervised learning, where we try to predict a specific answer, here we only have features. We are discovering the natural structure of the data.

The Toy Box Analogy: Think of a child given a massive box of mixed toys and told to "find the patterns." Without instructions, they group them naturally by similarity.

To the right, we have a raw dataset. Just points in space waiting to be understood.

Takeaway: Unsupervised learning is about revealing structure that is already hiding in the data.

stages.title: Measuring "Close"
stages.text:
STAGE 02 · UNDERSTAND
Measuring "Close"

Before we can group anything, we must define what "similar" means. The most common way is to measure the physical distance between data points.

We use the Euclidean distance (the straight-line distance) to find out who is closest to whom. It is common, but not the only option; Manhattan, cosine, or domain-specific distances can make more sense for different data.

d(A, B) = √[ (x₂ - x₁)² + (y₂ - y₁)² ]

By measuring the distance between every single pair of points, we build a "distance matrix"—a lookup table for similarity.

Takeaway: Clustering depends on your distance choice, because "close" is a design decision.

stages.title: The First Merge
stages.text:
STAGE 03 · BUILD
The First Merge

Hierarchical clustering (specifically the Agglomerative or "bottom-up" kind) starts with a simple rule:

Every point starts as its own separate cluster.
Find the two clusters that are closest together.
Merge them.

Watch as the algorithm scans all points, finds the single closest pair, and binds them into a new, single cluster.

Takeaway: Agglomerative clustering grows structure from the bottom up, one merge at a time.

stages.title: Defining Group Distance (Linkage)
stages.text:
STAGE 04 · BUILD

Linkage and distance are not interchangeable. Ward linkage is tied to Euclidean geometry and increases in within-cluster variance. Single linkage can chain; complete linkage favours compact groups; average linkage is a compromise. Dendrogram heights do not represent the same quantity for every method.

Defining Group Distance (Linkage)

Merging two individual points is easy. But how do you measure the distance between a single point and a group? Or between two groups?

This is called Linkage. The linkage method you choose changes the shape of the clusters.

Select a linkage method to re-calculate the merges:

Average
Single
Complete
Ward
Average: Mean distance between all pairs. Balanced clusters.
Worked Example: How is this calculated?
Average Linkage = mean(...)
STEP 1: BEFORE MERGE
	A	B	C
A	—	2	10
B		—	12
C			—
→
STEP 3: AFTER MERGING [A,B]
	[A,B]	C
[A,B]	—	11
C		—
Step 1: Find the smallest distance in the matrix. A and B are closest (distance = 2).
Step 2: Merge A and B into a new group: [A,B].
Step 3: Rebuild the matrix. We need the new distance between [A,B] and the remaining point C.
Step 4: Check old distances: A to C was 10, B to C was 12. Average uses the mean, so (10 + 12) / 2 = 11.

Takeaway: Linkage is the rulebook for deciding which groups are "closest" once clusters start to grow.

stages.title: The Process in Motion
stages.text:
STAGE 05 · UNDERSTAND
The Process in Motion

Now, the algorithm repeats the rule over and over. It constantly recalculates distances using the linkage method, finding the next closest pair of clusters, and merging them.

Slowly, tiny groups fuse into medium groups, which fuse into large groups. It only stops when everything becomes one giant family. Use the merge scrubber in the visual to step through the history one merge at a time.

17

NEXT MERGE DISTANCE

Takeaway: The algorithm keeps rebuilding the distance picture after every merge, so the path matters.

stages.title: The Family Tree (Dendrogram)
stages.text:
STAGE 06 · UNDERSTAND
The Family Tree (Dendrogram)

Instead of just looking at circles on a map, we can record the exact history of these merges in a tree structure called a Dendrogram.

As the points align at the bottom, watch the tree grow upwards. The vertical height of each branch is critical: it tells us exactly how far apart the two groups were when they merged.

Rule of thumb: A fusion low on the tree means the items were very similar. A fusion high up means they were quite different.

Takeaway: A dendrogram preserves the full merge history, and branch height tells you how costly each merge was.

stages.title: Cutting the Tree
stages.text:
STAGE 07 · UNDERSTAND
Cutting the Tree

What if you don't know how many clusters you need? That is the superpower of hierarchical clustering: you don't have to guess upfront.

By drawing a horizontal line across the dendrogram, you "cut" the branches. The number of vertical lines you intersect is your number of clusters (K).

How do you choose the cut? A good first strategy is to look for a big jump in merge height and cut just below it, because that often means the algorithm has started forcing together groups that were meaningfully different. If you want a more quantitative check, you can also compare several cuts with a metric such as silhouette score.

Cut Height (merge distance)
0.337
Resulting Clusters: 4

Takeaway: Choose cuts where the tree shows a natural separation, not just where a slider gives a convenient K.

stages.title: The Detective's Challenge
stages.text:
STAGE 08 · EXPLORE
The Detective's Challenge

Clustering is subjective detective work. Because there is no "true" answer (no target variable Y), the results rely entirely on your choices.

The "Socks and Computers" Problem

If variables use different units or their raw scales should not control distance, scale them using training data only. When variables share meaningful units and variance differences matter, standardisation may be undesirable.

Furthermore, an outlier can distort the tree, pulling a group away from its true members just to accommodate the stranger.

Takeaway: Scaling and outliers can change the tree dramatically, so preprocessing matters.

stages.title: Synthesis & Recap
stages.text:
STAGE 09 · REFLECT
Synthesis & Recap

Hierarchical clustering gives us a rich, explorable structure rather than a single flat answer. Let's compare it to the other famous method, K-Means:

FEATURE	HIERARCHICAL	K-MEANS
Setup	Pick K after	Pick K first
Output	Tree (Dendrogram)	Flat groups
Speed	Usually slower because it builds the full merge tree and repeatedly compares clusters	Faster

Final Advice: Never take one clustering result as absolute truth. Try different linkages and cut heights. If the same patterns emerge every time, you've found something truly interesting.

Takeaway: Hierarchical clustering is valuable when you want an explorable merge history, not just one fixed partition.

COMPLETE THE PICTURE
Scaling and cluster stability

Standardise features when their units differ, unless those units deliberately encode importance. Otherwise one large-scale variable can dominate every merge.

Dendrogram branches are descriptive, not automatically “true” clusters. Compare linkage choices, inspect stability, and use domain knowledge when selecting a cut height.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
The dendrogram records the order and distance of merges.
Linkage choice changes the geometry of the resulting groups.
Scaling and cut height must be justified, not selected because the picture looks pleasant.

Practical method checklist

Before you finish
Assumptions

A justified distance-linkage combination and meaningful feature scale.

When the method fails

Chaining, outliers, scale dominance, and unstable dendrogram branches.

Validation and leakage

Assess stability under resampling and reasonable preprocessing choices.

Interpretation cautions

Dendrogram heights differ in meaning across linkage methods.

What to report

Distance, linkage, scaling, cut rule, sensitivity, and cluster stability.

stages.title: The problem
stages.text:
STAGE 01

The problem
When positives are rare, a model can be highly accurate while missing every important case. Evaluation must reflect prevalence, asymmetric costs, and operational capacity.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.text:
STAGE 02

Intuition and objective
The threshold converts probabilities to actions. Lower thresholds increase recall and false positives; higher thresholds usually increase precision while missing more positives. Prevalence changes predictive values even when sensitivity and specificity stay fixed.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.text:
STAGE 03

Worked example
Fraud prevalence is 1%. A rule with 90% recall and 95% specificity flags 1,395 of 10,000 transactions: 90 true frauds and 1,305 false alarms. Precision is only 6.5%, so investigation capacity matters.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.text:
STAGE 04

Reasoning with the method

Sensitivity and specificity condition on actual class, while precision conditions on predicted positives; therefore precision changes strongly with prevalence. A small false-positive rate can still create an overwhelming number of alerts when negatives dominate. ROC and precision–recall curves show different trade-offs and neither chooses an operational threshold automatically. Weighting changes the training objective; resampling changes the examples seen. Synthetic cases must remain inside training folds and may be implausible. Calibration may need correction after altered sampling or prior shift. Confusion counts reveal workload that rates alone can hide.

A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

stages.text:
STAGE 05

Interactive laboratory

Adjust prevalence, threshold and false-negative cost. Watch precision, recall and expected cost respond.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.text:
STAGE 06

Assumptions and failure modes
Assumptions

Evaluation prevalence and case mix must match intended use. Labels and error costs must be credible; grouped or time structure must be preserved.

When the method fails

Accuracy and ROC-AUC can look healthy while positive predictions are unusable. Oversampling outside folds leaks, and resampling changes apparent prevalence and calibration.

stages.title: Practical workflow
stages.text:
STAGE 07

Practical workflow
Define positive class and action
Estimate realistic prevalence and costs
Use stratified plus group/time-aware validation
Resample or weight inside training folds
Calibrate probabilities when needed
Choose threshold on validation data
Evaluate once on test data

stages.title: Interpretation and reporting
stages.text:
STAGE 08

Interpretation and reporting

What to report: Report prevalence, confusion counts, precision, recall, specificity, PR-AUC, calibration, threshold, cost assumptions and uncertainty.

Common misuse: Balancing the test set and then reporting its precision as deployment precision.

stages.title: The Unlabeled Data
stages.text:
STAGE 01 · OBSERVE
The Unlabeled Data
BEFORE YOU START

K-Means searches for compact groups around centroids. It works best when Euclidean distance is meaningful and clusters are roughly spherical.

Imagine we have a list of customers. We know two things about each one: their Age and their Spending.

Let's draw them! Each customer becomes a dot on our map. Their age moves them left or right, and their spending moves them up or down.

Right now, there are no predefined group labels like ‘Cluster 1’ or ‘Cluster 2.’ The algorithm is simply looking at a scattered cloud of dots and trying to discover if some dots naturally sit close together in teams.

CUSTOMER	AGE	SPENDING
A	24	$ 420
B	48	$ 8,100
...	...	...
Plain-language takeaway: We turn our list of customers into dots on a map. Our goal is to figure out which dots naturally belong together in teams.

stages.title: The Blind Guess (Initialization)
stages.text:
STAGE 02 · UNDERSTAND
The Blind Guess (Initialization)

Before we can group the dots, we have to decide how many teams we want. We call this number K. But there is a catch: the algorithm needs a starting guess before it can ask which centroid (center star) is closest.

In this demo, we use Random Partition. Here is how it makes its first guess:

First, every dot is secretly assigned to a random, temporary team.
Next, it looks at all the dots in a team and finds their exact middle by averaging their x and y values.
Then, that average middle spot becomes the first centroid (star) for the team!

Because the first teams were completely random, these starting stars are usually in weird, unhelpful spots. That is okay, the algorithm will fix them soon!

Practical safeguard: use k-means++ to spread initial centroids intelligently, run multiple random restarts, and keep the solution with the lowest WCSS. Convergence reaches a local solution, so different starts can produce different clusters; empty clusters also need an explicit software rule.

Plain-language takeaway: The computer needs a starting guess. It puts dots into random teams, finds the exact middle of each random team, and places a star there to act as the first center.

stages.title: Nearest Neighbor Assignment
stages.text:
STAGE 03 · UNDERSTAND
Nearest Neighbor Assignment

Now that we have our starting stars, every dot looks around and asks a simple question: Which star is closest to me right now?

The dot measures the shortest straight-line distance to every star on the graph. The math formula below might look fancy, but it just calculates that simple, straight-line distance from one point to another.

Dist = √[ (x₂ - x₁)² + (y₂ - y₁)² ]

Every dot joins the team of the star that is closest to it. Hover over the dots on the canvas with your mouse to see their current distance to the star they joined!

Remember, this team choice is only temporary. When the stars move, the dots might change their minds.

Plain-language takeaway: Every dot measures the straight-line distance to all the stars. It then joins the team of the star that is closest to it.

stages.title: Recentering
stages.text:
STAGE 04 · BUILD
Recentering

After the dots pick their teams, each star is surrounded by its new points. But the star is probably not sitting in the true middle of its new team anymore.

So, the algorithm has to move the star to the perfect center of its dots. It does this by finding the average position of all the points assigned to that cluster.

Here is a simple worked example of how that works:
• Imagine a team has two dots.
• One dot is at (2, 4) and the other is at (4, 8).
• We average the x-values: (2 + 4) / 2 = 3.
• We average the y-values: (4 + 8) / 2 = 6.
• The star moves to the exact new middle at (3, 6)!

The star slides to this new spot. It does not need to sit on top of a real customer dot. It just moves to the mathematical center of its team.

Plain-language takeaway: The star looks at all the dots on its new team and slides over to sit perfectly in the middle of them.

stages.title: The Convergence Loop
stages.text:
STAGE 05 · UNDERSTAND
The Convergence Loop

When the stars move, the map changes! A dot that used to be closest to the Blue star might suddenly find that the Red star is closer.

So, K-Means repeats the same two steps over and over again:
First, dots join the nearest star.
Then, the stars move to the exact middle of their new teams.

This loop keeps going until the clustering becomes stable. In practice, the algorithm stops when almost nothing changes anymore. That stable stopping point is called convergence.

Convergence means things have settled down—but it doesn't guarantee this is the globally best clustering possible. Click the Step button to watch the loop happen!

Run Algorithm
Plain-language takeaway: The computer loops the same two steps over and over until the dots stop switching teams and everything finally settles down.

stages.title: Measuring Tightness (WCSS)
stages.text:
STAGE 06 · UNDERSTAND
Measuring Tightness (WCSS)

How do we judge whether our teams are tight or loose? We want the dots in a team to be packed closely around their star.

To measure this, K-Means uses a score called Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS). It measures the distance from every dot to its assigned star, squares that number, and adds them all up.

Why square the distances? Because squaring makes large distances count much more strongly than small ones. A point that sits very far away from its star hurts the score a lot.

We want this WCSS score to be as tiny as possible. Look at the Status Strip above the canvas. As the clustering improves, you will see the WCSS number move downward.

Plain-language takeaway: The computer scores the teams by measuring how far every dot is from its star. A lower score means the dots are tightly hugging their centers.

stages.title: The Elbow Heuristic
stages.text:
STAGE 07 · UNDERSTAND
The Elbow Heuristic

How do we choose K (the number of teams)? One common idea is to test out 1 team, then 2 teams, then 3 teams, and so on, recording the WCSS score for each.

As you add more teams, the dots naturally get closer to a star, so the score almost always drops. But we don't want a million teams! We are looking for the bend or elbow in the chart.

The elbow is a heuristic: it marks a possible point of diminishing returns, but it may be ambiguous or absent. Combine this chart with stability, silhouette scores, domain usefulness, and alternative clustering methods.

Important: the elbow method is just a helpful hint. Some datasets show a clear bend, while others do not. It helps guide us, but it is not a magical rule.

Plain-language takeaway: To find the best number of teams, we test different numbers and look for the "elbow" bend on a chart. It tells us when to stop adding more teams.

stages.title: The Scaling Trap
stages.text:
STAGE 08 · PREPARE
The Scaling Trap

K-Means measures distance with a simple ruler, but our data has a trap! Age ranges roughly from 20 to 60, while Spending is huge and ranges from 100 to 10,000.

If we use these numbers directly, the giant Spending numbers completely dominate the calculation. Look at the canvas: this is a demo visualization of scale imbalance. The dots look like a tall, squished line!

The computer is essentially ignoring Age because the numbers are too small to fight against the giant Spending numbers. This makes the distance calculation very unfair.

Standardization fixes this! It shrinks and stretches the numbers so Age and Spending are placed on a fair, equal playing field before we measure the distance.

Plain-language takeaway: If one category has giant numbers and another has tiny numbers, the giant ones take over. We have to standardize them so everything is fair.

stages.title: Limitations & Outliers
stages.text:
STAGE 09 · REFLECT
Limitations & Outliers

K-Means is super fast and helpful, but it has a few blind spots. Because it uses a single star and a simple ruler, it assumes every team is shaped like a neat, even circle.

If the real teams are shaped like bananas, stretched out, or very uneven, K-Means might force them into awkward slices. It is also very sensitive to outliers.

An outlier is a weird dot that sits super far away from everyone else. Because the star always moves to the average middle, one weird outlier can drag the star completely away from the main group.

In this demo, an outlier has been added. Watch how that one lonely dot pulls its centroid away from the main mass of points!

Check cluster stability across starts and resampled datasets, and report a silhouette score alongside domain usefulness. Compare Gaussian mixtures for probabilistic elliptical groups and density-based methods for irregular shapes or noise.

Plain-language takeaway: K-Means likes neat, round teams. A single weird dot that is very far away can easily trick the star and drag it in the wrong direction.
COMPLETE THE PICTURE
Run the algorithm more than once

K-Means can settle in a local solution that depends on its starting centroids. Use K-Means++ initialisation and several random starts, then retain the run with the lowest WCSS.

Also inspect stability: a useful clustering should not change completely after tiny perturbations or a different random seed.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
K-Means alternates point assignment and centroid recentering until stable.
Scaling changes distances and can change the clusters.
K, initialisation, outliers, and non-spherical structure all require judgement.

Practical method checklist

Before you finish
Assumptions

A distance and roughly centroid-shaped groups that suit the scientific question.

When the method fails

Outliers, unequal density or size, non-spherical groups, and unstable starts.

Validation and leakage

Fit scaling appropriately and examine resampled stability.

Interpretation cautions

The elbow is a heuristic, not the true number of clusters.

What to report

Scaling, initialisation, restarts, K rationale, silhouette, and stability.

stages.title: The Raw Data
stages.text:
STAGE 01 · OBSERVE
The Raw Data
BEFORE YOU START

KNN stores the training examples and predicts from nearby cases. Distance therefore defines what “similar” means.

Every machine learning model starts with data. Here we have measurements of fruits — each one scored on Sweetness and Color Intensity.

Each fruit is already labeled: it's either an Apple or an Orange. Because we have labels, this is supervised learning.

 Supervised learning means the model learns from examples where the answer is already known. Here, each fruit already has a known label: Apple or Orange. Later, KNN uses these known examples as its "memory" to classify any new, unknown fruit.

The Whole Idea of KNN

KNN stands for K-Nearest Neighbors. The concept is incredibly straightforward:

To classify a new unknown item, look at the K closest known examples (neighbors) in your dataset. Then, simply copy the label that appears most often among those neighbors!

Example: If we want to identify a mystery fruit, and its 3 closest neighbors are 
, 
, and 
, then Apple gets 2 votes and Orange gets 1 vote. KNN predicts Apple.


New unknown fruit → Find closest old fruits → Count their labels → Predict majority label
    
Tiny ML Dictionary

Before moving forward, let's establish a few basic terms:

• Feature: A measurement used to make a prediction (e.g., Sweetness or Color Intensity).
• Label: The correct answer already known for our examples (e.g., Apple or Orange).
• Class: The category we are trying to predict (e.g., Apple class vs. Orange class).
• Query Point: The new, unknown item we want to classify. In our visual plots, the query point is represented by a star 
.

"We know the query point's features, but we do not know its label yet. KNN tries to guess the label based on its neighbors."

Training Dataset
#	SWEETNESS	COLOR	LABEL
1	7.2	8.1	Apple
2	7.9	8.8	Apple
3	6.5	7	Apple
4	7.5	9	Apple
5	6	8.5	Apple
6	7.1	7.2	Apple
7	6.9	8.3	Apple

 KNN needs labeled examples to learn from. It doesn't build a formula — it simply remembers all the data and compares new points to what it already knows.

stages.title: Choosing Good Features
stages.text:
STAGE 02 · PREPARE
Choosing Good Features

Not every measurement helps separate classes. We pick features where the groups actually differ — like Sweetness and Color Intensity.

Bad features (random IDs, row numbers) add noise without signal. KNN is especially sensitive to irrelevant features because they pollute the distance calculation.

Why Feature Selection Matters

A good feature helps separate the classes clearly. A bad feature adds confusion and distorts the distance between points.

Useful Examples:

Sweetness helps because apples and oranges have different natural sweetness profiles.
Color Intensity helps separate reddish apples from yellowish-orange citrus fruits.

Not Useful Examples:

Row number is just the order in the table; it contains zero predictive power.
Day picked is unrelated to fruit sweetness or species and would only add noise.
Feature Quality

 Sweetness — The two fruit groups show different sweetness patterns

 Color Intensity — Apples score higher on red

 Row number — meaningless for prediction

 Day picked — no predictive power

 Notice how the two classes form somewhat distinct clusters on the plot — a good sign. KNN relies entirely on spatial proximity.

stages.title: Train / Test Split
stages.text:
STAGE 03 · PREPARE
Train / Test Split

We hold out a small test set (2 apples + 2 oranges) that the model will not see during training. The remaining points are used as the "memory" KNN will search through.

Testing on training data is one of the most common mistakes — it gives inflated confidence. A model that memorizes isn't smart; it's just a parrot.

Training vs. Testing Sets
• Training Set: The collection of examples KNN is allowed to remember and search through. This is the model's "memory".
• Test Set: Hidden examples set aside from the beginning, used ONLY at the very end to check if the model can accurately classify new, unseen data.

 Critical Warning (Data Leakage): Do not use the test set to choose K or tune features. If the model is exposed to the test set during its construction, your evaluation results are no longer honest. This is called data leakage!

22
TRAINING
4
TESTING (HELD-OUT)

stages.title: Feature Scaling
stages.text:
STAGE 04 · PREPARE
Feature Scaling

This is the most common mistake with KNN. If Sweetness ranges 0–10 but Color ranges 0–100, the Color feature would completely dominate distance calculations.

We use Min-Max Scaling to squish every feature into the 0–1 range, giving each feature equal voice.

Scaling is usually necessary when features use different units or magnitudes. If features already share meaningful units and scale, automatic rescaling may not be desirable. The distance metric and scaling choice together define what “near” means.

Scaled Value = (Value − Min) ÷ (Max − Min)

Example: Sweetness = 7, Min = 2, Max = 9
Scaled Value = (7 − 2) ÷ (9 − 2) = 5 ÷ 7 ≈ 0.71
Important: Scale Using Training Data Only

To prevent data leakage, we calculate the Minimum and Maximum values using only the training set. We then use this exact same scale factor for training, test, and any future query points.


Training Data finds Min/Max 
 same Min/Max scales training, test, and new query points
    

If we used the test set to calculate the scale range, information from the test set would leak into the training process, leading to over-optimistic performance estimates.

Concept Check

Why do we scale features before using KNN?

To make the dataset smaller and faster to process.
Because KNN relies on distances, and features with larger numeric ranges could unfairly dominate the calculations.
To make sure all values are converted into whole integers.
Scaling Parameters
2.2–7.9
SWEETNESS RANGE
2.2–9.0
COLOR RANGE
After scaling → both features in [0.00, 1.00]
Before / After Examples
FRUIT	LABEL	RAW SWEETNESS	RAW COLOR	SCALED SWEETNESS	SCALED COLOR
1	Apple	7.2	8.1	0.88	0.87
2	Orange	3.0	3.2	0.14	0.15
3	Orange	2.5	3.8	0.05	0.24

These sample rows use the training-set min and max only.

 Watch the points shift on the plot — they're being rescaled to [0, 1] on each axis. The order of points along each axis stays the same, but the scale changes. This makes distance fairer because Sweetness and Color now use comparable ranges.

Because KNN relies on distances, and features with larger numeric ranges could unfairly dominate the calculations.
To make sure all values are converted into whole integers.

stages.title: Measuring Distance
stages.text:
STAGE 05 · BUILD
Measuring Distance

KNN's entire logic boils down to one question: "Who lives closest to me?" To answer that, we need a way to measure distance between points.

The most common choice is Euclidean distance — the straight-line distance between two points.

Euclidean distance assumes each scaled direction should contribute through straight-line geometry. Manhattan, mixed-data, or domain-specific distances may be more appropriate. Scaling cannot rescue irrelevant features or the curse of dimensionality.

d(a, b) = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²]

This is just the Pythagorean theorem —
the same formula you learned in geometry class.
What Does Distance Mean Here?

In machine learning, distance represents dissimilarity between items:

Short distance means high similarity. The items have very similar features.
Long distance means high difference. The items are very dissimilar.
Step-by-Step Distance Calculation:

Let's calculate the distance between our mystery fruit and a training fruit manually:

Query point (Mystery Fruit 

Sweetness = 0.45, Color = 0.55

Training point (Known Fruit):
Sweetness = 0.50, Color = 0.65

Euclidean Distance Formula:
d = √[(0.50 − 0.45)² + (0.65 − 0.55)²]
d = √[(0.05)² + (0.10)²]
d = √[0.0025 + 0.0100]
d = √0.0125
d ≈ 0.1118 (the straight-line distance)

Note: While Euclidean distance is the straight-line default, other metrics exist (e.g., Manhattan distance, which calculates distance along grid paths like city streets). This page uses Euclidean distance.

Live Distance Calculation

Lines on plot show distances from 
 to all training points. The darker lines currently emphasize the nearest 3 neighbors from the teaching flow.

Closest point: Apple at (0.53, 0.53)
d = √[(0.45 − 0.53)² + (0.55 − 0.53)²]
d = 0.0790

stages.title: Choosing K
stages.text:
STAGE 06 · UNDERSTAND
Choosing K

K is one of the most important hyperparameters in KNN — the number of neighbors to consult before making a prediction.

Small K (e.g. K=1): Very sensitive to noise. One outlier can flip the prediction.
Large K (e.g. K=15): Too smooth. Local patterns get drowned out by distant voters.

We do not just guess K blindly. Later, in Stage 12, we compare several K values using cross-validation and look for a sensible choice.

Who Chooses K?

K is a hyperparameter. In machine learning, a hyperparameter is a setting selected using validation data or cross-validation, rather than a coefficient fitted directly during training.

The Trade-Off:

Too Small K (e.g., K=1): Extremely sensitive to outliers and noise. The model may overfit (memorize noise as pattern).
Too Large K (e.g., K=15): Overly smooth and generic. Local patterns are drowned out by far-away votes. The model may underfit (miss the actual pattern).
How a Machine Learning Task is Configured:
COMPONENT	WHO DECIDES?	MEANING
Features	Human / Designer	Measurements selected to describe items (e.g., Sweetness)
Scaling Method	Human choice	How feature ranges are made comparable (e.g., Min-Max)
Distance Metric	Human choice	Mathematical formula to measure closeness (e.g., Euclidean)
K value	Human choice	Number of neighboring votes allowed to participate
Training labels	Existing Data	The ground-truth answers for old examples
Prediction	KNN vote rule	Majority vote among the K closest neighbors
Concept Check

Who decides the value of K in K-Nearest Neighbors?

The KNN algorithm automatically discovers the best K during training.
K is a hyperparameter chosen using validation or cross-validation.
The query points themselves decide based on how far away they are.
Adjust K

3

K=3 is a balanced starting point. Try different values!

 Best practice: use an odd number for K to avoid ties. Use cross-validation to find the optimal K for your specific dataset.

stages.title: The Majority Vote
stages.text:
STAGE 08 · UNDERSTAND
The Majority Vote

Classification is now a democracy. Each of the K nearest neighbors gets one vote. The class with the most votes wins.

Equal Vote Democracy

In standard KNN, each neighbor inside the K-limit gets exactly one equal vote. The category with the highest vote count wins the prediction.

 Note: Vote share estimates probability. If K=3 and Apples win 2-1, the neighbor class proportion gives a local class-probability estimate of 66.7%. This estimate may be noisy or poorly calibrated, especially with small K; it is not a guaranteed probability for this fruit.

Why odd numbers for K?

In two-class (binary) classification, choosing an odd K guarantees there will be no ties. If we used an even number (like K=4) and got 2 Apple votes and 2 Orange votes, the model would require a complex, arbitrary tie-breaking rule. Using odd K values elegantly prevents this!

Current Vote Tally Breakdown:
Apple (d: 0.08)
Orange (d: 0.14)
Orange (d: 0.23)
Concept Check

If K=3 and the 3 nearest neighbors are Apple, Apple, Orange, what does KNN predict?

Orange, because it is the unique outlier.
Apple, because it wins the majority vote (2 votes to 1).
Undecided, because votes are split.
Vote Tally
1

2

Prediction:

If K=3 and the current neighbors are: 
 
 

→ Apple: 1 vote | Orange: 2 votes
→ Prediction:

 For regression tasks, instead of voting, KNN takes the average value of the K neighbors. But for classification like ours, it's pure democracy.

stages.title: Decision Boundary
stages.text:
STAGE 09 · BUILD
Decision Boundary

What if we classified every possible point on the plot? The result is a colorful map showing which regions belong to which class.

Unlike linear models, KNN boundaries are non-linear — they bend and curve around the data naturally. The boundary is just wherever the majority vote flips from one class to the other.

What is a Decision Boundary?

A Decision Boundary is the invisible dividing line or contour across the feature space where the model switches from predicting one class to another. Any point that falls on one side is predicted as Apple; any point on the other is Orange.

• Non-parametric: KNN has no underlying assumptions or mathematical weights to fit (unlike linear equations). The boundary adapts organically to the data density.
• Bias-Variance Tradeoff: Adjusting K alters this boundary:
K = 1 (High Variance / Low Bias):

Extremely flexible, wiggly, and complex boundary. It fits every outlier precisely, memorizing noise and likely overfitting.

Medium K (Balanced Tradeoff):

Smooth, reasonable boundary shapes that filter out minor noise while preserving genuine group clusters.

Large K (Low Variance / High Bias):

Highly smooth, almost straight boundaries. It ignores localized trends completely, risking underfitting.

Boundary Properties

The decision boundary emerges organically from the data — no formula is fitted. This is what makes KNN a non-parametric model.

 Small K = wiggly, complex boundaries. Large K = smoother boundaries. This is the classic bias-variance tradeoff.

Evaluating the Model

If Apple is the Positive Class, what does a False Positive mean in our fruit classification task?

The model predicted Orange, but the fruit was actually an Apple.
Performance Metrics (Apple = positive class)
100%
ACCURACY
(TP + TN) ÷ Total
Percentage correct.
100%

TP ÷ (TP + FP)
Of predicted Apples, how many real?
100%
RECALL

Of actual Apples, how many found?

These results come from a tiny 4-point held-out test set, so treat them as illustrative rather than stable performance estimates.

 With imbalanced data, accuracy alone can be misleading. Precision tells you "of all predicted apples, how many were actually apples?" Recall tells you "of all actual apples, how many did the model find?"

stages.title: The Effect of K
stages.text:
STAGE 12 · EXPLORE
The Effect of K

K is one of the most important tuning knobs. Watch how the decision boundary changes as K increases.

Start with Five-Fold Cross-Validation

Five-fold cross-validation is the usual practical starting point. Ten-fold cross-validation is also common. In either case, the training data is divided into folds, and each candidate K is scored several times using different train/validation folds.

 This toy dataset is very small, so this lesson demonstrates leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) instead. That is a small-data teaching choice, not the usual default. With a larger dataset, five-fold or ten-fold CV would typically be more practical.

Cross-Validation Compares K; It Does Not Choose K for You

Cross-validation is a loop: try several candidate values of K, calculate an average validation score for each one, then choose the K with the strongest average score. The procedure produces the comparison; the modelling workflow makes the selection.

Illustrative five-fold example:

CANDIDATE K	AVERAGE CV ACCURACY	WHAT WE DO
K = 1	75%	Compare
K = 3	88%	Compare
K = 5	92%	Best average score
K = 7	90%	Compare

In this example, we carry K = 5 forward because it has the highest average CV score. The live chart below uses LOOCV because this toy training set is tiny.

Recommended Workflow Order
Split once: Separate the full dataset into training and test sets. Keep the test set hidden.
Cross-validate on training only: Run five-fold CV for several candidate Ks. In this demonstration, use LOOCV because the training set is very small.
Choose K: Compare the average CV scores and select the best-performing candidate.
Retrain: Fit KNN on all of the training data using the selected K.
Test once: Evaluate that locked model once on the untouched test set.
Elbow / Knee: A Secondary Heuristic

An elbow or knee is where the CV curve begins to flatten as K increases. It can help you read the curve, but it is a heuristic, not a rule. In most cases, start with the K that has the best average cross-validation score. Use the elbow only as a secondary aid when nearby K values perform similarly, then document the tie-breaker you used.

Example: If K = 5 has the highest average CV score and the curve also starts flattening after K = 5, the knee supports the choice. It does not replace the score comparison or select K automatically.

 Do not choose K from a single split, from the curve's shape alone, or by repeatedly checking the final test set.

Compare K Values
K =
1

Very noisy boundary — each point creates its own island. High variance, low bias.

K vs Cross-Validation Accuracy

Each point shows the average cross-validation accuracy for one candidate K. Use the highest average score as the primary selection signal; the knee marker is only a secondary visual aid.

Demo note: This chart uses leave-one-out cross-validation on the training set only because the toy training set is very small. In practice, start with five-fold or ten-fold CV.

 Try several Ks → compare average CV scores → pick the best. The elbow/knee can support the decision, but it is not an automatic rule.

Big Picture

Try several Ks → cross-validation on train only → pick the best average score → retrain on all train → test once.

stages.title: Strengths and Weaknesses
stages.text:
STAGE 13 · REFLECT
Strengths and Weaknesses

Before using K-Nearest Neighbors in practice, it is vital to know when it shines and where it struggles.

 Strengths
Simple to understand: Intuitive to explain to stakeholders.
No Parameter-Learning Phase: KNN does not fit weights or coefficients. It stores the training examples and uses them during prediction.
Highly Flexible: Can easily construct complex, non-linear decision boundaries.
Naturally Multi-class: Works seamlessly for predicting 3 or more classes.
 Weaknesses & Limitations
Sensitive to Scale: Scaling is usually necessary when features use different units or magnitudes; otherwise larger-scale features dominate distance.
The Curse of Dimensionality: When there are too many features, distance often becomes less useful because many points start to seem similarly far apart. This makes it harder for KNN to find truly meaningful neighbors.
Slow at Scale: Must calculate distance to every single stored point for every new query. High memory and computing costs.
Class Imbalance: If you have 95% Apples and 5% Oranges, votes will naturally skew heavily to Apple.
The Whole Story in Plain English

Here is the complete machine learning workflow we walked through today:

Labeled Examples: Start with known data (fruits with known categories).
Feature Selection: Select high-quality, relevant properties (sweetness, color).
Train/Test Split: Set aside a final held-out test set to keep final evaluation fair.
Feature Scaling: Fit an appropriate scaling transformation using the training data when feature units or magnitudes would otherwise dominate the distance calculation. Standardisation, min-max scaling, robust scaling and domain-specific transformations are all possible choices; apply the fitted transformation unchanged to validation and test data.
Mystery Input: Introduce an unknown query point 
 on the plot.
Distance Measuring: Run Euclidean distance against all stored training examples.
Hyperparameter K: Choose K (the count of voting neighbors) using validation or cross-validation.
Locate Neighbors: Gather the K nearest samples.
Tally Votes: Perform a democratic, equal-weight majority vote.
Predict: Assign the winning class to the unknown query point.
Independent Testing: Run the held-out test points to check the model's accuracy.
Evaluate Quality: Read the confusion matrix, recall, precision, and F1 metrics.
Tune K: Use cross-validation inside the training memory to find the best K.
Analyze Trade-offs: Know KNN's limits, such as scale sensitivity and the curse of dimensionality.

Ties, weighting, and efficient prediction

Use an odd K for a two-class problem when practical to reduce ties. Distance-weighted KNN can give closer neighbours more influence than distant ones.

Prediction becomes expensive as the training set grows because neighbours must be searched at prediction time. Approximate-neighbour indexes can help, but scaling and cross-validated K still matter.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
Scaling is usually necessary when feature units or magnitudes differ.
Small K gives a flexible boundary; large K smooths it.
Tune K on validation data and evaluate on untouched test data.

Practical method checklist

Before you finish
Assumptions

A meaningful distance and locally similar observations.

When the method fails

High dimensions, irrelevant variables, missingness, imbalance, and expensive prediction.

Validation and leakage

Fit scaling and imputation in folds; tune K and weighting on validation data.

Interpretation cautions

Odd K only prevents equal votes in binary classification.

What to report

Distance, scaling, K, weighting, resampling, metrics, and uncertainty.

stages.title: The Raw Data
stages.text:
STAGE 01 · OBSERVE
The Raw Data
BEFORE YOU START

LDA is a probabilistic classifier. It models each class and then compares posterior scores for a new observation.

Every machine learning model starts with data. Here we have measurements of fruits — each one scored on Sweetness and Color.

Each fruit is already labeled: it's either an Apple or an Orange. Because we have labels, this is supervised learning.

The Whole Idea of LDA

Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) is a supervised classification method. It uses labeled examples to learn a straight-line rule that separates classes.

Simple Idea: LDA looks for a direction (projection axis) where:
• Different class centers are as far apart as possible.
• Points inside each class are as tightly bunched (low spread) as possible.

LDA General Pipeline:
Labeled Data → Class Centers → Class Spread → Optimal Direction → Boundary → Prediction

"LDA is like looking at a messy 2D cloud of points from the best angle so the two groups look as separated as possible."

Tiny LDA Dictionary
Feature: A measurement used to make a prediction (e.g., Sweetness or Color).
Label: The known category of an example (e.g., Apple or Orange).
Class: The target group we want to predict (Apple class or Orange class).
Mean (μ): The average position or center of a class point cloud.
Variance: How much a single feature fluctuates.
Covariance: How two features move in relation to each other.
Scatter (S): A mathematical measure of data spread or messiness.
Projection: Squashing 2D coordinates down onto a single 1D axis.
Discriminant Score (δ): A numerical score LDA computes for each class; the highest score wins!

stages.title: Choosing Good Features
stages.text:
STAGE 02 · PREPARE
Choosing Good Features

Not every measurement helps separate classes. We pick features where the groups actually show different patterns — like Sweetness and Color Score.

Bad features (random IDs, row numbers) add noise without signal. LDA works best when features genuinely explain class differences.

Feature Quality Evaluation

• Sweetness: In this toy dataset, the two fruit groups show different sweetness patterns.

• Color Score: In this toy dataset, apples and oranges have different color score patterns.

• Row Number: Completely meaningless for classification.

• Day of Entry: No predictive power.

 Warning: Bad or irrelevant features can seriously confuse LDA because they add noise to the calculated means, covariances, and final decision boundary.

stages.title: Train / Test Split
stages.text:
STAGE 03 · PREPARE
Train / Test Split

We hold out a small test set (2 apples + 2 oranges) that the model will not see during training. The remaining 20 points are used to learn the pattern.

The test points are completely hidden until the evaluation stage. A model that only memorizes training data isn't actually smart — it's just a parrot with ambitions.

20
TRAINING
4
TESTING (HIDDEN)

How the sets are used:

 Training Set: Used to learn means, covariance, priors, and the decision rule.
 Test Set: Used exactly once at the very end to check whether the learned rule works on unseen, new data.

 Data Leakage Warning: The test set must stay absolutely hidden until final evaluation. Do not use the test set to choose features, tune settings, or adjust the model. If the test set influences training decisions, the final evaluation score becomes dishonest!

stages.title: Group by Class
stages.text:
STAGE 04 · UNDERSTAND
Group by Class

LDA first separates the training data by label. All apples together, all oranges together. Now it can study each group independently.

Why group by class? This step is critical because LDA calculates a separate center (mean) and spread (scatter) for each individual class.

Class Groups
10
APPLES
10
ORANGES

Understanding the hulls:

A convex hull is just a visual outline drawn around the training points in a class. It is not the LDA model itself! It only helps us see where each class cloud lives in our feature space.

stages.title: Compute Class Means
stages.text:
STAGE 05 · BUILD
Compute Class Means

The mean is the center of each class — its average position in feature space. LDA uses these to understand where each group lives.

Class Means (Centers)
μ_apple = [ 7.32, 7.98 ]
μ_orange = [ 3.39, 2.51 ]

Each mean is computed by averaging the Sweetness and Color scores of all training points in that class.

Mean = Class Center

The class mean is the average location of all points in that class. It is like the center of gravity of the class cloud.

Example: If most apples have high Sweetness and high Color Score, the apple mean center (μ_apple) will appear right in the middle of the apple cluster.

μ_apple = average position of all apple training points
μ_orange = average position of all orange training points

 The  markers on the plot show each class center. The gap between them is what LDA will try to exploit.

Concept Check: Class Mean

What does a class mean (μ) represent in LDA?

A) The single most sweet fruit in the dataset.
B) The average center of a class.
C) The line that separates the two classes.
D) The number of points in the dataset.

controls.label: A) The single most sweet fruit in the dataset.
B) The average center of a class.
C) The line that separates the two classes.
D) The number of points in the dataset.

stages.title: Within-Class Scatter
stages.text:
STAGE 06 · BUILD
Within-Class Scatter

Not all apples are identical. SW measures how much the points in each class wiggle around their own mean.

The covariance ellipses on the plot show the spread shape. Diagonal entries = how much each feature varies. Off-diagonal = how features vary together.

Within-Class Scatter Matrix SW
S_W = (n₁ − 1)·Σ_apple + (n₂ − 1)·Σ_orange

S_W = ⎡ 8.685  2.645 ⎤
      ⎣ 2.645  8.565 ⎦

Each class covariance is weighted by (n_k − 1) before summing. Diagonal: variance of each feature. Off-diagonal: how features co-vary within a class.

What does within-class scatter mean?

Within-class scatter tells us how messy or spread out each class is inside itself.
• If all apples are clustered tightly together, apple scatter is small.
• If apples are spread out all over the plot, apple scatter is large.

What is covariance?
Covariance tells us whether Sweetness and Color move together:
• Positive covariance: Sweetness goes up, and Color Score also tends to go up.
• Negative covariance: One goes up, while the other goes down.
• Near Zero: They do not move together in any pattern.

Understanding the Scatter Matrix:
• Diagonal entries: How much each feature varies by itself (variance).
• Off-diagonal entries: How much the two features move together (covariance).

Concept Check: Within-Class Scatter

What does within-class scatter measure?

A) The distance between the Apple center and Orange center.
B) How spread out or messy points are inside each class.
C) The accuracy of the final predictions on unseen data.
D) The total count of features we selected.

controls.label: A) The distance between the Apple center and Orange center.
B) How spread out or messy points are inside each class.
C) The accuracy of the final predictions on unseen data.
D) The total count of features we selected.

stages.title: The Shared Covariance Assumption
stages.text:
STAGE 07 · PREPARE
The Shared Covariance Assumption

Here's LDA's key assumption: all classes share the same covariance shape. The groups can have different centers, but their spread is assumed to be roughly the same.

So LDA pools the individual covariance matrices into one shared estimate. Watch the ellipses morph into a single shape.

Pooled Covariance Matrix Σ
Σ = S_W / (n − 2)

Σ = ⎡ 0.482  0.147 ⎤
    ⎣ 0.147  0.476 ⎦
Why does LDA pool covariance?

LDA assumes that the classes have similar spread shapes. Instead of keeping separate shapes for Apple and Orange, it combines them into one shared covariance estimate.

Simple meaning: Different centers, same general spread shape.

LDA vs. QDA Comparison:
• LDA (Linear): Assumes shared covariance → Draws a straight decision line.
• QDA (Quadratic): Allows different covariances per class → Can draw a curved decision line.

 Warning: If the class clouds actually have very different shapes, LDA's shared covariance assumption is violated. LDA may struggle, and QDA (Quadratic Discriminant Analysis) might fit the data much better.

Concept Check: Shared Covariance

What is LDA’s shared covariance assumption?

A) Every fruit in the dataset has the exact same sweetness value.
B) The test set must have the same size as the training set.
C) Classes can have different centers, but they are assumed to have similar spread shapes.
D) The decision boundary must always be curved.

controls.label: A) Every fruit in the dataset has the exact same sweetness value.
B) The test set must have the same size as the training set.
C) Classes can have different centers, but they are assumed to have similar spread shapes.
D) The decision boundary must always be curved.

stages.title: Between-Class Scatter
stages.text:
STAGE 08 · BUILD
Between-Class Scatter

SB measures how far apart the class centers are. The further apart, the easier it is for LDA to separate them.

LDA's goal is to maximize the ratio of between-class scatter to within-class scatter:

Between-class scatter = gap between class centers

Let's contrast the two scatter metrics:
• Within-class scatter asks: "How messy and spread out is each class inside itself?"
• Between-class scatter asks: "How far apart are the class centers (means)?"

LDA's Ultimate Goal: We want the gap between classes to be BIG, and the messiness inside each class to be SMALL!

J(w) = wᵀ S_B w / wᵀ S_W w

In simple terms, J(w) is maximized when:
1. Projected class means are far apart.
2. Projected class spreads are small.
Between-Class Scatter SB
S_B = (n₁·n₂/n) · (μ₁ − μ₂)(μ₁ − μ₂)ᵀ

S_B = ⎡ 77.224  107.485 ⎤
      ⎣ 107.485  149.604 ⎦

stages.title: The Optimal Direction
stages.text:
STAGE 09 · UNDERSTAND
The Optimal Direction

In this 2-class example, LDA gives one main discriminant direction w — the angle where classes appear most separated.

What is projection and why do we do it?

Projection means dropping every 2D point (Sweetness, Color) down onto a single 1D line or direction.

This turns a 2D pair of numbers into a single 1D score:

Fruit (Sweetness, Color) → [Project] → One LDA Score

Why project? If the projected Apple scores sit neatly on one side of the line and the projected Orange scores sit on the other side, LDA has found an excellent direction for separation!

w ∝ S_W⁻¹ (μ₁ − μ₂)

This isn't just the straight line between means.
It also tilts to avoid the direction of maximum within-class spread.
Optimal Direction w
w = S_W⁻¹ · (μ₁ − μ₂) → [ 0.4594, 0.8883 ]

This direction maximizes the Fisher criterion J(w). Points projected onto it show maximum class separation.

stages.title: The Decision Boundary
stages.text:
STAGE 10 · BUILD
The Decision Boundary

Because LDA is linear, the boundary between classes is a straight line (in 2D). Everything on one side is classified as Apple, the other as Orange.

Discriminant Scores: Highest Score Wins

LDA calculates a separate scoring function for each class, called the Discriminant Score (δ):

δ_apple(x) = Score indicating how much point x looks like an Apple
δ_orange(x) = Score indicating how much point x looks like an Orange

For any point, LDA compares the two scores: whichever score is higher is the predicted class!

Example Fruit Prediction:

(Simple illustrative example, not a live value from the current dataset)
• Apple Score (δ_apple) = 2.31
• Orange Score (δ_orange) = -1.44
 Since 2.31 is higher than -1.44, LDA predicts Apple!
What are priors (π_k)?

The prior probability (π_k) represents the class probability before observing its features. Priors may be estimated from training prevalence or specified externally.
• If apples and oranges are equally common, priors are equal (50% each).
• If we estimate priors from 90% apples in training, the apple score gets a prior boost, shifting the boundary slightly to favor Apple predictions.

δ_k(x) = xᵀ Σ⁻¹ μ_k − ½ μ_kᵀ Σ⁻¹ μ_k + log(π_k)

Predict class k with the highest δ_k(x)
Decision Rule
Prior π_apple = 0.50
Prior π_orange = 0.50

The boundary is where δ_apple(x) = δ_orange(x). Points on the apple side get a higher apple score.

Concept Check: Decision Rule

How does LDA decide the final predicted class of a point?

A) It checks which class is physically closer using plain Euclidean distance.
B) It calculates a discriminant score for each class and chooses the highest one.
C) It always predicts the class that has more training samples.
D) It uses random guessing when a point is near the boundary.

stages.title: Assumptions & Limitations
stages.text:
STAGE 14 · PREPARE
Assumptions & Limitations

To use LDA effectively, you need to understand when it thrives and when it falls short.

LDA Works Best When:
Linearity: A straight-line boundary is a reasonable way to separate classes.
Normality: Each class looks like a symmetrical oval cloud (multivariate normal distribution).
Equal Spread: All classes share roughly the same spread/covariance shape.
Independence: Data samples are collected independently.
Data Volume: There are many more rows than features.
No Outliers: Extreme values are absent (outliers pull means away easily).
LDA Struggles When:
The true dividing boundary is highly curved.
Classes have very different shapes or spreads (e.g., one is a tight circle, the other is a giant flat ellipse).
There are severe outliers that skew centers.
You have too many features and not enough rows (overfitting).
Features are redundant or highly correlated (collinearity).
Alternative Methods

If LDA doesn't fit, consider these standard alternatives:

 QDA (Quadratic Discriminant Analysis): Excellent if class spreads are highly unequal.
 Logistic Regression: Also estimates class probabilities, but avoids LDA’s Gaussian class-conditional and shared-covariance assumptions.
 KNN or Decision Trees: Great for highly complex, non-linear boundaries.
COMPLETE THE PICTURE
Posterior probabilities and regularised LDA

The discriminant scores can be converted into posterior class probabilities. These probabilities are useful for ranking and threshold decisions, not merely producing a hard label.

When the covariance estimate is unstable because there are many features or limited data, shrinkage or regularised LDA can trade a little bias for much lower variance.
